# Overview



**GPUMD** (Graphics Processing Units Molecular Dynamics) is a highly efficient, general-purpose molecular dynamics package fully implemented on GPUs using CUDA C++. It combines production-ready MD simulation capabilities with a built-in machine-learned potential framework called **Neuroevolution Potential (NEP)**, enabling users to train, validate, and deploy ML potentials within a single cohesive toolchain. The package is distributed under the GNU General Public License v3 and currently stands at **version 5.7**.

![GPUMD Logo](https://github.com/brucefan1983/GPUMD/raw/master/logo/logo-main-arctic.png)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L161), [main.cu](/src/main_gpumd/main.cu#L60-L79)

## What GPUMD Does

GPUMD serves two primary roles in computational materials science, delivered through two distinct executables built from the same source tree:

| Executable | Purpose | Entry Point | Key Capability |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gpumd` | Run MD simulations | `src/main_gpumd/` | Dynamics, minimization, phonon, heat transport, measurement |
| `nep` | Train & predict NEP models | `src/main_nep/` | Neuroevolution potential training, dataset prediction, TNEP/qNEP support |

A third executable, `gnep`, is optionally buildable and provides an alternative training scheme (GNEP) using gradient-based optimization.

The `gpumd` executable reads a `run.in` file containing a sequence of keyword-driven commands — each command specifying a potential, ensemble, measurement, or other operation — and executes them in order. Multiple "runs" can be chained in a single `run.in`, enabling complex multi-stage workflows (e.g., equilibrate → measure → deform) without scripting.

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt](/CMakeLists.txt#L1-L69), [main.cu](/src/main_gpumd/main.cu#L42-L58), [run.cu](/src/main_gpumd/run.cu#L175-L209)

## Architecture at a Glance

The `gpumd` executable follows a classic MD loop architecture, fully resident on the GPU. The main simulation loop in `Run::perform_a_run()` orchestrates four subsystems in each timestep: **Integration** (half-step velocity update), **Force** (potential evaluation), **Measurement** (observables), and **Integration** (second half-step). A fifth subsystem, **Monte Carlo**, interleaves trial moves for hybrid MC/MD simulations.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "gpumd Executable"
        MAIN["main.cu<br/>Entry Point"] --> RUN["Run<br/>run.in Parser &<br/>Simulation Driver"]
        RUN --> INIT["Initialize<br/>Positions, Velocities,<br/>GPU Memory"]
        INIT --> LOOP["perform_a_run()<br/>Main MD Loop"]
        
        subgraph LOOP["MD Time Step Loop"]
            direction TB
            I1["Integrate.compute1()<br/>Velocity half-step"] --> F["Force.compute()<br/>Potential & Forces"]
            F --> AUX["Auxiliary Forces<br/>Spring, E-field,<br/>Random, Electron-stop"]
            AUX --> M["Measure.process()<br/>Observables & I/O"]
            M --> I2["Integrate.compute2()<br/>Velocity full-step + Thermostat"]
            I2 --> MC["MC.compute()<br/>Monte Carlo trials"]
        end
    end
    
    subgraph "Core Subsystems"
        FORCE["Force Subsystem<br/>Potential dispatch &<br/>Neighbor list"]
        INTG["Integrate Subsystem<br/>Ensemble & Thermostat"]
        MEAS["Measure Subsystem<br/>Compute & Dump"]
        MCSUB["MC Subsystem<br/>Canonical & SGC"]
    end
    
    LOOP --> FORCE
    LOOP --> INTG
    LOOP --> MEAS
    LOOP --> MCSUB
```

Sources: [run.cu](/src/main_gpumd/run.cu#L211-L348), [force.cuh](/src/force/force.cuh#L34-L87), [integrate.cuh](/src/integrate/integrate.cuh#L28-L120), [measure.cuh](/src/measure/measure.cuh#L28-L69)

## Source Code Organization

The source tree under `src/` is organized by functional responsibility, with each module compiled as `.cu` CUDA source files:

| Directory | Responsibility | Key Classes | Count |
|---|---|---|---|
| `main_gpumd/` | Simulation driver, run.in parser, velocity/deposition | `Run`, `Velocity`, `Deposition` | 10 files |
| `force/` | All interatomic potentials & neighbor list | `Force`, `Potential` (abstract), `NEP`, `Tersoff1988`, ... | 30 files |
| `integrate/` | Ensemble thermostats & barostats | `Ensemble` (abstract), `Ensemble_NVE`, `Ensemble_NHC`, ... | 34 files |
| `measure/` | Observables, I/O, heat transport | `Measure`, `HAC`, `HNEMD_Kappa`, `DOS`, ... | 46 files |
| `model/` | Atom data, simulation box, groups | `Atom`, `Box`, `Group` | 8 files |
| `minimize/` | Energy minimization (SD, FIRE) | `Minimizer_SD`, `Minimizer_FIRE` | 8 files |
| `mc/` | Monte Carlo sampling | `MC`, `MC_Ensemble_Canonical` | 9 files |
| `phonon/` | Hessian & phonon computation | `Hessian` | 2 files |
| `utilities/` | GPU vectors, error handling, I/O | `GPU_Vector`, `read_file` | 12 files |
| `main_nep/` | NEP training & prediction | `SNES`, `Fitness`, `Parameters` | 18 files |
| `main_gnep/` | GNEP gradient-based training | `GNEP`, `Adam` | 15 files |

Sources: [get_repo_structure src](/src), [atom.cuh](/src/model/atom.cuh#L27-L57)

## Supported Interatomic Potentials

GPUMD supports a rich set of potentials through a polymorphic `Potential` base class. The `Force` class dispatches computation to one or more `Potential` instances, enabling hybrid combinations. Potentials are selected at runtime by reading the first keyword in the potential file:

| Category | Potentials | Hybrid Combinations |
|---|---|---|
| **Machine-Learned** | NEP3, NEP4, NEP5 (+ ZBL variants), qNEP (dynamic charge), TNEP (dipole/polarizability) | NEP+ILP, NEP+ZBL, NEP+D3 |
| **Empirical Many-Body** | Tersoff (1988, 1989, mini), EAM (Zhou 2004, Dai 2006, alloy), ADP | Tersoff+ILP, SW+ILP |
| **Pairwise** | Lennard-Jones (LJ) | — |
| **Special Purpose** | FCP (force constant potential), Deep Potential (DP), NNAP | — |

> [!TIP]
> The `Force` class holds a `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Potential>>`, meaning multiple potentials can be active simultaneously in a single simulation — for example, a NEP model for intralayer interactions combined with an ILP model for interlayer Van der Waals forces.

Sources: [force.cu](/src/force/force.cu#L58-L200), [potential.cuh](/src/force/potential.cuh#L30-L114)

## Ensemble & Integration Methods

The integration subsystem uses a two-step split-operator pattern (`compute1` / `compute2`) enabling Velocity Verlet with interleaved thermostat/barostat operations. Available ensembles span equilibrium, non-equilibrium, and advanced sampling regimes:

| Ensemble Type | Class | Use Case |
|---|---|---|
| NVE | `Ensemble_NVE` | Microcanonical dynamics |
| NVT (Langevin) | `Ensemble_Lan` | Stochastic thermostat |
| NVT (NHC) | `Ensemble_NHC` | Nosé-Hoover chain thermostat |
| NVT (BER) | `Ensemble_Ber` | Berendsen thermostat |
| NVT (QTB) | `Ensemble_QTB` | Quantum thermal bath |
| NPT (MTTK) | `Ensemble_MTTK` | Martyna-Tuckerman-Tobias-Klein |
| NPT (SCR) | `Ensemble_NPT_SCR` | Stochastic cell rescaling |
| NPT (BAO) | `Ensemble_BAO` | BAOAB integrator |
| Heat (NEMD) | `Ensemble_Heat_Hybrid` | Non-equilibrium heat transport |
| HNEMD | Multiple | Homogeneous NEMD for thermal conductivity |
| MSST | `Ensemble_MSST` | Multi-scale shock simulation |
| NPHug | `Ensemble_NPHug` | Shock Hugoniot |
| PIMD | `Ensemble_PIMD` | Path-integral molecular dynamics |
| TTM | `Ensemble_TTM` | Two-temperature model |
| Thermodynamic Integration | `Ensemble_TI` variants | Free energy calculations |

Sources: [ensemble.cuh](/src/integrate/ensemble.cuh#L27-L158), [integrate.cuh](/src/integrate/integrate.cuh#L28-L120)

## Measurement & Analysis Capabilities

The `Measure` subsystem aggregates a collection of `Property` objects that compute and output observables during simulation. This is where GPUMD's strength in heat transport becomes evident:

| Capability | Class | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **Heat Transport** | `HAC`, `HNEMD_Kappa`, `HNEMDEC_Kappa`, `SHC` | EMD (HAC), HNEMD, spectral heat current |
| **Structural** | `RDF`, `ADF`, `Angular_RDF`, `OrientOrder` | Radial/angular distribution, order parameters |
| **Dynamical** | `MSD`, `SDC`, `DOS`, `Viscosity` | Mean-square displacement, density of states |
| **I/O** | `Dump_Thermo`, `Dump_XYZ`, `Dump_Restart`, `Dump_NetCDF` | Trajectory and restart output |
| **Electronic** | `LSQT`, `Iron_Conductivity` | Linear-scaling quantum transport |
| **Special** | `Plumed`, `Extrapolation`, `Modal_Analysis` | Enhanced sampling, model monitoring, modal analysis |

Sources: [measure.cuh](/src/measure/measure.cuh#L28-L69), [run.cu](/src/main_gpumd/run.cu#L29-L62)

## NEP Training Pipeline

The `nep` executable implements a complete training workflow: it reads a `train.xyz` dataset in extended XYZ format, optimizes NEP model parameters using the SNES (separable natural evolution strategy) optimizer, and writes the resulting potential file. The pipeline supports prediction mode (evaluating a trained model on a dataset) and training for TNEP (tensorial models for dipole/polarizability) and qNEP (dynamic charge models).

```mermaid
graph LR
    DATA["train.xyz<br/>Training Dataset"] --> PAR["Parameters<br/>nep.in Parsing"]
    PAR --> FIT["Fitness<br/>Loss Evaluation<br/>on GPU"]
    FIT --> OPT["SNES / Adam<br/>Parameter Optimization"]
    OPT -->|"converged?"| FIT
    OPT -->|"yes"| MODEL["nep.model.txt<br/>Trained Potential"]
    MODEL --> GPUMD["gpumd<br/>Production MD"]
```

Sources: [main.cu (nep)](/src/main_nep/main.cu#L42-L84)

## GPU & Platform Requirements

| Requirement | Minimum | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| NVIDIA GPU | Compute capability ≥ 3.5 | Kepler generation and above |
| CUDA Toolkit | ≥ CUDA 9.0 | C++17 and CUDA 17 standards |
| OS | Linux (GCC) / Windows (MSVC) | Full support on both |
| Libraries | cuBLAS, cuSOLVER, cuFFT | Auto-linked via CMake |

Multi-GPU parallelism is supported for NEP-based simulations via domain decomposition along the thickest box dimension (overridable with `x`/`y`/`z` specifier). Good efficiency requires ≥10⁵ atoms per GPU.

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt](/CMakeLists.txt#L1-L30), [README.md](/README.md#L19-L23)

## Ecosystem & Extensions

GPUMD connects to a broader ecosystem of tools and interfaces:

- **Python Interfaces**: `calorine` (NEP construction & MD analysis), `gpyumd` (GPUMD I/O), `pyNEP` (NEP Python interface)
- **Format Converters**: 13+ converters for VASP, CP2K, CASTEP, ABACUS, ORCA, LAMMPS (MTP/Runner), GROMACS, DeepMD, and more
- **LAMMPS Integration**: Standalone [NEP_CPU](https://github.com/brucefan1983/NEP_CPU) provides a C++ NEP engine with LAMMPS pair style
- **MDI Interface**: `gpumd-mdi` enables coupling with other codes (e.g., VASP) via the MolSSI Driver Interface
- **PySAGES Integration**: GPU-native enhanced sampling on NEP potentials
- **Colab Tutorial**: End-to-end NEP workflow runnable on Google Colab

Sources: [tools/readme.md](/tools/readme.md#L1-L33), [README.md](/README.md#L30-L38)

```
GPUMD/
├── src/                  ← CUDA C++ source code (all .cu/.cuh files)
│   ├── main_gpumd/      ← gpumd executable: simulation driver
│   ├── main_nep/        ← nep executable: NEP training
│   ├── main_gnep/       ← gnep executable: gradient-based NEP (optional)
│   ├── main_mdi/        ← MDI interface executable
│   ├── force/           ← Potential models & neighbor list
│   ├── integrate/       ← Ensemble thermostats & barostats
│   ├── measure/         ← Observables, I/O, heat transport
│   ├── model/           ← Atom, Box, Group data structures
│   ├── minimize/        ← Energy minimizers (SD, FIRE)
│   ├── mc/              ← Monte Carlo sampling
│   ├── phonon/          ← Hessian & phonon computation
│   └── utilities/       ← GPU vectors, error handling, I/O
├── examples/            ← Minimal working examples
├── potentials/          ← Pre-packaged potential parameter files
├── tools/               ← Format converters, analysis scripts, utilities
├── tests/               ← Bash/Batch integration tests
├── tests_pytest/        ← Python pytest regression & conservation tests
├── doc/                 ← Sphinx-based documentation & manual
├── developers/          ← Developer class topology diagrams
├── CMakeLists.txt       ← CMake build system
├── Dockerfile           ← Containerized build
└── LICENCE              ← GPL v3
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L161)

# Quick Start



Get GPUMD compiled, configured, and running your first simulation in minutes. This guide walks you through the complete lifecycle — from building the executables to executing a molecular dynamics run and training a Neuroevolution Potential (NEP) model — using the repository's own example datasets.

## Prerequisites at a Glance

Before compiling GPUMD, ensure your environment meets these requirements:

| Requirement | NVIDIA (CUDA) | AMD (ROCm/HIP) |
|---|---|---|
| **GPU** | Compute capability ≥ 3.5 | Any ROCm-supported GPU |
| **Toolkit** | CUDA ≥ 9.0 | ROCm (with hipcc) |
| **C++ Compiler (Linux)** | GCC with C++14+ support | hipcc (C++17 default) |
| **C++ Compiler (Windows)** | MSVC `cl.exe` + 64-bit `make.exe` | Not supported |
| **Additional libs** | cuBLAS, cuSOLVER, cuFFT | hipBLAS, hipSOLVER, hipFFT |

> [!TIP]
> On Windows, if you encounter `c1xx : fatal error C1083` errors during compilation, remove the `-Xcompiler "/wd 4819"` flag from the makefile. For GPUs with compute capability < 6.0, add `-DUSE_KEPLER` to `CFLAGS`.

Sources: [makefile](/src/makefile#L1-L15), [makefile.hip](/src/makefile.hip#L1-L15), [installation.rst](/doc/installation.rst#L10-L30)

## Step 1 — Build the Executables

GPUMD produces two primary executables: **`gpumd`** (the MD simulation engine) and **`nep`** (the NEP training/prediction tool). A third optional executable, **`gnep`**, supports gradient-based NEP training.

### Option A: Make (Recommended)

```bash
cd src
make              # builds gpumd and nep
```

To target a specific GPU architecture, edit the `CUDA_ARCH` variable at the top of the makefile before building:

```makefile
CUDA_ARCH = -arch=sm_80    # e.g., sm_80 for A100, sm_89 for RTX 4090
```

### Option B: CMake (Pre-release)

```bash
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build --config Release --parallel
```

The executables appear in the `build/` directory. Target a specific GPU architecture at configure time:

```bash
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=80
```

### Option C: AMD GPU via ROCm/HIP

```bash
cd src
make -f makefile.hip                    # defaults to gfx90a
make -f makefile.hip HIP_ARCH=gfx1100  # override for your GPU
```

### Option D: Docker

A Dockerfile based on `nvidia/cuda:13.1.1-devel-ubuntu24.04` is provided for containerized builds, pre-loaded with Python testing and documentation dependencies:

```bash
docker build -t gpumd .
docker run --gpus all -it gpumd
```

After any build method, verify success:

```bash
ls src/gpumd src/nep    # or ls build/gpumd build/nep for CMake
```

Sources: [makefile](/src/makefile#L49-L62), [CMakeLists.txt](/CMakeLists.txt#L1-L69), [makefile.hip](/src/makefile.hip#L9-L20), [Dockerfile](/Dockerfile#L1-L38), [installation.rst](/doc/installation.rst#L34-L62)

## Step 2 — Understand the Input Files

Every GPUMD simulation requires exactly **two input files** in the working directory:

| File | Purpose | Format |
|---|---|---|
| **`model.xyz`** | Atomic configuration (positions, lattice, species) | Extended XYZ |
| **`run.in`** | Simulation protocol (potential, ensemble, outputs) | Keyword-parameter lines |

For NEP training, the `nep` executable uses a different pair:

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **`train.xyz`** | Training dataset (structures with energies, forces, virials in extended XYZ) |
| **`nep.in`** | NEP training configuration (atom types, hyperparameters) |

### The `model.xyz` File

This file follows the [extended XYZ convention](https://github.com/libAtoms/extxyz). A minimal example for 250 atoms of PbTe:

```
250
Lattice="0.0 16.426 16.426 16.426 0.0 16.426 16.426 16.426 0.0" Properties=species:S:1:pos:R:3:force:R:3
Te  3.379  3.216  3.349  -0.830  0.522 -0.420
Pb 32.611 16.673 16.724   0.085 -1.242 -0.371
...
```

- **Line 1**: Number of atoms
- **Line 2**: Key-value pairs — `Lattice` (9 components of cell vectors in Å), `Properties` (column definitions), optional `pbc` (default `"T T T"`)
- **Line 3+**: One row per atom with the columns defined by `Properties`

Units: positions in **Å**, velocities in **Å/fs**, masses in **amu**.

### The `run.in` File

This file drives the simulation as a sequence of keyword commands. Blank lines and `#` comments are ignored. The overall structure follows a strict logical order:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["potential  nep.txt"] --> B["velocity  300"]
    B --> C["ensemble  nvt_lan 300 300 100"]
    C --> D["time_step  1"]
    D --> E["dump_thermo  10"]
    E --> F["run  10000"]
    F --> G{More runs?}
    G -->|Yes| C
    G -->|No| H[Done]

    style A fill:#e1f5fe
    style B fill:#fff3e0
    style C fill:#f3e5f5
    style F fill:#e8f5e9
```

**Key keywords for your first simulation:**

| Keyword | Syntax | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `potential` | `potential <file> [x\|y\|z]` | Set the interatomic potential (NEP, Tersoff, EAM, LJ, etc.) |
| `velocity` | `velocity <T_K> [seed <n>]` | Initialize velocities at temperature T (K) |
| `ensemble` | `ensemble <type> <params...>` | Choose integrator (nve, nvt_lan, npt_ber, etc.) |
| `time_step` | `time_step <dt>` | Set integration timestep (fs) |
| `dump_thermo` | `dump_thermo <interval>` | Write thermodynamic output every N steps |
| `dump_xyz` | `dump_xyz <interval> <file> force` | Dump positions + forces to XYZ |
| `run` | `run <N_steps>` | Execute N MD steps |

Sources: [run_in.rst](/doc/gpumd/input_files/run_in.rst#L1-L80), [model_xyz.rst](/doc/gpumd/input_files/model_xyz.rst#L1-L80), [potential.rst](/doc/gpumd/input_parameters/potential.rst#L1-L36), [velocity.rst](/doc/gpumd/input_parameters/velocity.rst#L1-L37), [ensemble.rst](/doc/gpumd/input_parameters/ensemble.rst#L1-L41)

## Step 3 — Run Your First MD Simulation

The repository ships ready-to-run examples. The simplest path is the **dynamic simulation** example for PbTe using a pre-trained NEP model:

```bash
cd examples/gpumd_dynamic
../../src/gpumd
```

This reads `model.xyz` and `run.in`, where `run.in` contains:

```
potential   ../nep_train/nep.txt    # use the pre-trained NEP model
velocity    300                      # initialize at 300 K

ensemble    nvt_lan 300 300 100     # NVT Langevin thermostat at 300 K
time_step   1                        # 1 fs timestep
dump_thermo 10                       # output thermo every 10 steps
run         10000                    # run 10,000 steps
```

After completion, you'll find `thermo.out` with columns of time, temperature, pressure, and energy data.

### Static Calculation Example

For a single-point force/energy evaluation:

```bash
cd examples/gpumd_static
../../src/gpumd
```

The `run.in` here uses `ensemble nve` with `time_step 0` and `run 1` — a zero-step "run" that just computes forces:

```
potential   ../nep_train/nep.txt
velocity    1

ensemble nve
time_step 0
dump_xyz 1 dump.xyz force precision double
run 1
```

Sources: [gpumd_dynamic/run.in](/examples/gpumd_dynamic/run.in#L1-L8), [gpumd_static/run.in](/examples/gpumd_static/run.in#L1-L8), [readme.md](/examples/readme.md#L1-L50)

## Step 4 — Train a NEP Model

The NEP (Neuroevolution Potential) framework lets you train machine-learned interatomic potentials from ab initio data. The workflow has two phases:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["train.xyz<br/>(DFT structures)"] --> B["nep.in<br/>(config)"]
    B --> C["nep executable<br/>(training)"]
    C --> D["nep.txt<br/>(trained model)"]
    D --> E["gpumd<br/>(production MD)"]

    style A fill:#fff3e0
    style C fill:#f3e5f5
    style D fill:#e8f5e9
    style E fill:#e1f5fe
```

### Training

```bash
cd examples/nep_train
../../src/nep
```

The `nep.in` file is minimal for this example:

```
type         2 Te Pb     # 2 atom types: Te and Pb
generation   20000        # run 20,000 generations
```

The `nep` executable reads `train.xyz` (training data in extended XYZ with energies and forces) and `nep.in`, then produces `nep.txt` (the trained potential model) and `loss.out` (training metrics).

### Prediction (Validation)

To evaluate the trained model against the training data:

```bash
cd examples/nep_prediction
../../src/nep
```

With `nep.in`:

```
type         2 Te Pb
prediction   1            # run in prediction mode instead of training
```

This writes `force.out` and `energy.out` comparing NEP predictions against reference values.

> [!TIP]
> By default, both `gpumd` and `nep` use **all visible GPUs**. Control GPU selection with `export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0` (single GPU) or `export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,2` (multi-GPU). For multi-GPU runs, use GPUs of the same type to avoid slow-GPU bottlenecks. Good parallel efficiency for `gpumd` requires >100k atoms per GPU.

Sources: [nep_train/nep.in](/examples/nep_train/nep.in#L1-L3), [nep_prediction/nep.in](/examples/nep_prediction/nep.in#L1-L3), [readme.md](/examples/readme.md#L12-L40)

## Available Built-in Potentials

GPUMD ships with a rich set of pre-parametrized potentials in the `potentials/` directory, ready to use by pointing `potential` to the file path:

| Category | Potentials | Example Files |
|---|---|---|
| **NEP** | Machine-learned (NEP1–NEP4, UNEP) | `nep/C_2024_NEP4.txt`, `nep/Si_2022_NEP4_3body.txt` |
| **Tersoff** | Empirical many-body | `tersoff/Si_Tersoff_1989.txt`, `tersoff/Graphene_Lindsay_2010.txt` |
| **EAM** | Embedded atom method | `eam/Cu_Zhou_2004.txt`, `eam/CuNi.eam.alloy` |
| **LJ** | Lennard-Jones | `lj/Ar_10A.txt`, `lj/Ar_20A.txt` |
| **Hybrid** | NEP+ILP, SW+ILP, Tersoff+ILP | `hybrid_nep_ilp/hybrid_nep_ilp_gr_hbn_ILP_oywg_2018.txt` |

Use them directly in `run.in`:

```
potential  ../../potentials/tersoff/Si_Tersoff_1989.txt
```

Sources: [potentials/](/potentials), [potential.rst](/doc/gpumd/input_parameters/potential.rst#L16-L36)

## Quick Reference — Complete Workflow

| Step | Command | What Happens |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Build | `cd src && make` | Produces `gpumd` and `nep` executables |
| 2. Prepare | Create `model.xyz` + `run.in` | Define your system and simulation protocol |
| 3. Run MD | `path/to/gpumd` | Executes simulation, writes output files |
| 4. Train NEP | Create `train.xyz` + `nep.in`, then `path/to/nep` | Produces `nep.txt` model file |
| 5. Validate | Set `prediction 1` in `nep.in`, then `path/to/nep` | Compares predictions to reference data |
| 6. Production | Use `nep.txt` in `run.in` with `potential nep.txt` | Full MD with ML potential |

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

| Problem | Solution |
|---|---|
| `nvcc: command not found` | Install CUDA toolkit and add to PATH |
| `undefined reference to cuBLAS` | Ensure CUDA toolkit is fully installed (includes libs) |
| Wrong GPU architecture | Set `-arch=sm_XX` in makefile matching your GPU (e.g., sm_80 for A100) |
| Slow multi-GPU performance | Use same-type GPUs; ensure >100k atoms per GPU for `gpumd` |
| `c1xx : fatal error C1083` (Windows) | Remove `-Xcompiler "/wd 4819"` from makefile |
| Kepler GPU (cc < 6.0) | Add `-DUSE_KEPLER` to `CFLAGS` in makefile |

Sources: [makefile](/src/makefile#L1-L15), [installation.rst](/doc/installation.rst#L34-L62), [readme.md](/examples/readme.md#L12-L40)

## Where to Go Next

Now that you can compile and run GPUMD, explore the deeper architecture and capabilities:

# Input File Format



GPUMD requires a small, declarative set of input files to define a simulation. At minimum, you need **two files**: `model.xyz` (the atomic configuration) and `run.in` (the simulation protocol). Two optional files — `kpoints.in` and `eigenvector.in` — support phonon and modal analysis calculations. GPUMD reads these files sequentially, executes commands top-to-bottom, and terminates with an error if any command is invalid. This page provides a complete reference for all four input files, their syntax, and the execution semantics that govern how they interact.

Sources: [index.rst](doc/gpumd/input_files/index.rst#L1-L17), [run_in.rst](doc/gpumd/input_files/run_in.rst#L1-L10)

## File Inventory at a Glance

| File | Required | Purpose | Format |
|------|----------|---------|--------|
| `model.xyz` | **Yes** | Atomic positions, velocities, box, boundary conditions | Extended XYZ |
| `run.in` | **Yes** | Simulation protocol: potentials, ensembles, runs, output | Keyword-parameter lines |
| `kpoints.in` | No | k-point paths for phonon dispersion calculations | Space-separated coordinates + labels |
| `eigenvector_in` | No | Eigenvectors for modal analysis | Specialized format |

Sources: [index.rst](doc/gpumd/input_files/index.rst#L1-L17)

## Execution Architecture

The relationship between input files and GPUMD's execution flow follows a strict sequential pipeline. The diagram below illustrates how `model.xyz` is consumed at startup, how `run.in` drives the simulation loop, and how optional files integrate into specific calculation types:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Startup["Startup Phase"]
        MODEL["model.xyz<br/>(atomic configuration)"] --> PARSE["Parse extended XYZ<br/>→ positions, velocities,<br/>box, groups"]
    end
    subgraph Protocol["run.in Protocol Execution"]
        PARSE --> POT["potential<br/>(set interaction model)"]
        POT --> MIN{minimize?<br/>Optional}
        MIN -->|Yes| EMIN["Energy Minimization<br/>(FIRE or SD)"]
        MIN -->|No| STATIC{Static<br/>Calculations?}
        EMIN --> STATIC
        STATIC -->|Yes| SC["compute_cohesive<br/>compute_elastic<br/>compute_phonon"]
        STATIC -->|No| MD["MD Simulation Loop"]
        SC --> MD
        subgraph MDLoop["Repeated MD Run Blocks"]
            MD --> VEL["velocity<br/>(initialize velocities)"]
            VEL --> ENS["ensemble<br/>(set integrator)"]
            ENS --> SETTINGS["time_step, compute,<br/>dump_*, fix, deform..."]
            SETTINGS --> RUN["run N<br/>(execute N steps)"]
            RUN -->|More blocks| ENS
        end
    end
    subgraph Optional["Optional Input Files"]
        KP["kpoints.in"] -.->|phonon calc| SC
        EV["eigenvector_in"] -.->|modal analysis| SETTINGS
    end
```

Sources: [run_in.rst](doc/gpumd/input_files/run_in.rst#L12-L45)

---

## The `model.xyz` File

The `model.xyz` file defines the complete initial state of the simulation system. It uses the **extended XYZ format** — a widely adopted standard in atomistic simulation. The file has a rigid three-section structure: a header line with the atom count, a lattice/properties line, and then one line per atom.

Sources: [model_xyz.rst](doc/gpumd/input_files/model_xyz.rst#L1-L15)

### Line 1: Atom Count

The first line contains a single integer: the total number of atoms *N* in the system.

```
250
```

Sources: [model_xyz.rst](doc/gpumd/input_files/model_xyz.rst#L17-L19)

### Line 2: Lattice, Boundary Conditions, and Properties

The second line consists of `keyword=value` pairs separated by spaces. Spaces around `=` are allowed. Values containing spaces must be enclosed in double quotes (e.g., `keyword="value_1 value_2"`). All characters are **case-insensitive**. The recognized keywords are:

| Keyword | Required | Syntax | Description |
|---------|----------|--------|-------------|
| `lattice` | **Yes** | `lattice="ax ay az bx by bz cx cy cz"` | Nine components of the three cell vectors **a**, **b**, **c** in Å |
| `pbc` | No | `pbc="pbc_a pbc_b pbc_c"` | Periodic boundary conditions: `T` (periodic) or `F` (free/open) per direction. Default: `"T T T"` |
| `properties` | **Yes** | `properties=property_name:data_type:count[:...]` | Defines per-atom data columns (see below) |
| `energy` | No | `energy=<value>` | Total energy in eV (informational; not used by GPUMD) |
| `config_type` | No | `config_type=<string>` | Configuration label (informational) |

**Cell vector interpretation**: The nine lattice components define three vectors in Cartesian coordinates:

> **a** = a_x **ê**_x + a_y **ê**_y + a_z **ê**_z  
> **b** = b_x **ê**_x + b_y **ê**_y + b_z **ê**_z  
> **c** = c_x **ê**_x + c_y **ê**_y + c_z **ê**_z

**Periodic boundary conditions**: For non-NEP potentials, GPUMD uses the minimum-image convention, requiring the box to be at least twice the potential cutoff in each periodic direction. For NEP potentials, sufficiently many periodic images are automatically considered, so this constraint is relaxed.

Sources: [model_xyz.rst](doc/gpumd/input_files/model_xyz.rst#L21-L55)

### Property Definitions

The `properties` keyword defines what data columns appear on each atom line (Line 3+). Properties are concatenated with colons:

| Property | Data Type | Columns | Required | Description |
|----------|-----------|---------|----------|-------------|
| `species` | `S` | 1 | **Yes** | Element symbol (e.g., `C`, `Si`, `Te`) |
| `pos` | `R` | 3 | **Yes** | Position vector (x, y, z) in Å |
| `mass` | `R` | 1 | No | Mass in amu (default values used if missing) |
| `charge` | `R` | 1 | No | Charge in units of e (default: 0) |
| `vel` | `R` | 3 | No | Velocity vector in Å/fs |
| `group` | `I` | *n* | No | *n* grouping methods (integer labels) |

**Grouping methods** are integer labels that partition atoms into groups. Multiple grouping methods can coexist, each providing a different partitioning (e.g., method 0 = left/right half, method 1 = per-atom, method 2 = all-atoms-one-group). These groups are referenced by `compute` and `dump` keywords in `run.in`.

Sources: [model_xyz.rst](doc/gpumd/input_files/model_xyz.rst#L46-L55)

### Lines 3+: Per-Atom Data

Each subsequent line contains the data columns defined by the `properties` keyword, in the same order. Every line must have the same number of values.

Sources: [model_xyz.rst](doc/gpumd/input_files/model_xyz.rst#L57-L58)

### Units Summary

| Quantity | Unit |
|----------|------|
| Mass | unified atomic mass unit (amu) |
| Charge | elementary charge e |
| Position / Cell dimensions | Ångstrom (Å) |
| Velocity | Å/fs |
| Energy (if present) | eV |
| Force (if present) | eV/Å |

Sources: [model_xyz.rst](doc/gpumd/input_files/model_xyz.rst#L60-L66)

### `model.xyz` Example

A minimal example with 10 atoms, periodic in x only, with 3 grouping methods:

```
10
pbc="T F F" lattice="4 0 0 0 1 0 0 0 1" properties=species:S:1:pos:R:3:group:I:3
C  0 0 0 0 0 0
Si 1 0 0 0 1 0
C  2 0 0 0 2 0
Si 3 0 0 0 3 0
C  4 0 0 0 4 0
Si 5 0 0 1 5 0
C  6 0 0 1 6 0
Si 7 0 0 1 7 0
C  8 0 0 1 8 0
Si 9 0 0 1 9 0
```

A real-world example from the repository (250-atom PbTe system with forces):

```
250
energy=-930.7339 config_type=nep2xyz pbc="T T T" Lattice="0.0 16.42598 16.42598 16.42598 0.0 16.42598 16.42598 16.42598 0.0" Properties=species:S:1:pos:R:3:force:R:3
Te 3.271619 3.093816 3.354722 0.4178623 -0.03671069 -0.04290853
Te 3.726119 6.524911 6.853489 -1.835852 -0.5027356 -0.4577284
...
```

Sources: [model_xyz.rst](doc/gpumd/input_files/model_xyz.rst#L68-L103), [model.xyz](examples/gpumd_static/model.xyz#L1-L3)

---

## The `run.in` File

The `run.in` file defines the **simulation protocol** — the sequence of operations GPUMD executes. Blank lines and lines starting with `#` are ignored (enabling inline comments). All other lines follow the form:

```
keyword parameter_1 parameter_2 ...
```

> [!TIP]
> The overall structure of `run.in` is not arbitrary — it follows a strict ordering: (1) `potential` → (2) optional `minimize` → (3) optional static calculations → (4) MD simulation blocks. Each MD block must contain an `ensemble` keyword followed by a `run` keyword, with configuration keywords in between. This block can be repeated for multi-stage simulations.

Sources: [run_in.rst](doc/gpumd/input_files/run_in.rst#L5-L30)

### Keyword Execution Semantics

Every keyword falls into one of two execution categories, indicated by the **Exec.** column in the tables below:

- **Yes (Immediate)**: The command is executed as soon as it is encountered. It does not depend on a subsequent `run` keyword.
- **No (Deferred)**: The command configures settings for the next `run` block. It takes effect only when `run` is encountered.

Additionally, some keywords are **propagating** (**Prop.** = Yes), meaning their setting persists from one `run` block to the next. Most keywords are non-propagating and must be re-specified for each `run` block.

Sources: [run_in.rst](doc/gpumd/input_files/run_in.rst#L32-L45)

### Simulation Setup Keywords

These keywords configure the fundamental simulation parameters before any calculation begins:

| Keyword | Brief Description | Exec. | Prop. |
|---------|-------------------|-------|-------|
| `potential` | Set the interatomic potential model | Yes | N/A |
| `velocity` | Set initial velocities from a temperature | Yes | N/A |
| `dftd3` | Add DFT-D3 dispersion correction to NEP | Yes | N/A |
| `change_box` | Change the simulation box | Yes | N/A |
| `deform` | Deform the simulation box | No | No |
| `ensemble` | Specify the integrator for an MD run | No | No |
| `fix` | Fix (freeze) atoms | No | No |
| `time_step` | Set the integration time step | No | **Yes** |

Sources: [run_in.rst](doc/gpumd/input_files/run_in.rst#L47-L75)

### Action Keywords

These keywords trigger calculations or advance the simulation:

| Keyword | Brief Description | Exec. | Prop. |
|---------|-------------------|-------|-------|
| `minimize` | Perform energy minimization (FIRE or SD) | Yes | N/A |
| `run` | Run N MD steps | Yes | No |
| `compute` | Compute time/space-averaged quantities | No | No |
| `compute_cohesive` | Compute cohesive energy curve | Yes | N/A |
| `compute_elastic` | Compute elastic constants | Yes | N/A |
| `compute_dos` | Compute phonon density of states | No | No |
| `compute_gkma` | Compute modal heat current (GKMA) | No | No |
| `compute_hac` | Compute thermal conductivity (EMD/HAC) | No | No |
| `compute_hnema` | Compute modal thermal conductivity (HNEMA) | No | No |
| `compute_hnemd` | Compute thermal conductivity (HNEMD) | No | No |
| `compute_hnemdec` | Compute multicomponent conductivity (HNEMDEC) | No | No |
| `compute_phonon` | Compute phonon dispersion | Yes | N/A |
| `compute_sdc` | Compute self-diffusion coefficient | No | No |
| `compute_msd` | Compute mean-square displacement | No | No |
| `compute_shc` | Compute spectral heat current | No | No |

Sources: [run_in.rst](doc/gpumd/input_files/run_in.rst#L77-L145)

### Output Keywords

These keywords control what data is written and how frequently:

| Keyword | Brief Description | Exec. | Prop. |
|---------|-------------------|-------|-------|
| `active` | On-the-fly active learning | No | No |
| `dump_observer` | Write observer NEP potential data | No | No |
| `dump_netcdf` | Write positions in netCDF format | No | No |
| `dump_restart` | Write restart file | No | No |
| `dump_thermo` | Write thermodynamic quantities | No | No |
| `dump_xyz` | Write per-atom data in extended XYZ | No | No |

Sources: [run_in.rst](doc/gpumd/input_files/run_in.rst#L147-L190)

---

## Key `run.in` Keywords — Syntax Reference

This section provides the exact syntax for the most commonly used keywords. Each entry shows the parameter format, units, and a working example.

### `potential` — Set Interatomic Potential

```
potential <potential_filename>
```

Specifies the potential file path (relative or absolute). Supported models include: Tersoff (1988/1989/mini), EAM, FCP, Lennard-Jones, NEP, hybrid NEP+ILP, SW+ILP, Tersoff+ILP, and Deep Potential (DP).

**Example:**
```
potential ../nep_train/nep.txt
```

Sources: [potential.rst](doc/gpumd/input_parameters/potential.rst#L1-L36)

### `velocity` — Initialize Velocities

```
velocity <initial_temperature> [seed <seed_number>]
```

| Parameter | Unit | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `initial_temperature` | K | Target temperature for velocity initialization |
| `seed` | — | Optional random seed for reproducibility |

The generated velocities do **not** follow the Maxwell distribution initially, but converge to it during simulation. Total linear and angular momenta are set to zero. If velocities are already present in `model.xyz`, those are used instead and the temperature parameter is ignored. If this keyword is missing and `model.xyz` has no velocities, a default temperature of 300 K is used.

**Example:**
```
velocity 300
velocity 10 seed 42
```

Sources: [velocity.rst](doc/gpumd/input_parameters/velocity.rst#L1-L37)

### `ensemble` — Set Integrator

```
ensemble <method> <method_parameters...>
```

**Standard ensembles:**

| Method | Parameters | Description |
|--------|------------|-------------|
| `nve` | (none) | Micro-canonical (no thermostat) |
| `nvt_ber` | `T_1 T_2 T_coup` | NVT with Berendsen thermostat |
| `nvt_nhc` | `T_1 T_2 T_coup` | NVT with Nosé-Hoover chain |
| `nvt_bdp` | `T_1 T_2 T_coup` | NVT with Bussi-Donadio-Parrinello |
| `nvt_lan` | `T_1 T_2 T_coup` | NVT with Langevin thermostat |
| `nvt_bao` | `T_1 T_2 T_coup` | NVT with Langevin BAOAB splitting |
| `npt_ber` | `T_1 T_2 T_coup {pressure_params}` | NPT with Berendsen barostat |
| `npt_scr` | `T_1 T_2 T_coup {pressure_params}` | NPT with stochastic cell rescaling |

**Units**: Temperature in K, pressure in GPa. The coupling constant `T_coup` = τ_T/Δt (relaxation time / time step); a good choice is ~100. The pressure coupling `p_coup` = τ_p/Δt; a good choice is ~1000.

**Example:**
```
ensemble nvt_lan 300 300 100
ensemble nve
```

Sources: [ensemble.rst](doc/gpumd/input_parameters/ensemble.rst#L1-L41), [ensemble_standard.rst](doc/gpumd/input_parameters/ensemble_standard.rst#L1-L98)

### `time_step` — Set Integration Time Step

```
time_step <dt_in_fs> [<max_distance_per_step>]
```

| Parameter | Unit | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `dt_in_fs` | fs | Time step for integration (default: 1 fs) |
| `max_distance_per_step` | Å | Optional: maximum atom displacement per step |

This keyword is **propagating** — its value carries over to subsequent `run` blocks without re-specification.

**Example:**
```
time_step 1
time_step 0.5
time_step 2.0 0.05
```

Sources: [time_step.rst](doc/gpumd/input_parameters/time_step.rst#L1-L51)

### `minimize` — Energy Minimization

```
minimize <method> <force_tolerance> <max_steps> [<box_change> [<hydrostatic_strain>]]
```

| Parameter | Unit | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `method` | — | `sd` (steepest descent) or `fire` (FIRE algorithm) |
| `force_tolerance` | eV/Å | Convergence criterion (use negative value to force max_steps) |
| `max_steps` | — | Maximum number of iterations |
| `box_change` | — | `1` = optimize box (FIRE only) |
| `hydrostatic_strain` | — | `1` = use hydrostatic strain for box change |

**Example:**
```
minimize fire 1.0e-5 1000
minimize fire 1.0e-5 1000 1 1
```

Sources: [minimize.rst](doc/gpumd/input_parameters/minimize.rst#L1-L83)

### `run` — Execute MD Steps

```
run <number_of_steps>
```

Each `run` keyword defines a self-contained MD block. The block encompasses all keywords from the preceding `ensemble` (or the start of the file) up to and including `run` itself. Multiple blocks can be chained for multi-stage simulations.

**Example:**
```
run 10000
run 1000000
```

Sources: [run.rst](doc/gpumd/input_parameters/run.rst#L1-L42)

### `dump_thermo` — Write Thermodynamic Output

```
dump_thermo <interval>
```

Writes global thermodynamic quantities to `thermo.out` every `interval` steps. **Non-propagating** — must be re-specified for each `run` block.

**Example:**
```
dump_thermo 10
```

Sources: [dump_thermo.rst](doc/gpumd/input_parameters/dump_thermo.rst#L1-L30)

### `dump_xyz` — Write Per-Atom Data

```
dump_xyz <interval> <filename> [group <grouping_method> <group_id>] [precision <single|double>] {<property_1> <property_2> ...}
```

| Parameter | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| `interval` | Output interval in steps |
| `filename` | Output file path (append `*` to write one file per frame) |
| `group` | Restrict output to a specific group |
| `precision` | `single` (9 digits, default) or `double` (17 digits) |
| properties | `mass`, `velocity`, `force`, `potential`, `virial`, `charge`, `bec`, `group_labels`, `unwrapped_position` |

Wrapped positions are always included. **Non-propagating**. Can be invoked multiple times per `run` block.

**Example:**
```
dump_xyz 1000 positions.xyz
dump_xyz 100 properties.xyz group 1 0 mass velocity potential force virial
dump_xyz 100 forces.xyz precision double force
```

Sources: [dump_xyz.rst](doc/gpumd/input_parameters/dump_xyz.rst#L1-L66)

---

## The `kpoints.in` File (Optional)

This file specifies k-point paths for phonon dispersion calculations invoked by `compute_phonon` in `run.in`. Each line defines a high-symmetry point with three fractional coordinates and a label name:

```
k_x k_y k_z label
```

A **blank line** separates distinct k-point paths (useful for plotting discontinuous segments in the Brillouin zone).

**Example — 2D hexagonal lattice:**
```
0 0 0 G
0.5 0 0 M
0.333 0.333 0 K
0 0 0 G
```

**Example — FCC lattice (two paths):**
```
0 0 0 G
0.5 0 0.5 X
0.625 0.25 0.625 U

0.375 0.375 0.75 K
0 0 0 G
0.5 0.5 0.5 L
0.5 0.25 0.75 W
0.5 0 0.5 X
```

Sources: [kpoints_in.rst](doc/gpumd/input_files/kpoints_in.rst#L1-L53)

---

## The `eigenvector_in` File (Optional)

This file provides eigenvector data for modal analysis calculations. It is only needed when performing specialized modal decomposition and is referenced indirectly through `compute` keywords in `run.in`.

Sources: [eigenvector_in.rst](doc/gpumd/input_files/eigenvector_in.rst#L1-L8)

---

## Complete Working Examples

### Static Calculation (Force Evaluation)

```
potential   ../nep_train/nep.txt
velocity    1

ensemble nve
time_step 0
dump_xyz 1 dump.xyz force precision double
run 1
```

This evaluates forces on the initial configuration using an NEP potential and writes them to `dump.xyz`. The `time_step 0` and `run 1` combination ensures no actual time integration occurs — this is a single-point calculation.

Sources: [run.in](examples/gpumd_static/run.in#L1-L8)

### Dynamic NVT Simulation

```
potential   ../nep_train/nep.txt
velocity    300

ensemble    nvt_lan 300 300 100
time_step   1
dump_thermo 10
run         10000
```

This runs a 10,000-step NVT simulation at 300 K using the Langevin thermostat with a coupling constant of 100. Thermodynamic data is written every 10 steps. The velocity initialization at 300 K matches the target temperature.

Sources: [run.in](examples/gpumd_dynamic/run.in#L1-L8)

### Multi-Stage MD with Minimization

A typical multi-stage workflow combines minimization, equilibration, and production:

```
potential nep.txt

# Stage 1: Energy minimization
minimize fire 1.0e-5 1000

# Stage 2: Equilibrate at 300 K (NVT)
velocity 300
ensemble nvt_lan 300 300 100
time_step 1
dump_thermo 100
run 20000

# Stage 3: Production run (NVE)
ensemble nve
dump_thermo 10
dump_xyz 1000 traj.xyz velocity force
compute_hnemd 10 0.0001
run 1000000
```

Sources: [run.rst](doc/gpumd/input_parameters/run.rst#L28-L42), [minimize.rst](doc/gpumd/input_parameters/minimize.rst#L64-L83)

---

## `run.in` Execution Model — Key Rules

Understanding these rules prevents common configuration errors:

1. **Sequential execution**: Commands in `run.in` are processed top-to-bottom. An invalid command causes immediate termination with an error message.
2. **Immediate vs. deferred**: Immediate keywords (`potential`, `velocity`, `minimize`, `compute_cohesive`, `compute_elastic`, `compute_phonon`) execute when encountered. Deferred keywords (`ensemble`, `time_step`, `compute`, `dump_*`, `fix`, `deform`) configure the next `run` block.
3. **Propagation**: Only `time_step` propagates across `run` blocks. All other deferred keywords must be re-specified for each block.
4. **One ensemble per run**: Exactly one `ensemble` keyword must precede each `run` keyword.
5. **Comment syntax**: Lines starting with `#` and blank lines are ignored. Inline comments after `#` are supported.
6. **Required ordering**: `potential` must come before `minimize`. `minimize` must come before MD runs. `velocity` must come before the first `ensemble`/`run` block.

> [!TIP]
> When debugging a `run.in` file, check whether you've forgotten to re-specify non-propagating keywords (like `dump_thermo` or `compute`) in subsequent `run` blocks — this is the most common source of "missing output" issues.

Sources: [run_in.rst](doc/gpumd/input_files/run_in.rst#L5-L45), [time_step.rst](doc/gpumd/input_parameters/time_step.rst#L40-L51)

---

# Architecture Overview



GPUMD (Graphics Processing Units Molecular Dynamics) is a **GPU-first molecular dynamics framework** built entirely in CUDA C++ / HIP C++, designed from the ground up to exploit massive data parallelism on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. The codebase compiles into three distinct executables — `gpumd` (production MD), `nep` (Neuroevolution Potential training), and `gnep` (gradient-based NEP training) — each with a focused entry point but sharing the `utilities` module for common GPU abstractions. The architectural philosophy is strikingly minimalist: virtually zero external dependencies (only optional NetCDF and PLUMED), no MPI layer, and a deliberate preference for single-GPU computation with domain-decomposition multi-GPU as an opt-in feature for NEP potentials only. This design achieves exceptional kernel occupancy and memory coherence by keeping the simulation state resident on the GPU across the entire time-stepping loop, with minimal host-device synchronization points.

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L1-L69), [developers/readme.md](developers/readme.md#L50-L105)

## Top-Level Executable Architecture

The three executables form a **train-then-deploy** workflow: the `nep` executable trains machine-learning interatomic potentials from ab initio datasets, producing a compact `.nep` model file; the `gpumd` executable then consumes that model (or any of the built-in empirical potentials) to perform production molecular dynamics simulations. The `gnep` executable provides an alternative training path using Adam-based gradient optimization rather than the default separable natural evolution strategy (SNES).

| Executable | Entry Point | Purpose | Key Link Libraries |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gpumd` | `src/main_gpumd/main.cu` | Production MD simulation | CUDA::cublas, cusolver, cufft |
| `nep` | `src/main_nep/main.cu` | NEP potential training | CUDA::cublas, cusolver, cufft |
| `gnep` | `src/main_gnep/main.cu` | Gradient-based NEP training | CUDA::cublas, cusolver, cufft |

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt](CMakeLists.txt#L28-L56), [src/main_gpumd/main.cu](src/main_gpumd/main.cu#L34-L60), [src/main_nep/main.cu](src/main_nep/main.cu#L35-L65)

## Core Simulation Pipeline: The `Run` Orchestrator

The `Run` class is the **top-level orchestrator** for the entire `gpumd` simulation lifecycle. It is instantiated in `main()` and owns — either directly or indirectly — every major subsystem. The constructor performs a three-phase bootstrap: (1) read `model.xyz` to initialize atomic positions and types, (2) allocate GPU memory for per-atom data, and (3) parse and execute `run.in` line-by-line. The simulation itself proceeds in `perform_a_run()`, which implements the canonical MD time-stepping loop with a **velocity-Verlet split** across `integrate.compute1()` and `integrate.compute2()`.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["main()"] --> B{"Has deposition?"}
    B -- No --> C["Run constructor"]
    B -- Yes --> D["Deposition loop"]
    D --> C
    C --> E["Read model.xyz"]
    E --> F["Allocate GPU memory"]
    F --> G["execute_run_in()"]
    G --> H["Parse run.in keywords"]
    H --> I["perform_a_run()"]
    I --> J["integrate.initialize()"]
    J --> K["measure.initialize()"]
    K --> L["Initial force.compute()"]
    L --> M["Time-stepping loop"]
    M --> N["integrate.compute1()"]
    N --> O["force.compute()"]
    O --> P["External force modifiers"]
    P --> Q["measure.process()"]
    Q --> R["integrate.compute2()"]
    R --> M
    M -- Done --> S["measure.finalize()"]
```

The time-stepping loop in `perform_a_run()` follows a precise ordering that is critical for correctness: the first half-kick of velocity-Verlet (`integrate.compute1`), full force evaluation (`force.compute`), application of external perturbations (electron stopping, added forces, springs, random forces, electric fields), measurement sampling, then the second half-kick (`integrate.compute2`), followed by optional Monte Carlo swaps. The loop also supports **adaptive time-stepping** by computing the maximum atomic velocity and capping the maximum distance per step.

Sources: [src/main_gpumd/run.cuh](src/main_gpumd/run.cuh#L40-L80), [src/main_gpumd/run.cu](src/main_gpumd/run.cu#L211-L350), [src/main_gpumd/main.cu](src/main_gpumd/main.cu#L34-L60)

## Class Ownership and Composition Hierarchy

The `Run` class holds **all core simulation state** through direct member composition. This flat ownership model — as opposed to deep nesting — keeps data flow explicit and avoids virtual dispatch overhead for cross-module communication. The only two polymorphic hierarchies (`Potential` and `Ensemble`) are accessed through `unique_ptr` vectors/holders within their respective manager classes (`Force` and `Integrate`).

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Run {
        +Atom atom
        +Box box
        +vector~Group~ group
        +Force force
        +Integrate integrate
        +Measure measure
        +MC mc
        +GPU_Vector thermo
        +Velocity velocity
        +Electron_Stop electron_stop
        +Add_Force add_force
        +Add_Spring add_spring
        +Add_Random_Force add_random_force
        +Add_Efield add_efield
    }
    class Force {
        +vector~unique_ptr~Potential~~ potentials
        +compute()
    }
    class Integrate {
        +unique_ptr~Ensemble~ ensemble
        +compute1() compute2()
    }
    class Measure {
        +vector~unique_ptr~Property~~ properties
        +process() process_dynamics()
    }
    class MC {
        +unique_ptr~MC_Ensemble~ mc_ensemble
        +compute()
    }
    Run *-- Force : holds
    Run *-- Integrate : holds
    Run *-- Measure : holds
    Run *-- MC : holds
    Run *-- Atom : holds
    Run *-- Box : holds
    Run "1" o-- "0..*" Group : holds vector
```

> [!TIP]
> The `Run` class deliberately does **not** hold `Minimize` or `Hessian` as members. These are instantiated as **stack-local objects** inside `parse_one_keyword()` and execute synchronously before returning control — they are one-shot computations, not part of the time-stepping loop.

Sources: [src/main_gpumd/run.cuh](src/main_gpumd/run.cuh#L40-L80), [src/force/force.cuh](src/force/force.cuh#L36-L87), [src/integrate/integrate.cuh](src/integrate/integrate.cuh#L27-L120), [src/measure/measure.cuh](src/measure/measure.cuh#L31-L69)

## The Model Layer: Atom, Box, and Group

The **model layer** (`src/model/`) defines the geometric and topological state of the simulation system. `Atom` is the central data structure — it holds all per-atom quantities as `GPU_Vector` objects (position, velocity, force, virial, potential energy, heat current) directly in GPU device memory, with corresponding CPU-side `std::vector` mirrors for type, mass, and charge that are used only during initialization. For path-integral molecular dynamics (PIMD), `Atom` also manages per-bead replicated arrays (`position_beads`, `velocity_beads`, `force_beads`, etc.).

`Box` encapsulates the simulation cell geometry with support for both **orthogonal and triclinic** cells. The box matrix `cpu_h[18]` stores both the cell vectors (entries 0–8) and their inverse (entries 9–17), enabling efficient minimum-image convention (MIC) computation via the inline `apply_mic()` device function — a function that appears in both `double` and `float` overloads and is called from virtually every force kernel.

`Group` implements the **atom grouping system** that partitions atoms into labeled subsets for targeted operations (fixing, thermostating, heat source/sink assignment, Monte Carlo species swaps). Multiple grouping methods can coexist, each stored as a separate `Group` instance in `Run::group`.

| Class | Key GPU Data | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `Atom` | `position_per_atom`, `velocity_per_atom`, `force_per_atom`, `virial_per_atom`, `potential_per_atom`, `heat_per_atom` | Per-atom physical state (all GPU-resident) |
| `Box` | `cpu_h[18]`, `float_h[18]` | Simulation cell matrix + inverse (CPU-cached, device-accessible) |
| `Group` | `GPU_Vector<int> label` | Atom-to-group mapping for selective operations |

Sources: [src/model/atom.cuh](src/model/atom.cuh#L22-L57), [src/model/box.cuh](src/model/box.cuh#L13-L47), [src/model/group.cuh](src/model/group.cuh)

## The Force Computation Subsystem

The force subsystem employs a **strategy pattern** with `Potential` as the abstract base class defining a virtual `compute()` interface. The `Force` manager class holds a `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Potential>>` called `potentials`, enabling **multiple simultaneous potentials** — for example, combining a Tersoff bulk potential with an interlayer potential (ILP) for 2D materials, or running NEP alongside ZBL repulsion at short range. The `Force::compute()` method iterates over all registered potentials and accumulates forces and energies additively.

The `Potential::compute()` signature is uniform: it receives box, type, position arrays and outputs per-atom potential energy, force, and virial. This interface is implemented by over **15 concrete potential classes**, spanning empirical potentials (EAM, Tersoff, LJ, ADP), machine-learned potentials (NEP, DP, NNAP), harmonic force constant potentials (FCP), and composite hybrid potentials (ILP+Tersoff, ILP+SW, ILP+NEP). Each concrete potential internally manages its own `Neighbor` object for GPU-accelerated cell-list neighbor construction.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Potential {
        <<abstract>>
        +compute(box, type, pos, pot, force, virial)*
        +rc : double
    }
    class NEP { +compute() }
    class NEP_Charge { +compute() }
    class NEP_MULTIGPU { +compute() }
    class Tersoff1989 { +compute() }
    class Tersoff1988 { +compute() }
    class EAM { +compute() }
    class LJ { +compute() }
    class ILP_TERSOFF { +compute() }
    class ILP_NEP { +compute() }
    class FCP { +compute() }
    Potential <|-- NEP
    Potential <|-- NEP_Charge
    Potential <|-- NEP_MULTIGPU
    Potential <|-- Tersoff1989
    Potential <|-- Tersoff1988
    Potential <|-- EAM
    Potential <|-- LJ
    Potential <|-- ILP_TERSOFF
    Potential <|-- ILP_NEP
    Potential <|-- FCP
```

Sources: [src/force/potential.cuh](src/force/potential.cuh#L28-L114), [src/force/force.cuh](src/force/force.cuh#L36-L87), [src/force/force.cu](src/force/force.cu#L1-L200)

## The Integration and Ensemble Subsystem

Time integration follows the same strategy pattern: `Ensemble` is the abstract base with pure virtual `compute1()` and `compute2()` methods implementing the **two-step velocity-Verlet** decomposition. The `Integrate` manager holds a single `std::unique_ptr<Ensemble>` representing the currently active ensemble, selected at parse time from the `ensemble` keyword in `run.in`. The ensemble type integer (`Integrate::type`) determines the integration scheme, with values ≥31 triggering PIMD bead-mode computation.

The concrete ensemble classes form the richest hierarchy in the codebase with over **20 variants**, covering NVE, NVT (Nose-Hoover chain, Langevin, Bussi-Damped), NPT (MTTK, Berendsen, SCR barostat), heat transport (NEMD, HNEMD), shock (MSST, NPHug), and advanced methods (PIMD, ECO-PIMD, QTBot, TTM two-temperature model, thermodynamic integration ensembles). All ensembles inherit the protected `velocity_verlet()` method from the `Ensemble` base class, ensuring a consistent integration kernel across all thermostat/barostat combinations.

| Ensemble Category | Classes | Key Feature |
|---|---|---|
| Microcanonical | `Ensemble_NVE` | Energy conservation, no thermostat |
| Canonical NVT | `Ensemble_LAN`, `Ensemble_NHC`, `Ensemble_BDP`, `Ensemble_BER` | Langevin, Nose-Hoover, Bussi, Berendsen |
| Isothermal-isobaric NPT | `Ensemble_MTTK`, `Ensemble_NPT_SCR`, `Ensemble_NPT_QTB` | MTTK, Stochastic Cell Rescaling |
| Heat transport | `Ensemble_Heat_Hybrid`, `Ensemble_TI`, `Ensemble_TI_*` | NEMD, HNEMD, thermodynamic integration |
| PIMD | `Ensemble_PIMD`, `ECO_PIMD` | Ring-polymer bead dynamics |
| Shock | `Ensemble_MSST`, `Ensemble_NPHUG` | Multi-Scale Shock, Hugoniot |

Sources: [src/integrate/ensemble.cuh](src/integrate/ensemble.cuh#L30-L158), [src/integrate/integrate.cuh](src/integrate/integrate.cuh#L27-L120)

## The Measurement and Property Subsystem

The measurement subsystem mirrors the force/integrate pattern: `Property` is the abstract base with a three-phase lifecycle — `preprocess()`, `process()`, and `postprocess()` — plus an optional `process_dynamics()` for measurements that need to sample within the integration split (e.g., heat current). The `Measure` manager holds a `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Property>>` called `properties`, and each `run.in` keyword like `compute_hac`, `compute_msd`, or `dump_thermo` appends a new `Property` subclass instance to this vector.

This design enables **composable, on-the-fly analysis**: multiple measurements execute simultaneously during the same MD run without interfering with each other, as each `Property` maintains its own internal accumulation buffers. The measurement catalog is extensive, covering structural analysis (RDF, ADF, orientational order), dynamical properties (MSD, SDC, VACF, DOS), transport coefficients (HAC for thermal conductivity, HNEMD κ, viscosity), phonon analysis (LSQT, modal analysis), and I/O (XYZ dump, thermo dump, restart, NetCDF trajectories).

Sources: [src/measure/property.cuh](src/measure/property.cuh#L28-L74), [src/measure/measure.cuh](src/measure/measure.cuh#L31-L69)

## NEP Training Pipeline Architecture

The `nep` executable follows a radically simpler architecture compared to `gpumd` — there is no time-stepping loop. Instead, the training pipeline is a three-step sequential process: (1) `Parameters para` reads the `nep.in` configuration file, (2) `Fitness fitness(para)` loads training/test datasets (`train.xyz`, `test.xyz`) and establishes the loss function, and (3) `SNES snes(para, &fitness)` runs the **Separable Natural Evolution Strategy** optimizer, which evolves a population of candidate NEP parameter vectors by mutating mean and step-size parameters, evaluating fitness on GPU, ranking by utility, and updating distribution parameters. The entire evolutionary search runs inside `SNES::compute()`, which is called automatically at the end of the `SNES` constructor.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["nep.in"] --> B["Parameters"]
    C["train.xyz / test.xyz"] --> D["Fitness"]
    B --> D
    D --> E["SNES optimizer"]
    B --> E
    E --> F["Population evolution loop"]
    F --> G["GPU fitness evaluation"]
    G --> H["Rank & update μ, σ"]
    H --> F
    F --> I["loss.out / nep.txt"]
```

Sources: [src/main_nep/main.cu](src/main_nep/main.cu#L35-L65), [src/main_nep/snes.cuh](src/main_nep/snes.cuh#L35-L82)

## GPU Memory Model and Portable Abstraction

GPUMD's entire computational state resides in **GPU device memory** through the `GPU_Vector<T>` template class, which wraps raw device allocations with RAII semantics and provides `data()` pointers for direct kernel access. The `Atom` class exemplifies this pattern: positions, velocities, forces, virials, and potentials are all `GPU_Vector<double>`, transferred to the device once during initialization and remaining resident throughout the simulation. CPU-side mirrors exist only for initialization data (`cpu_type`, `cpu_mass`, `cpu_position_per_atom`).

Portability across NVIDIA (CUDA) and AMD (HIP) GPUs is achieved through the **macro abstraction layer** in `gpu_macro.cuh`, which defines conditional compilation macros that map CUDA API calls to their HIP equivalents (e.g., `CHECK()` wraps both `cudaGetLastError` and `hipGetLastError`). All source files use the `.cu` / `.cuh` extension convention regardless of backend, and the build system selects between `makefile` (CUDA) and `makefile.hip` (HIP). The codebase requires C++17 and CUDA 17 standards.

Sources: [src/utilities/gpu_macro.cuh](src/utilities/gpu_macro.cuh), [src/utilities/gpu_vector.cuh](src/utilities/gpu_vector.cuh), [developers/readme.md](developers/readme.md#L58-L75)

## Source Module Map

The following table provides a definitive mapping of each source directory to its architectural role, the key classes it defines, and its relationship to the `Run` orchestrator.

| Directory | Role | Key Classes | Owned By |
|---|---|---|---|
| `src/model/` | Geometric & topological state | `Atom`, `Box`, `Group`, `Read_XYZ` | `Run` (direct members) |
| `src/force/` | Interatomic force computation | `Force`, `Potential` (abstract), `NEP`, `Tersoff*`, `EAM`, `LJ`, `Neighbor`, ... | `Run::force` |
| `src/integrate/` | Time integration & thermostat/barostat | `Integrate`, `Ensemble` (abstract), `Ensemble_NVE`, `Ensemble_LAN`, ... | `Run::integrate` |
| `src/measure/` | On-the-fly property computation & I/O | `Measure`, `Property` (abstract), `HAC`, `MSD`, `RDF`, `Dump_XYZ`, ... | `Run::measure` |
| `src/minimize/` | Energy minimization | `Minimize`, `Minimizer_FIRE`, `Minimizer_SD` | Instantiated locally in `Run::parse_one_keyword()` |
| `src/mc/` | Hybrid Monte Carlo / MD | `MC`, `MC_Ensemble`, `MC_Ensemble_Canonical`, `MC_Ensemble_SGC` | `Run::mc` |
| `src/phonon/` | Phonon / Hessian computation | `Hessian` | Instantiated locally in `Run::parse_one_keyword()` |
| `src/utilities/` | Cross-cutting GPU & I/O utilities | `GPU_Vector`, `gpu_macro.cuh`, `Error`, `Read_File`, `cusolver_wrapper` | Shared by all modules |
| `src/main_nep/` | NEP training pipeline | `Parameters`, `Fitness`, `SNES`, `NEP`, `Structure`, `Dataset` | `nep` executable only |
| `src/main_gnep/` | Gradient NEP training | `Parameters`, `Fitness`, `Adam`, `Gradients`, `Structure`, `Dataset` | `gnep` executable only |

Sources: [developers/readme.md](developers/readme.md#L80-L100), [src/main_gpumd/run.cuh](src/main_gpumd/run.cuh#L40-L80)

## Architectural Design Principles

Several deliberate design choices distinguish GPUMD from conventional MD codes and are worth understanding before diving into subsystem-specific documentation:

- **GPU-resident data**: Per-atom arrays never leave device memory during the time loop. This eliminates the dominant bottleneck in heterogeneous MD codes — host-device data transfer — and enables the ~100× speedups GPUMD achieves over LAMMPS for NEP potentials on a single GPU.
- **Flat polymorphism via `unique_ptr` vectors**: The `Force`, `Integrate`, and `Measure` managers each hold polymorphic objects through `std::unique_ptr`, but the managers themselves are flat members of `Run`. This avoids deep virtual call chains while still supporting runtime extensibility.
- **Cell-list neighbor finding on GPU**: The `Neighbor` class implements a fully GPU-resident cell-list construction algorithm with optional skin distance for Verlet-style reuse. The neighbor list (`NN`, `NL` arrays) lives entirely in device memory and is reconstructed each force evaluation.
- **No MPI, single-GPU default**: The codebase deliberately avoids MPI for inter-node communication. Multi-GPU support exists only for NEP via spatial domain decomposition (`NEP_MULTIGPU`), activated when `gpuGetDeviceCount() > 1`.
- **Internal unit system**: Energy in eV, length in Å, mass in Dalton, temperature in K, charge in e. This choice aligns with materials science conventions and avoids floating-point scaling in the most performance-critical kernels.

> [!TIP]
> The `GPU_Vector<T>` template is the single most important data structure to understand when reading GPUMD source code. Every per-atom quantity flowing through the simulation pipeline — positions, velocities, forces, virials — is a `GPU_Vector`. It provides `size()`, `data()` (returning a raw device pointer), and automatic RAII deallocation, but no host-side element access: kernel code accesses it via raw pointers obtained from `data()`.

Sources: [developers/readme.md](developers/readme.md#L88-L105), [src/force/neighbor.cuh](src/force/neighbor.cuh#L90-L161), [src/utilities/gpu_vector.cuh](src/utilities/gpu_vector.cuh)

# Force and Potential System



The Force and Potential System is the computational backbone of GPUMD, responsible for evaluating interatomic forces, per-atom potential energies, and per-atom virial tensors that drive every molecular dynamics step. It is organized as a **two-tier hierarchy**: the `Force` class acts as the top-level orchestrator that parses potential inputs, dispatches computation, and applies post-processing corrections, while the `Potential` abstract base class defines the interface that each concrete potential model must implement. This separation ensures that adding a new potential requires only subclassing `Potential` and registering the model name in the `Force::parse_potential` factory — the rest of the simulation pipeline remains untouched.

Sources: [force.cuh](src/force/force.cuh#L1-L87), [potential.cuh](src/force/potential.cuh#L1-L114)

## Architecture Overview

The force computation pipeline follows a strict sequence: periodic boundary conditions are applied, per-atom properties are initialized to zero, each potential's `compute` method is invoked, optional HNEMD driving forces are injected, and finally the total force is corrected to guarantee a zero net force. The following diagram captures the class hierarchy and the data flow through the `Force::compute` method:

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Force {
        "-vector<unique_ptr<Potential>> potentials"
        -bool is_fcp
        -bool has_non_nep
        -string multiple_potentials_mode_
        +"parse_potential(param, box, N)"
        +"compute(box, pos, type, group, pe, f, virial)"
        +"set_hnemd_parameters(...)"
        +"set_multiple_potentials_mode(mode)"
    }

    class Potential {
        <<abstract>>
        +int N1, N2
        +double rc
        +int nep_model_type
        +int ilp_flag
        +"compute(box, type, pos, pe, f, virial)"*
        +"compute_ilp(box, type, pos, pe, f, virial, group)"
        #find_properties_many_body(...)
    }

    class LJ
    class Tersoff1989
    class Tersoff1988
    class Tersoff_mini
    class EAM
    class EAMAlloy
    class ADP
    class FCP
    class NEP
    class NEP_Charge
    class NEP_MULTIGPU
    class ILP_NEP
    class ILP_TERSOFF
    class ILP_TMD_SW
    class DP
    class NNAP

    Force --> Potential : owns 1..N via unique_ptr
    Potential <|-- LJ
    Potential <|-- Tersoff1989
    Potential <|-- Tersoff1988
    Potential <|-- Tersoff_mini
    Potential <|-- EAM
    Potential <|-- EAMAlloy
    Potential <|-- ADP
    Potential <|-- FCP
    Potential <|-- NEP
    Potential <|-- NEP_Charge
    Potential <|-- NEP_MULTIGPU
    Potential <|-- ILP_NEP
    Potential <|-- ILP_TERSOFF
    Potential <|-- ILP_TMD_SW
    Potential <|-- DP
    Potential <|-- NNAP
```

The `Force` class owns a `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Potential>>` named `potentials`, enabling polymorphic dispatch. Each concrete potential stores its own `Neighbor` object (except FCP, which bypasses neighbor lists entirely) and GPU-allocated parameter and scratch space. The `Potential` base class provides the shared `find_properties_many_body` kernel that reduces **partial pairwise forces** (the `f12` arrays) into per-atom forces and the 9-component virial tensor, eliminating code duplication across all many-body potentials.

Sources: [force.cuh](src/force/force.cuh#L63-L78), [force.cu](src/force/force.cu#L37-L68)

## The Force::compute Pipeline

When `Force::compute` is called each timestep, it executes the following sequence as a single GPU-side pipeline with no host-device round-trips between stages:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Apply PBC<br/>(gpu_apply_pbc)"] --> B["Initialize Properties<br/>force=0, pe=0, virial=0"]
    B --> C{Multiple Potentials<br/>Mode?}
    C -->|observe| D["Compute potentials[0]<br/>(single dispatch)"]
    C -->|average| E["Compute ALL potentials<br/>(accumulate) → Divide by count"]
    D --> F{HNEMD active?}
    E --> F
    F -->|yes| G["Add Driving Force<br/>(gpu_add_driving_force)"]
    F -->|no| H{Force correction<br/>needed?}
    G --> H
    H -->|yes: HNEMD or FCP| I["Sum total force →<br/>Subtract mean per atom<br/>(gpu_correct_force)"]
    H -->|no| J["Return forces,<br/>energies, virials"]
    I --> J
```

**PBC application** maps all atom positions back into the simulation box using the inverse box matrix stored in `box.cpu_h[9..17]`. This is skipped for FCP potentials since they operate on equilibrium displacement vectors rather than absolute positions. **Property initialization** zeros out the 3 force components, 1 potential energy, and 9 virial components per atom in a single kernel launch.

Sources: [force.cu](src/force/force.cu#L473-L560), [force.cu](src/force/force.cu#L327-L375)

## Potential Dispatch and Multiple Potential Support

The `parse_potential` method serves as a **factory function** that reads the first token from each potential file and constructs the appropriate `Potential` subclass. The complete dispatch table is:

| Potential Name String | Class | Category | Requires Neighbor List |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lj` | `LJ` | Empirical (pair) | Yes |
| `tersoff_1989` | `Tersoff1989` | Empirical (many-body) | Yes |
| `tersoff_1988` | `Tersoff1988` | Empirical (many-body) | Yes |
| `tersoff_mini` | `Tersoff_mini` | Empirical (many-body) | Yes |
| `eam_zhou_2004` | `EAM` | Empirical (many-body) | Yes |
| `eam_dai_2006` | `EAM` | Empirical (many-body) | Yes |
| `eam/alloy` | `EAMAlloy` | Empirical (many-body) | Yes |
| `adp` | `ADP` | Empirical (many-body) | Yes |
| `fcp` | `FCP` | Lattice dynamics | No |
| `nep3`, `nep4`, `nep5` (and variants) | `NEP` / `NEP_MULTIGPU` | Machine learning | Yes |
| `nep4_charge1/2/3` (and ZBL variants) | `NEP_Charge` | Machine learning (charged) | Yes |
| `nep_ilp` | `ILP_NEP` | Hybrid (ILP + NEP) | Yes (dual) |
| `tersoff_ilp` | `ILP_TERSOFF` | Hybrid (ILP + Tersoff) | Yes (dual) |
| `sw_ilp` | `ILP_TMD_SW` | Hybrid (ILP + SW) | Yes (dual) |
| `dp` | `DP` | Machine learning (DeepMD) | No (built-in) |
| `nnap` | `NNAP` | Machine learning (NN) | No (built-in) |

**Multiple potential support** is restricted to NEP potentials only — the `has_non_nep` flag tracks whether any non-NEP potential has been parsed, and the system raises an error if a second potential is added while `has_non_nep` is true. When multiple NEPs are active, the `multiple_potentials_mode_` string (set via `set_multiple_potentials_mode`) controls behavior:

- **`"observe"`** (default): Only `potentials[0]` is computed. The remaining potentials exist in memory but are not evaluated — useful for on-the-fly model comparison without performance penalty.
- **`"average"`**: All potentials are computed and their per-atom forces, energies, and virials are accumulated, then divided by the number of potentials. This enables model averaging for uncertainty quantification.

Sources: [force.cu](src/force/force.cu#L60-L190), [force.cu](src/force/force.cu#L497-L530)

## The Potential Base Class and Force Reduction

The `Potential` abstract base class defines the contract that every concrete potential must fulfill. Its key virtual methods are:

| Method | Signature | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `compute` (pure virtual) | `(Box&, type, pos, pe, force, virial)` | Standard force evaluation |
| `compute` (virtual, default empty) | `(temperature, Box&, type, pos, pe, force, virial)` | Temperature-dependent (NEP free energy) |
| `compute_ilp` (virtual, default empty) | `(Box&, type, pos, pe, force, virial, group)` | ILP-aware computation with group labels |

Each concrete potential implements `compute` by first building or refreshing its neighbor list, then launching GPU kernels that compute **partial pairwise forces** `f12[i]` — the force contribution from atom *i* toward its neighbor *j*, stored as `(f12x, f12y, f12z)` arrays indexed by `[neighbor_index * N + atom_index]`. The base class method `find_properties_many_body` then performs the reduction:

$$F_i = \sum_j (f_{ij} - f_{ji})$$
$$W_{i,\alpha\beta} = \sum_j r_{ij,\alpha} \cdot f_{ji,\beta}$$

This reduction is implemented in the `gpu_find_force_many_body` CUDA kernel, which iterates over each atom's neighbor list, looks up the reciprocal partial force `f21` via a neighbor-list offset search (linear scan for `double` precision, binary search for `float` precision), and accumulates per-atom force and virial components. The **9-component virial** is stored in a flat array with the mapping `{xx→0, yy→1, zz→2, xy→3, xz→4, yz→5, yx→6, zx→7, zy→8}`.

> [!TIP]
> The `float` precision variant of `find_properties_many_body` uses **binary search** to find the reciprocal neighbor offset, while the `double` variant uses a **linear scan**. This is because the `float` path is used by NEP potentials which have sorted neighbor lists, enabling O(log n) lookup versus O(n) for unsorted lists.

Sources: [potential.cuh](src/force/potential.cuh#L43-L80), [potential.cu](src/force/potential.cu#L32-L155)

## Concrete Potential Categories

### Pair Potentials: Lennard-Jones

The `LJ` class is the simplest concrete potential. It stores pre-computed parameters `s6e4[i][j]`, `s12e4[i][j]`, and `cutoff_square[i][j]` for each type pair in a `LJ_Para` struct (with `MAX_TYPE = 10` supported type pairs). These are the coefficients of the 12-6 Lennard-Jones expression after pulling out common factors for GPU efficiency. The `Neighbor` object manages the full neighbor list at the LJ cutoff radius.

### Many-Body Empirical Potentials: Tersoff and EAM

The **Tersoff** family (`Tersoff1989`, `Tersoff1988`, `Tersoff_mini`) follows a two-pass computation pattern: the first kernel computes bond-order values `b` and their derivatives `bp` for each pair, and the second kernel uses these to accumulate the partial forces `f12`. The `Tersoff1989_Data` struct stores `b`, `bp`, and `f12` arrays as `GPU_Vector<double>`, plus its own `Neighbor` object.

The **EAM** potentials (`EAM`, `EAMAlloy`) use a similar two-pass approach: the first pass accumulates electron density at each atom, and the second pass computes forces using the derivative of the embedding function `F'(ρ)` stored in `EAM_Data::Fp`. The `EAM2004Zhou` parameter struct carries all analytic embedding and pair function coefficients for the Zhou 2004 formulation, while `EAMAlloy` reads tabulated potential files in LAMMPS-compatible format. The **ADP** potential extends EAM with additional dipole and quadrupole terms.

### Lattice Dynamics: Force Constant Potential (FCP)

The `FCP` class is architecturally distinct — it does **not** use a neighbor list. Instead, it reads force constant matrices up to 6th order (`phi2` through `phi6`) and equilibrium positions `r0`, then computes forces as a Taylor expansion in atomic displacements. The `FCP_Data` struct stores multi-body index arrays (`i2/j2/index2` through `i6/j6/k6/l6/m6/n6/index6`) that encode which atoms participate in each force-constant term. Because FCP uses absolute displacements rather than neighbor-based interactions, the `Force` class skips PBC application when `is_fcp` is true, and always applies force correction to remove any residual net force.

### Machine Learning Potentials: NEP Family

The `NEP` class is the most complex concrete potential, supporting NEP3, NEP4, and NEP5 model versions with multiple model types (energy, dipole, polarizability, temperature-dependent free energy). Its architecture features:

- **Separate radial and angular neighbor lists** (`NN_radial`/`NL_radial` and `NN_angular`/`NL_angular`) with different cutoff radii, managed by the `Neighbor` object
- **Two box-size code paths**: `compute_small_box` for systems that fit in the expanded-box approach, and `compute_large_box` for larger systems — the small-box path uses an `ExpandedBox` struct with replicated cell data for reduced neighbor-list overhead
- **ANN parameters** stored as raw `float*` pointers in the `ANN` struct (`w0`, `b0`, `w1`, `b1`, `c` per element type), enabling direct GPU constant-memory access
- **Optional ZBL repulsion** for short-range correction, controlled by `ZBL::enabled` and `ZBL::flexibled` flags
- **Optional DFT-D3 dispersion** via the `dftd3` sub-object
- **Multi-GPU support** through the `NEP_MULTIGPU` subclass, which partitions the simulation domain along a user-specified direction (x, y, or z)

The `NEP_Charge` variant adds charge-equilibration logic on top of the base NEP framework. When multiple GPUs are detected and the potential name is a NEP variant, `parse_potential` automatically constructs `NEP_MULTIGPU` instead of `NEP`, unless `num_gpus == 1`.

### Hybrid ILP Potentials

The ILP (interlayer potential) hybrids combine a short-range intralayer potential with a long-range interlayer potential for layered materials. Three variants exist:

| Class | Intralayer Part | Interlayer Part | Target Materials |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ILP_NEP` | NEP (multiple models via map file) | ILP (Kolmogorov-Crespi type) | C, h-BN, TMD |
| `ILP_TERSOFF` | Tersoff 1988 | ILP (Kolmogorov-Crespi type) | C, h-BN |
| `ILP_TMD_SW` | Stillinger-Weber | ILP (Kolmogorov-Crespi type) | TMD |

These are the only potentials that override `compute_ilp` instead of (or in addition to) `compute`. The `compute_ilp` method receives a `std::vector<Group>` reference that provides **group labels** distinguishing different layers — the ILP interlayer force is only computed between atoms in different groups, while the intralayer potential acts within groups. Each ILP variant manages **two separate neighbor lists**: a standard neighbor list for the intralayer potential and a specialized ILP neighbor list (`ilp_NN`/`ilp_NL`) built with `find_neighbor_ilp` that respects the layer-group partitioning.

The `ILP_NEP` variant supports **multiple NEP models** mapped to different groups via a NEP map file, enabling different parameterizations for different layer types (e.g., MoS₂ with different NEP models for Mo-S and S-S interactions).

Sources: [lj.cuh](src/force/lj.cuh#L38-L50), [tersoff1989.cuh](src/force/tersoff1989.cuh#L33-L57), [eam.cuh](src/force/eam.cuh#L64-L83), [fcp.cuh](src/force/fcp.cuh#L33-L57), [nep.cuh](src/force/nep.cuh#L28-L185), [ilp_nep.cuh](src/force/ilp_nep.cuh#L140-L200), [ilp_tersoff.cuh](src/force/ilp_tersoff.cuh#L55-L96)

## HNEMD Driving Force and Force Correction

After all potentials have been evaluated, the `Force::compute` method applies two optional post-processing steps:

**HNEMD (Homogeneous Non-Equilibrium Molecular Dynamics)** adds an external driving force proportional to the per-atom virial tensor to induce a heat current. The `gpu_add_driving_force` kernel computes:

$$F_{i,\alpha}^{\text{drive}} = \sum_\beta f_{e,\beta} \cdot W_{i,\beta\alpha}$$

where $f_e$ is the driving force vector `hnemd_fe_[3]` and $W$ is the virial. Two HNEMD variants are supported: the standard method (`compute_hnemd_`) and the enhanced color conductivity method (`compute_hnemdec_`), which uses type-dependent coefficients stored in the `coefficient` GPU vector.

**Force correction** ensures the total force on the system is exactly zero, which is required for proper center-of-mass conservation. The `gpu_sum_force` kernel computes the total force vector using a parallel reduction, and `gpu_correct_force` subtracts the mean force `F_tot / N` from each atom. This correction is applied when: (1) HNEMD is active, or (2) the potential is FCP.
