The NEP framework extends beyond scalar potential energy surfaces into two powerful variant architectures: **qNEP** (charge-augmented NEP) introduces self-consistent atomic charges with electrostatic long-range interactions, and **TNEP** (tensorial NEP) predicts rank-1 and rank-2 tensorial properties—dipoles and polarizabilities—using the same descriptor infrastructure. Both variants inherit the core NEP descriptor computation and SNES optimization pipeline but diverge in their output heads, loss functions, and physical semantics, enabling NEP to serve not merely as an interatomic potential but as a unified framework for multi-property machine-learning potentials.

## Variant Taxonomy and Dispatch Architecture

The model variant is determined at construction time by the `Fitness` class, which inspects three independent configuration flags—`train_mode`, `charge_mode`, and `vdw`/`charge_vdw`—to instantiate the correct `Potential` subclass. The dispatch logic follows a strict priority chain:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Fitness Constructor] --> B{train_mode?}
    B -->|1 dipole / 2 polarizability| C[TNEP]
    B -->|0 potential| D{charge_vdw?}
    D -->|yes| E[NEP_Charge_VDW]
    D -->|no| F{charge_mode?}
    F -->|1 or 2| G[NEP_Charge<br/>qNEP]
    F -->|0| H{vdw?}
    H -->|yes| I[NEP_VDW]
    H -->|no| J[NEP<br/>standard]

    style C fill:#e8d5b7,stroke:#b8860b
    style E fill:#b7d5e8,stroke:#1e6fa0
    style G fill:#b7d5e8,stroke:#1e6fa0
    style I fill:#d5b7e8,stroke:#6a1e9a
    style J fill:#d5e8b7,stroke:#2d8a1e
```

All variants inherit from the abstract `Potential` base class, which declares a pure virtual `find_force` interface. This polymorphic design ensures the SNES optimizer interacts uniformly with any variant through `potential->find_force(...)`, while variant-specific computation kernels handle the distinct physics internally.

| Variant Class | Source File | `train_mode` | `charge_mode` | `vdw` | `charge_vdw` | Output Properties |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `NEP` | nep.cu | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | Energy, Force, Virial |
| `NEP_VDW` | nep_vdw.cu | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 | + Environment-dependent vdW |
| `NEP_Charge` | nep_charge.cu | 0 | 1 or 2 | 0 | 0 | + Electrostatics (qNEP) |
| `NEP_Charge_VDW` | nep_charge_vdw.cu | 0 | 1 or 2 | 0 | 1 | + Electrostatics + vdW |
| `TNEP` | tnep.cu | 1 or 2 | — | — | — | Dipole / Polarizability |

Sources: [fitness.cu](src/main_nep/fitness.cu#L130-L141), [potential.cuh](src/main_nep/potential.cuh#L27-L33)

## qNEP: Charge-Augmented NEP

### Physical Model

The qNEP model augments the standard NEP potential with **environment-dependent atomic charges** computed from the same descriptor vector via a separate ANN head. The total energy includes an electrostatic contribution evaluated using Ewald summation, split into real-space and reciprocal-space components. The atomic charge $q_i$ is predicted from the local descriptor $\mathbf{q}_i$ through a per-element single-hidden-layer ANN, identical in architecture to the energy-predicting ANN but with independent weights.

Two charge modes control which electrostatic contributions are included:

| `charge_mode` | Real-space | Reciprocal-space | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | — | — | Standard NEP (no charges) |
| 1 | ✓ | ✓ | Song et al. (2024b) — full Ewald |
| 2 | — | ✓ | Cheng (2025) — reciprocal only |

Mode 2 omits the real-space contribution, which is physically justified when the short-range NEP potential already implicitly captures the real-space electrostatic effects through its parametric flexibility. This reduces computational cost while maintaining accuracy for systems where the charge–dipole and charge–charge interactions at short range are absorbed into the short-range NEP parameters.

> [!TIP]
> When training a qNEP model, target charges are **not** required as training data. The charges emerge self-consistently from the descriptor–ANN mapping. However, you may optionally provide target Born effective charges (BEC), though this typically works reliably only for a single-phase system because the model assumes a constant high-frequency dielectric constant $\epsilon_\infty$ across the entire training dataset.

### Ewald Summation Infrastructure

The `NEP_Charge_Data` struct reveals the GPU-side Ewald summation data structures: reciprocal-space k-vectors (`kx`, `ky`, `kz`), structure factors (`S_real`, `S_imag`), and the reciprocal-space energy density (`G`, `D_real`). The `Charge_Para` struct controls the Ewald splitting parameter $\alpha = 0.5$ Å⁻¹ and the maximum k-point count (`num_kpoints_max = 50000`). The method `find_k1k2k3()` precomputes the reciprocal-space k-vector mesh, which remains fixed throughout training since it depends only on the simulation cell geometry.

### qNEP + van der Waals (NEP_Charge_VDW)

The `NEP_Charge_VDW` class combines charge electrostatics with environment-dependent van der Waals interactions. Its data struct extends `NEP_Charge_Data` with `C6`, `C6_derivative`, and `D_C6` GPU vectors for the dispersion coefficients, plus `G_vdw` and `G_vdw_virial` for the vdW reciprocal-space contribution and its virial. The `ParaMB` struct stores per-element `c6_ref_sqrt` reference dispersion coefficients, from which environment-dependent $C_6$ values are predicted via the ANN.

### Training Configuration

A minimal qNEP training input (`nep.in`) requires only the `charge_mode` keyword:

```
type         2 Te Pb
cutoff       8 4
charge_mode  2
generation   20000
```

The relevant loss-function weights for qNEP are `lambda_q` (total charge loss, default 0.1) and `lambda_z` (BEC loss, default 0.5). The `import_q_scaler` keyword allows reusing a pre-computed descriptor scaler from an existing `nep.txt` file rather than recomputing it, which is useful for fine-tuning workflows.

Sources: [nep_charge.cuh](src/main_nep/nep_charge.cuh#L37-L119), [nep_charge_vdw.cuh](src/main_nep/nep_charge_vdw.cuh#L37-L122), [charge_mode.rst](doc/nep/input_parameters/charge_mode.rst#L1-L29), [qnep_train/nep.in](examples/qnep_train/nep.in#L1-L5), [lambda_q.rst](doc/nep/input_parameters/lambda_q.rst#L1-L16), [lambda_z.rst](doc/nep/input_parameters/lambda_z.rst#L1-L16)

## TNEP: Tensorial Neuroevolution Potential

### Physical Model and Tensorial Outputs

The TNEP model repurposes the NEP descriptor infrastructure to predict **tensorial properties** rather than scalar potential energies. It supports two output modes selected by `train_mode`:

| `train_mode` | Property | Tensor Rank | Components | Physical Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Dipole moment $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ | 1 (vector) | 3 ($\mu_x, \mu_y, \mu_z$) | Electric dipole per structure |
| 2 | Polarizability $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ | 2 (symmetric tensor) | 6 ($\alpha_{xx}, \alpha_{yy}, \alpha_{zz}, \alpha_{xy}, \alpha_{yz}, \alpha_{zx}$) | Dielectric response |

TNEP is fundamentally an **observer model**: it does not replace the potential energy surface but runs alongside it, reading the same atomic positions and computing tensorial observables on-the-fly. In a GPUMD simulation, this is configured by specifying two `potential` lines in `run.in`—the PES model first, then the TNEP observer model second.

### Multi-Layer ANN Architecture

Unlike the standard NEP and qNEP which use a single-hidden-layer ANN, TNEP supports **up to two hidden layers** controlled by `num_hidden_layers` and `num_neurons2`. The `TNEP::ANN` struct stores `num_neurons1`, `num_neurons2`, and `num_hidden_layers`, and the parameter count `one_ann_no_bias` adjusts accordingly:

- **1 hidden layer**: `one_ann_no_bias = (dim + 2) × num_neurons1`
- **2 hidden layers**: `one_ann_no_bias = (dim + 1) × num_neurons1 + (num_neurons1 + 2) × num_neurons2`

For polarizability (`train_mode = 2`), a **second independent ANN** (`wb_pol`, `b_pol`) predicts the scalar part of the polarizability, while the first ANN predicts the tensorial part. This separation ensures the scalar trace and anisotropic components are learned with appropriate flexibility.

### Descriptor Computation and Per-Type Cutoffs

TNEP computes the same radial and angular descriptors as standard NEP, but supports **per-element cutoff distances** stored as arrays `rc_radial[NUM_ELEMENTS]` and `rc_angular[NUM_ELEMENTS]`. For a pair of atom types $t_1$ and $t_2$, the effective cutoff is the arithmetic mean: $r_c = (r_c^{t_1} + r_c^{t_2}) / 2$. This type-dependent cutoff scheme allows finer control over the descriptor's spatial sensitivity for chemically heterogeneous systems.

The `apply_ann` kernel dispatches between `apply_ann_one_layer` and `apply_ann_two_layers` based on `num_hidden_layers`, and for polarizability mode, a separate `apply_ann_pol` kernel handles the scalar ANN head followed by the tensorial ANN head, writing results into the `g_virial` buffer (repurposed for polarizability storage).

### Rotational Self-Consistency

A critical physical constraint on TNEP predictions is their correct transformation behavior under rotations. The test suite verifies:

- **Dipole** (rank-1): $\boldsymbol{\mu}' = R \boldsymbol{\mu}$ — the dipole vector rotates as a vector.
- **Polarizability** (rank-2): $\boldsymbol{\alpha}' = R \boldsymbol{\alpha} R^T$ — the polarizability tensor transforms via congruence.

The test constructs a Rodrigues rotation, applies it to both positions and velocities, and confirms that TNEP outputs transform correctly within a tolerance of `rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-5`. A subtle implementation detail: `dump_dipole` and `dump_polarizability` only write output after a full velocity-Verlet step, so the tests embed pre-rotated velocities directly into the `model.xyz` input to ensure exact rotational consistency without stochastic velocity initialization interference.

Sources: [tnep.cuh](src/main_nep/tnep.cuh#L30-L89), [tnep.cu](src/main_nep/tnep.cu#L23-L31), [tnep.cu](src/main_nep/tnep.cu#L200-L260), [test_io_tnep_commands.py](tests_pytest/test_io_tnep_commands.py#L1-L75), [test_tnep_invariances.py](tests_pytest/test_tnep_invariances.py#L1-L139)

## Comparative Architecture: qNEP vs TNEP

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Potential {
        <<abstract>>
        +find_force(para, parameters, dataset, calculate_q_scaler, deviceCount)
    }
    class NEP {
        -ParaMB paramb
        -ANN annmb
        -NEP_Data nep_data
    }
    class NEP_Charge {
        -ParaMB paramb
        -ANN annmb
        -NEP_Charge_Data nep_data
        -Charge_Para charge_para
        +find_k1k2k3()
    }
    class NEP_Charge_VDW {
        -ParaMB paramb
        -ANN annmb
        -NEP_Charge_VDW_Data nep_data
        -Charge_Para charge_para
        +find_k1k2k3()
    }
    class NEP_VDW {
        -ParaMB paramb
        -ANN annmb
        -NEP_VDW_Data nep_data
        -VDW_Para vdw_para
    }
    class TNEP {
        -ParaMB paramb
        -ANN annmb
        -TNEP_Data nep_data
    }

    Potential <|-- NEP
    Potential <|-- NEP_Charge
    Potential <|-- NEP_Charge_VDW
    Potential <|-- NEP_VDW
    Potential <|-- TNEP

    note for NEP_Charge "qNEP: charge_mode 1 or 2\nEwald k-space summation"
    note for TNEP "train_mode 1 (dipole) or 2 (polarizability)\nObserver model, 1-2 hidden layers"
```

| Dimension | qNEP | TNEP |
|---|---|---|
| **Purpose** | Augment PES with electrostatics | Predict dipole / polarizability observables |
| **Role in simulation** | Replaces standard NEP as the PES | Runs alongside a separate PES (observer) |
| **ANN output** | Atomic charge $q_i$ (scalar per atom) | Dipole vector or polarizability tensor per atom |
| **ANN layers** | 1 hidden layer | 1 or 2 hidden layers |
| **Long-range treatment** | Ewald summation (real + reciprocal or reciprocal only) | None (local descriptor → tensor) |
| **Extra loss terms** | `lambda_q` (charge), `lambda_z` (BEC) | Standard energy/force/virial adapted for tensors |
| **Training data** | No target charges needed; BEC optional | Dipole or polarizability reference data |
| **Per-type cutoffs** | Single cutoff (qNEP) or per-type (qNEP+vdW) | Per-type cutoffs always |
| **Key GPU data** | k-vectors, structure factors, $G$, $S$, $D$ | Standard descriptors + `sum_fxyz` |

> [!TIP]
> The `NEP_Charge_VDW` variant is the most feature-rich model, combining electrostatics, environment-dependent dispersion, and per-type cutoffs. When all three extensions (charge, vdW, per-type cutoff) are needed, use `charge_vdw 1` in `nep.in` rather than setting `charge_mode` and `vdw` independently—the combined class ensures consistent reciprocal-space treatment of both electrostatic and dispersion contributions.

Sources: [fitness.cu](src/main_nep/fitness.cu#L130-L141), [nep_charge.cuh](src/main_nep/nep_charge.cuh#L37-L119), [nep_charge_vdw.cuh](src/main_nep/nep_charge_vdw.cuh#L37-L122), [nep_vdw.cuh](src/main_nep/nep_vdw.cuh#L28-L118), [tnep.cuh](src/main_nep/tnep.cuh#L30-L89), [parameters.cuh](src/main_nep/parameters.cuh#L38-L95)

## Configuration Reference

The following `nep.in` keywords are specific to or particularly relevant for qNEP and TNEP variants:

| Keyword | Applies To | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `charge_mode` | qNEP | 0 | 0=off, 1=full Ewald, 2=reciprocal only |
| `charge_vdw` | qNEP+vdW | 0 | 1=enable combined charge-vdW model |
| `vdw` | NEP+vdW | 0 | 1=enable environment-dependent vdW |
| `lambda_q` | qNEP | 0.1 | Weight for total charge loss |
| `lambda_z` | qNEP | 0.5 | Weight for BEC loss |
| `import_q_scaler` | qNEP | false | Reuse scaler from existing `nep.txt` |
| `model_type` | TNEP | 0 | 0=potential, 1=dipole, 2=polarizability |
| `num_neurons2` | TNEP | — | Second hidden layer size (2-layer ANN) |

For deeper understanding of the base descriptor computation shared across all variants, see [NEP Model Architecture](8-nep-model-architecture). For the training pipeline that orchestrates SNES optimization across these variants, see [NEP Training Pipeline](9-nep-training-pipeline). For how TNEP observer models are deployed alongside NEP potentials in production simulations, see [Force and Potential System](5-force-and-potential-system).


# Empirical Potentials



GPUMD implements a suite of **classical empirical interatomic potentials** optimized for GPU execution, covering pairwise, many-body, and embedded-atom formalisms. These potentials serve as the backbone for molecular dynamics simulations of crystalline solids, alloys, and simple fluids. Each implementation inherits from the abstract `Potential` base class and follows a unified computation contract: accept box, type, and position data; produce per-atom potential energy, force, and virial tensors. The entire force evaluation pipeline — from neighbor list construction through kernel launch — executes on the GPU with single-precision arithmetic for accumulated quantities and double-precision for positional data where it matters most.

Sources: [potential.cuh](/src/force/potential.cuh#L1-L114), [force.cu](/src/force/force.cu#L1-L200)

## Architecture and Unified Interface

All potentials in GPUMD descend from the `Potential` abstract base class, which defines the core virtual `compute()` method and shared infrastructure for many-body force accumulation. The `Force` driver class parses the `potential` command from the run input file, instantiates the correct concrete potential class based on the first token in the potential file, and manages the lifecycle of one or more potential objects.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Potential {
        <<abstract>>
        +int N1, N2
        +double rc
        +int nep_model_type
        +int ilp_flag
        +compute(box, type, pos, pot, force, virial)*
        #find_properties_many_body(...)
    }
    class LJ {
        +LJ_Para lj_para
        +Neighbor neighbor
        +compute(...)
    }
    class Tersoff1989 {
        +Tersoff1989_Parameters ters0..2
        +Tersoff1989_Data data
        +Neighbor neighbor
        +compute(...)
    }
    class Tersoff1988 {
        +GPU_Vector ters
        +Tersoff1988_Data data
        +Neighbor neighbor
        +compute(...)
    }
    class Tersoff_mini {
        +Tersoff_mini_Para para
        +Tersoff_mini_Data data
        +Neighbor neighbor
        +compute(...)
    }
    class EAM {
        +EAM2004Zhou eam2004zhou
        +EAM2006Dai eam2006dai
        +EAM_Data eam_data
        +Neighbor neighbor
        +compute(...)
    }
    class EAMAlloy {
        +EAMAlloy_Data eam_data
        +Neighbor neighbor
        +compute(...)
    }
    class ADP {
        +ADP_Data adp_data
        +compute(...)
    }
    Potential <|-- LJ
    Potential <|-- Tersoff1989
    Potential <|-- Tersoff1988
    Potential <|-- Tersoff_mini
    Potential <|-- EAM
    Potential <|-- EAMAlloy
    Potential <|-- ADP
```

The `Force::parse_potential()` method reads the potential file, identifies the model by its first token (e.g., `lj`, `tersoff_1989`, `eam_zhou_2004`, `adp`), and constructs the appropriate subclass via `std::unique_ptr<Potential>`. Each concrete class carries its own `Neighbor` object for neighbor list management, pre-computed parameter structs transferred to GPU constant memory or texture cache, and working `GPU_Vector` arrays for intermediate quantities like bond orders and partial forces. The `Potential` base class also provides the protected `find_properties_many_body()` helper, which reduces per-neighbor partial force arrays (`f12x`, `f12y`, `f12z`) into final per-atom force and virial — a pattern shared by all many-body potentials.

Sources: [potential.cuh](/src/force/potential.cuh#L59-L100), [force.cu](/src/force/force.cu#L82-L155), [potential.cu](/src/force/potential.cu#L35-L100)

## Lennard-Jones (LJ)

The **Lennard-Jones** potential is the simplest pairwise model in GPUMD, implementing the standard 12-6 form:

$$V(r_{ij}) = 4\varepsilon\left[\left(\frac{\sigma}{r_{ij}}\right)^{12} - \left(\frac{\sigma}{r_{ij}}\right)^{6}\right]$$

The implementation supports up to **10 atom types** (configurable via `MAX_TYPE`), with full cross-interaction matrices for ε, σ, and cutoff. Parameters are pre-computed into GPU-friendly `float` arrays (`s6e4 = 4εσ⁶`, `s12e4 = 4εσ¹²`, `cutoff_square`) at initialization to minimize runtime computation. The CUDA kernel uses **single-precision accumulation** for forces and virials within the neighbor loop, with double-precision positions for distance calculation. The LJ kernel directly computes per-atom potential energy and virial within the same pass — unlike many-body potentials that require a separate reduction step. A default neighbor list capacity of 700 neighbors per atom is allocated.

**Potential file format** — The file begins with `lj` followed by the number of types and element symbols, then an N×N matrix of `epsilon sigma cutoff` triplets:

```
lj 1
Ar
10.0 3.4 10.0
```

For multi-element systems, off-diagonal entries define cross-interactions using Lorentz-Berthelot or explicitly specified mixing rules.

Sources: [lj.cuh](/src/force/lj.cuh#L1-L50), [lj.cu](/src/force/lj.cu#L30-L120)

## Tersoff Potentials

GPUMD provides **three Tersoff variants** covering the major formulations in the literature. All three share the same computational pattern: a two-pass kernel structure where the first pass computes bond order `b_ij` and its derivative `b'_ij` for all pairs, and the second pass accumulates partial forces `f12` which are then reduced to per-atom quantities via `find_properties_many_body()`.

### Tersoff-1989

The **Tersoff-1989** potential implements the two-element formulation from Tersoff's seminal paper on multicomponent systems. It supports **1 or 2 atom types** with explicit parameter sets for same-type interactions and a mixing rule (geometric mean with χ scaling) for cross-type interactions. The bond-order function takes the form:

$$b_{ij} = \left(1 + \beta^n \zeta_{ij}^n\right)^{-1/2n}, \quad \zeta_{ij} = \sum_{k \neq i,j} f_c(r_{ik})\, g(\theta_{ijk})\, \exp\!\left[\lambda^3(r_{ij}-r_{ik})^3\right]$$

The angular function uses $g(\theta) = 1 + c^2/d^2 - c^2/(d^2 + (h - \cos\theta)^2)$. Pre-computed constants include `c2`, `d2`, `one_plus_c2overd2`, `pi_factor`, and `minus_half_over_n` to avoid redundant operations in the kernel. The implementation stores three `Tersoff1989_Parameters` structs (`ters0`, `ters1`, `ters2`) for the two pure types and the mixed type respectively, with a neighbor capacity factor of 50.

Sources: [tersoff1989.cuh](/src/force/tersoff1989.cuh#L1-L57), [tersoff1989.cu](/src/force/tersoff1989.cu#L1-L120)

### Tersoff-1988

The **Tersoff-1988** variant supports **arbitrary multi-element** systems through a flat parameter array (`GPU_Vector<double> ters`) indexed by type pairs. Unlike the 1989 variant which hard-codes type dispatch in device functions, Tersoff-1988 uses a **cell-list neighbor construction** (with `cell_count`, `cell_count_sum`, `cell_contents` arrays) for improved scalability with large cutoffs or dense systems. The parameter structure is more general, allowing different parameter sets for each (type_i, type_j, type_k) triplet combination.

Sources: [tersoff1988.cuh](/src/force/tersoff1988.cuh#L1-L54)

### Tersoff-mini

The **Tersoff-mini** is a **simplified Tersoff** variant that reduces the parameter set to essential terms. It uses a compact `Tersoff_mini_Para` struct with parameter arrays of size 3 (for up to 3 type-pair combinations), storing `a`, `b`, `lambda`, `mu`, `beta`, `n`, `h`, `r1`, `r2` and their derived constants. This variant is useful when the full Tersoff parameterization is unnecessary, offering faster initialization and lower memory footprint while maintaining the same two-pass kernel structure.

Sources: [tersoff_mini.cuh](/src/force/tersoff_mini.cuh#L1-L65)

## Embedded Atom Method (EAM)

GPUMD implements **two EAM formalisms**: an analytical parameterization (Zhou 2004 and Dai 2006) and a tabulated format (eam/alloy) compatible with LAMMPS. EAM potentials model the energy as an embedding function of the local electron density plus a pairwise repulsion:

$$E_i = F(\bar{\rho}_i) + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{j \neq i} \phi(r_{ij}), \quad \bar{\rho}_i = \sum_{j \neq i} \rho(r_{ij})$$

### EAM Zhou 2004 / Dai 2006

The **analytical EAM** implementation supports up to **18 elements** (via `MAX_NUM_ELEMENTS_EAM`), using the Zhou 2004 parameterization for multi-component alloys. The `EAM2004Zhou` struct stores per-element parameters as `float` arrays for GPU efficiency: `re_inv`, `fe`, `rho_e_inv`, `alpha`, `beta`, `A`, `B`, `kappa`, `lambda`, plus embedding function coefficients `Fn0..Fn3`, `F0..F3`, `eta`, `Fe`. The Dai 2006 single-element parameterization uses a simpler `EAM2006Dai` struct with 10 scalar parameters. Both variants compute `F'(ρ)` as an intermediate per-atom quantity stored in `EAM_Data::Fp` during the density accumulation pass, which is then used in the force computation pass.

### EAM/alloy (Tabulated)

The **EAM/alloy** potential reads tabulated function data in the LAMMPS eam/alloy format, supporting arbitrary multi-element systems. The tabulated functions — embedding function `F(ρ)`, electron density `ρ(r)`, and pair potential `φ(r)` — are stored as `float4` arrays (`F_rho_g`, `rho_r_g`, `phi_r_g`) on the GPU, enabling coalesced memory access during spline interpolation. The implementation uses uniform grid spacing (`drho`, `dr`) for efficient index computation from continuous values. A configurable `max_neighbor` parameter (default 400, maximum 1024) controls neighbor list capacity and can be specified as an optional second argument to the `potential` command.

**Potential file format for eam/alloy:**

```
eam/alloy
<number_of_elements> <element_names...>
<nrho> <drho> <nr> <dr> <rc>
<tabulated F, rho, phi data>
```

Sources: [eam.cuh](/src/force/eam.cuh#L1-L83), [eam_alloy.cuh](/src/force/eam_alloy.cuh#L1-L58)

## Angular Dependent Potential (ADP)

The **ADP** potential extends EAM with **dipole (u)** and **quadrupole (w)** distortion terms that capture directional bonding, following Mishin et al. (Acta Mater. 53, 4029, 2005). The total energy per atom is:

$$E_i = F(\bar{\rho}_i) + \frac{1}{2}\sum_j \phi(r_{ij}) + \sum_{\alpha} \mu_i^{\alpha}\mu_j^{\alpha} u(r_{ij}) + \sum_{\alpha,\beta} \lambda_i^{\alpha\beta}\lambda_j^{\alpha\beta} w(r_{ij})$$

where μ and λ are per-atom dipole and quadrupole tensors accumulated from neighbors, analogous to the scalar electron density in standard EAM. The `ADP_Data` struct stores these per-atom tensors as `GPU_Vector<double>` arrays (`mu` with 3 components, `lambda` with 6 components following xx,yy,zz,yz,xz,xy ordering) alongside the standard EAM quantities (`Fp`, embedding derivative). The implementation uses **cubic spline interpolation** with pre-computed spline coefficients (`a`, `b`, `c`, `d` arrays) for all five tabulated functions (F, ρ, φ, u, w), uploaded to the GPU as separate `GPU_Vector<double>` arrays. A `pair_index_map_g` lookup table maps (type_i, type_j) pairs to their corresponding function table indices for O(1) access.

Sources: [adp.cuh](/src/force/adp.cuh#L1-L98)

## Supported Potentials Summary

| Potential | Keyword | Types | Formalism | Key Features |
|-----------|---------|-------|-----------|-------------|
| Lennard-Jones | `lj` | 1–10 | Pairwise | 12-6 form, cross-interaction matrix |
| Tersoff-1989 | `tersoff_1989` | 1–2 | Many-body (bond-order) | Two-element with χ mixing rule |
| Tersoff-1988 | `tersoff_1988` | Multi | Many-body (bond-order) | Cell-list neighbor, general multi-element |
| Tersoff-mini | `tersoff_mini` | Multi | Many-body (simplified) | Reduced parameter set |
| EAM Zhou 2004 | `eam_zhou_2004` | 1–18 | Embedded-atom | Analytical, up to 18 elements |
| EAM Dai 2006 | `eam_dai_2006` | 1 | Embedded-atom | Analytical, single element |
| EAM/alloy | `eam/alloy` | Multi | Embedded-atom (tabulated) | LAMMPS-compatible format, spline interp |
| ADP | `adp` | Multi | Angular-dependent | Dipole + quadrupole terms, spline interp |

Sources: [force.cu](/src/force/force.cu#L97-L155)

## GPU Computation Patterns

All empirical potentials in GPUMD share a common computational architecture optimized for GPU throughput. The execution pattern follows two distinct strategies depending on whether the potential is pairwise or many-body.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Force::compute called] --> B[Initialize force/virial/PE to zero]
    B --> C{Potential type?}
    C -->|Pairwise LJ| D[Single-pass kernel]
    D --> D1[Loop over neighbors per atom]
    D1 --> D2[Compute pair energy + force inline]
    D2 --> D3[Accumulate per-atom force, virial, PE]
    C -->|Many-body Tersoff/EAM/ADP| E[Two-pass kernel]
    E --> F[Pass 1: Compute intermediate quantities]
    F --> F1[Bond orders b_ij / electron density ρ_i]
    F1 --> G[Pass 2: Compute partial forces f12]
    G --> G1[Loop over neighbor pairs + triplets]
    G1 --> H[find_properties_many_body reduction]
    H --> H1[Reduce f12 arrays to per-atom force + virial]
    D3 --> I[Apply HNEMD driving force if active]
    H1 --> I
    I --> J[Correct total force to zero sum]
```

**Pairwise potentials** (LJ) use a **single-pass kernel**: each atom iterates over its neighbors, computes pair energy and force directly, and accumulates results into per-atom arrays. The factor of 0.5 in the energy term accounts for double-counting, while forces are computed as `f12x - f21x` using Newton's third law with the half-pair formalism.

**Many-body potentials** (Tersoff, EAM, ADP) require a **two-pass structure**: the first pass computes environment-dependent intermediate quantities (bond orders for Tersoff, electron density for EAM, density tensors for ADP), and the second pass uses these intermediates to compute partial force arrays `f12x/y/z`. The final reduction from partial forces to per-atom forces and virials is handled by the shared `Potential::find_properties_many_body()` kernel, which iterates over each atom's neighbors, applies the minimum image convention, and accumulates both the net force vector and the 9-component virial tensor.

> [!TIP]
> All empirical potentials use **single-precision (float)** accumulation for forces and virials within GPU kernels, while positions remain in **double-precision**. This mixed-precision strategy provides ~2× throughput improvement on GPU hardware while maintaining sufficient accuracy for MD simulations. The `find_properties_many_body` helper has overloads for both `float*` and `double*` f12 arrays to support this pattern.

Sources: [potential.cu](/src/force/potential.cu#L35-L100), [lj.cu](/src/force/lj.cu#L100-L190), [force.cu](/src/force/force.cu#L260-L340)

## Potential File Format and Initialization

Each empirical potential is specified in the GPUMD run input via the `potential` command, which takes the path to a potential parameter file. The first line of this file contains the **potential keyword** that determines which class is instantiated. The `Force::parse_potential()` method reads this keyword, opens the file, and dispatches to the appropriate constructor:

```
# In run.in:
potential /path/to/potential.txt
```

For potentials requiring additional files (e.g., hybrid potentials combining an intralayer model with an interlayer potential), a second parameter specifies the companion file:

```
# EAM/alloy with custom neighbor capacity:
potential /path/to/eam_file.txt 500

# Hybrid Tersoff+ILP (covered in Hybrid Potentials page):
potential /path/to/ilp.txt /path/to/tersoff.txt
```

The initialization sequence for each potential follows a consistent pattern: (1) read and validate the keyword and element count, (2) parse element-specific parameters into pre-computed constants, (3) determine the global cutoff `rc` from the largest interaction range, and (4) initialize the `Neighbor` object with this cutoff and an estimated neighbor capacity. The `Neighbor::initialize()` call pre-allocates GPU memory for the neighbor list arrays based on the cutoff and a per-atom neighbor estimate that varies by potential type (700 for LJ, 50×N for Tersoff-1989).

Sources: [force.cu](/src/force/force.cu#L82-L155), [lj.cu](/src/force/lj.cu#L35-L60), [tersoff1989.cu](/src/force/tersoff1989.cu#L30-L100)

## Available Potential Parameter Files

The `potentials/` directory in the repository provides pre-validated parameter files for common materials:

| Directory | Contents | Potential Type |
|-----------|----------|---------------|
| `potentials/lj/` | Ar (10Å, 20Å cutoffs) | LJ |
| `potentials/tersoff/` | Si, C, Ge, BN, SiC, SiGe, GaN, SiO, Sn, BNC (17 files) | Tersoff-1989 |
| `potentials/eam/` | Cu (Zhou 2004, Dai 2006), CuNi alloy, 18-element Zhou set | EAM |
| `potentials/adp/` | AlCu, CuTa, Ta, U_Mo | ADP |

These files serve as both reference examples and ready-to-use inputs. The Tersoff directory is particularly rich, covering semiconductors (Si with Erhart, Fan, and original Tersoff parameterizations), carbon allotropes (graphene with Lindsay 2010 and modified variants), compound semiconductors (BN, SiC, GaN), and novel materials (Sn with Cherukara 2016, Ge with Dong 2021).

Sources: [potentials/](/potentials)

## Relationship to Other Potential Types

Empirical potentials form one pillar of GPUMD's three-category potential system. The **NEP (Neuroevolution Potential)** family — covered in [NEP Model Architecture](8-nep-model-architecture) — provides machine-learned potentials with superior accuracy and transferability. The **hybrid potentials** — covered in [Hybrid and Composite Potentials](12-hybrid-and-composite-potentials) — combine an intralayer empirical potential (Tersoff, SW, or NEP) with an interlayer potential (ILP) for layered materials. The force computation infrastructure enforces a key constraint: **multiple potentials can only be used simultaneously if all are NEP-type** (as checked by `has_non_nep` flag in `Force::parse_potential()`), since the multiple-potential averaging/observation mode relies on NEP's consistent per-atom energy decomposition.

> [!TIP]
> When choosing between empirical potentials for a new system, prefer **EAM/alloy** for metals (best balance of accuracy and performance), **Tersoff-1989** for covalent semiconductors with 1–2 elements, and **Tersoff-1988** for multi-element covalent systems. For layered materials like graphene or MoS₂, use the hybrid potentials from [Hybrid and Composite Potentials](12-hybrid-and-composite-potentials) rather than a standalone Tersoff.

Sources: [force.cu](/src/force/force.cu#L155-L170)

## Next Steps

- **[Hybrid and Composite Potentials](12-hybrid-and-composite-potentials)** — Learn how empirical potentials combine with interlayer potentials for layered materials
- **[Force and Potential System](5-force-and-potential-system)** — Understand the full force computation pipeline including neighbor lists and HNEMD
- **[CUDA Kernel Design](13-cuda-kernel-design)** — Dive into the GPU kernel optimization strategies used across all potentials

# Hybrid and Composite Potentials



GPUMD implements three **hybrid potential models** that decompose interatomic interactions into **intralayer** (within a single 2D layer) and **interlayer** (between separate layers) contributions. Each hybrid pairs a distinct intralayer potential with the shared **Interlayer Potential (ILP)** formalism, enabling accurate simulation of van der Waals heterostructures — systems where covalent bonding within layers coexists with weak dispersion forces between layers. This architectural separation is both physically motivated and computationally advantageous: the intralayer term operates on a short-range neighbor list while the ILP term requires a much larger cutoff (typically ~16 Å), and the two computations are dispatched through distinct GPU kernel pathways.

## Architectural Overview

All three hybrid potentials inherit from the abstract `Potential` base class and expose a `compute_ilp()` virtual method that accepts group information — the mechanism by which atoms are partitioned into layers and sublayers. The `Force` driver class detects the `ilp_flag` member at runtime and routes computation through `compute_ilp()` rather than the standard `compute()` interface.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Potential {
        <<abstract>>
        +int N1, N2
        +double rc
        +int nep_model_type
        +int ilp_flag
        +"compute(box, type, pos, pot, force, virial)*"
        +"compute_ilp(box, type, pos, pot, force, virial, group)"
    }
    
    class ILP_NEP {
        +ILP_Para ilp_para
        +ILP_Data ilp_data
        +vector~ParaMB~ parambs
        +vector~ANN~ annmbs
        +GPU_Vector~int~ nep_map
        +GPU_Vector~int~ type_map
        +"compute_ilp()"
    }
    
    class ILP_TERSOFF {
        +ILP_CBN_Para ilp_para
        +ILP_CBN_Data ilp_data
        +Tersoff1988_Data tersoff_data
        +int ilp_group_method
        +"compute_ilp()"
    }
    
    class ILP_TMD_SW {
        +ILP_TMD_Para ilp_para
        +ILP_TMD_Data ilp_data
        +SW2_Para sw2_para
        +SW2_Data sw2_data
        +"compute_ilp()"
    }
    
    Potential <|-- ILP_NEP : inherits
    Potential <|-- ILP_TERSOFF : inherits
    Potential <|-- ILP_TMD_SW : inherits
```

The dispatch logic in `Force::compute()` inspects `potentials[0]->ilp_flag`: when set to `1`, the call routes to `compute_ilp()` with the group vector, enabling layer-aware force evaluation. This is a critical architectural branch — standard potentials never require group information, but hybrid ILP potentials depend on it to distinguish intra- from inter-layer atom pairs.

Sources: [force.cu](src/force/force.cu#L499-L522), [potential.cuh](src/force/potential.cuh#L40-L62)

## The Shared Interlayer Potential (ILP)

All three hybrids share the identical ILP mathematical formulation from Ouyang et al. (2018, 2020). The ILP site potential is:

**U_i^ILP = Tap(r_ij) × [U^att(r_ij) + U^rep(r_ij, n_i, n_j)]**

The **taper function** `Tap(r_ij)` provides a smooth cutoff with a 7th-order polynomial ensuring C² continuity. The **attractive term** captures van der Waals dispersion via a C₆/r⁶ dependence modulated by a Fermi-like switching function. The **repulsive term** encodes Pauli exclusion with anisotropic dependence on the normal vectors **n_i**, **n_j** of each layer — this anisotropy is what distinguishes ILP from isotropic Lennard-Jones–type models and is essential for capturing the orientation-dependent corrugation of interlayer adhesion.

The lateral distances ρ_ij and ρ_ji are computed by projecting out the normal component, yielding:

**ρ²_ij = r²_ij − (r_ij · n_i)²**

This projection makes the repulsion sensitive to the local registry (AA vs. AB stacking), a physical effect that purely distance-based potentials cannot reproduce.

Sources: [nep_ilp.rst](doc/potentials/nep_ilp.rst#L25-L65), [sw_ilp.rst](doc/potentials/sw_ilp.rst#L22-L65), [tersoff_ilp.rst](doc/potentials/tersoff_ilp.rst#L22-L65)

## Hybrid Potential Catalog

| Hybrid | Intralayer Term | Interlayer Term | Supported Materials | Files Required | `run.in` Syntax |
|--------|----------------|-----------------|---------------------|----------------|-----------------|
| **NEP+ILP** | NEP (NEP3 or NEP4) | ILP | Graphene, h-BN, TMDs (homo- & heterostructures) | ILP file + NEP map file | `potential <ilp> <nep_map>` |
| **Tersoff+ILP** | Tersoff (1988) | ILP | Graphene, h-BN (homo- & heterostructures) | ILP file + Tersoff file | `potential <ilp> <tersoff>` |
| **SW+ILP** | Modified Stillinger-Weber | ILP | TMD homostructures (MX₂) | ILP file + SW file | `potential <ilp> <sw>` |

### NEP+ILP — Machine-Learning Intralayer

The NEP+ILP hybrid is the most flexible variant, pairing the **Neuroevolution Potential** for intralayer interactions with ILP for interlayer coupling. Its distinguishing capability is the **NEP mapping file**, which assigns different NEP models to different layer groups — enabling heterostructures where, for example, an h-BN layer uses one NEP and a MoS₂ layer uses another.

The class `ILP_NEP` maintains vectors of `ParaMB` and `ANN` structures — one per NEP model — along with GPU-resident `nep_map` and `type_map` arrays that route each atom to its correct parameter set at kernel execution time. This multi-NEP architecture is unique among the three hybrids.

**ILP file format** (`nep_ilp`):
```
nep_ilp <num_types> <element_list>
<group_method_layers> <group_method_sublayers>
beta alpha delta epsilon C d sR reff C6 S rcut1 rcut2
```

**NEP mapping file format**:
```
<group_method_layers> <num_nep_files> <nep_file_0> <nep_file_1> ...
<num_groups>
<NEP_id for group_0>
<NEP_id for group_1>
...
```

The `group_method_sublayers` field is critical for TMDs: a single MoS₂ monolayer contains three sublayers (Mo + 2S), and the ILP normal vector calculation must know which atoms belong to the same sublayer to correctly orient **n_i**. For graphene/h-BN systems where each monolayer is a single sublayer, this value equals the layer group method.

Sources: [ilp_nep.cuh](src/force/ilp_nep.cuh#L96-L215), [nep_ilp.rst](doc/potentials/nep_ilp.rst#L68-L140)

### Tersoff+ILP — Empirical Intralayer for Carbon/BN

The Tersoff+ILP hybrid restricts its domain to graphene and h-BN systems, where the well-parameterized Tersoff (1988) potential provides reliable intralayer forces. The class `ILP_TERSOFF` composes an `ILP_CBN_Para` struct (ILP parameters with `MAX_TYPE_ILP_TERSOFF = 3` for C, B, N) with a `Tersoff1988_Data` struct for the intralayer component.

Only **one group method** is required (for layers), since graphene and h-BN monolayers each constitute a single sublayer — the sublayer concept is unnecessary here.

**ILP file format** (`tersoff_ilp`):
```
tersoff_ilp <num_types> <element_list>
<group_method_layers>
beta alpha delta epsilon C d sR reff C6 S rcut1 rcut2
```

The Tersoff potential file uses the standard Tersoff (1988) parameter format with parameters `A, B, λ, μ, β, n, c, d, h, R, S, m, α, γ` for each triplet type.

Sources: [ilp_tersoff.cuh](src/force/ilp_tersoff.cuh#L30-L96), [tersoff_ilp.rst](doc/potentials/tersoff_ilp.rst#L68-L127)

### SW+ILP — Empirical Intralayer for TMDs

The SW+ILP hybrid targets **transition metal dichalcogenide homostructures** (MoS₂, MoSe₂, WSe₂, etc.). It pairs a modified Stillinger-Weber potential — with a specialized cutoff function `f_C(δ)` that excludes unphysical angle types in TMD structures — with ILP for interlayer coupling. The modification uses thresholds δ₁ = 0.25 and δ₂ = 0.35, defined as compile-time constants in `ilp_tmd_sw.cuh`.

The class `ILP_TMD_SW` composes `ILP_TMD_Para` (with `MAX_TYPE_ILP_TMD_SW = 4` for Mo, S, Se, Te variants) with `SW2_Para` and `SW2_Data` for the intralayer SW component. Two group methods are mandatory: one for layers, one for sublayers (since each TMD monolayer contains three sublayers).

**ILP file format** (`sw_ilp`):
```
sw_ilp 2 M X
beta_MM alpha_MM delta_MM epsilon_MM C_MM d_MM sR_MM reff_MM C6_MM S_MM rcut1_MM rcut2_MM
beta_MX alpha_MX ... (cross terms)
beta_XX alpha_XX ... (X-X terms)
```

The SW file contains two-body parameters (`A, B, a, σ, γ` for each pair) and three-body parameters (`λ, cos0` for each triplet), with the element order matching the ILP file.

> [!TIP]
> The SW+ILP hybrid is restricted to **homostructures only** — all layers must be the same TMD material. For TMD heterostructures, use NEP+ILP with separate NEP models per layer.

Sources: [ilp_tmd_sw.cuh](src/force/ilp_tmd_sw.cuh#L30-L116), [sw_ilp.rst](doc/potentials/sw_ilp.rst#L68-L131)

## Layer Identification via Group Methods

All hybrid potentials require **group methods** defined in `model.xyz` to partition atoms into layers (and optionally sublayers). This is the mechanism that enables the ILP to distinguish intralayer neighbor pairs (same group) from interlayer pairs (different groups). The group method indices specified in the potential files must match those in `model.xyz`.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[model.xyz with group_methods] --> B{Hybrid Type?}
    B -->|NEP+ILP| C[Layer group + Sublayer group]
    B -->|Tersoff+ILP| D[Layer group only]
    B -->|SW+ILP| E[Layer group + Sublayer group]
    C --> F[ILP: uses both groups for normal vectors]
    D --> G[ILP: uses layer group; single sublayer assumed]
    E --> H[ILP: uses both groups for normal vectors]
    F --> I[NEP: mapping file assigns NEP model per layer]
    G --> J[Tersoff: single intralayer potential for all layers]
    H --> K[SW: single intralayer potential for all layers]
```

**Layer group method**: Atoms in the same 2D material layer share the same `group_id`. For a bilayer graphene system, atoms in layer 1 have `group_id = 0` and atoms in layer 2 have `group_id = 1`.

**Sublayer group method**: Atoms in the same atomic plane within a single layer share the same `group_id`. For MoS₂, the Mo plane is one sublayer and each S plane is a separate sublayer, yielding three sublayers per monolayer. For graphene, each monolayer is a single sublayer, so the sublayer group method equals the layer group method.

Sources: [nep_ilp.rst](doc/potentials/nep_ilp.rst#L90-L120), [tersoff_ilp.rst](doc/potentials/tersoff_ilp.rst#L90-L110), [sw_ilp.rst](doc/potentials/sw_ilp.rst#L75-L100)

## ILP Parameter Specification

The ILP parameters are pair-wise and follow a consistent format across all three hybrids. Each line specifies 12 parameters for one atom type pair:

| Parameter | Symbol | Description |
|-----------|--------|-------------|
| `beta` | β | Equilibrium interlayer distance (z₀) |
| `alpha` | α | Exponential decay rate in repulsive term |
| `delta` | δ | Controls width in repulsive exponent denominator |
| `epsilon` | ε | Well depth / energy scale |
| `C` | C | Additional repulsive coefficient |
| `d` | d | Fermi function steepness for attractive term |
| `sR` | S_R | Scaling factor for effective distance |
| `reff` | r_eff | Effective interlayer distance |
| `C6` | C₆ | Dispersion coefficient |
| `S` | S | Scale factor |
| `rcut1` | — | Cutoff for normal vector calculation (~3–4 Å) |
| `rcut2` | — | Cutoff for ILP interactions (typically 16 Å) |

For an N-element system, the ILP file contains N² parameter lines covering all type pairs. The `rcut2` value (typically 16 Å) defines the ILP neighbor list radius — substantially larger than intralayer cutoffs, requiring a dedicated neighbor list construction within each hybrid potential class.

Sources: [nep_ilp.rst](doc/potentials/nep_ilp.rst#L102-L112), [ilp_nep.cuh](src/force/ilp_nep.cuh#L73-L88)

## GPU Data Layout and Constants

Each hybrid potential class defines compile-time constants that bound GPU memory allocation for the ILP neighbor list. These reflect the structural differences between carbon/BN materials and TMDs:

| Constant | C/BN Value | TMD Value | Purpose |
|----------|-----------|-----------|---------|
| `MAX_TYPE_ILP_*` | 3 | 4–7 | Maximum atom types |
| `CUDA_MAX_NL_ILP_*` | 1024–2048 | 2048 | Max interlayer neighbors per atom |
| `MAX_ILP_NEIGHBOR_*` | 3 | 6 | Neighbors for normal vector calculation |
| `MAX_BIG_ILP_NEIGHBOR_*` | 128 | 128 | Extended neighbor buffer |

The `MAX_ILP_NEIGHBOR` difference (3 vs. 6) is physically meaningful: graphene's sp² bonding gives each atom 3 nearest in-plane neighbors for normal vector determination, while TMDs have 6 nearest neighbors in the chalcogen sublattice. These constants are used to size shared memory and loop bounds in CUDA kernels.

> [!TIP]
> The ILP neighbor list is constructed independently from the intralayer neighbor list because its cutoff (16 Å) is much larger. Each hybrid class builds this list using a cell-list approach stored in `ILP_Data::cell_count`, `cell_count_sum`, and `cell_contents`.

Sources: [ilp_nep.cuh](src/force/ilp_nep.cuh#L34-L42), [ilp_tersoff.cuh](src/force/ilp_tersoff.cuh#L30-L36), [ilp_tmd_sw.cuh](src/force/ilp_tmd_sw.cuh#L30-L38)

## Potential Dispatch and Multiple Potentials

The `Force::parse_potential()` method identifies hybrid potentials by reading the first token of the potential file:

- `nep_ilp` → constructs `ILP_NEP(file_ilp, file_nep_map, num_types, N)`
- `tersoff_ilp` → constructs `ILP_TERSOFF(file_ilp, file_tersoff, num_types, N)`
- `sw_ilp` → constructs `ILP_TMD_SW(file_ilp, file_sw, num_types, N)`

Each hybrid requires exactly **two file parameters** in the `potential` command. The first file is always the ILP parameter file; the second is either a NEP mapping file (for NEP+ILP) or an intralayer potential file (for Tersoff+ILP and SW+ILP).

GPUMD also supports **multiple independent potentials** via repeated `potential` commands, but this mode is restricted to NEP-only combinations. When `potentials.size() > 1` and any non-NEP potential is present, the parser raises an error. Hybrid ILP potentials therefore cannot be combined with additional potentials — they must stand alone.

Sources: [force.cu](src/force/force.cu#L156-L205), [force.cu](src/force/force.cu#L206-L218)

## NEP+ILP Example: Bilayer Graphene

Given three files — `C.ilp` (ILP parameters), `C.nep` (NEP3 potential), and `map.nep` (NEP mapping):

**`run.in`:**
```
potential C.ilp map.nep
```

**`C.ilp`:**
```
nep_ilp 1 C
0 0
beta_CC alpha_CC delta_CC epsilon_CC C_CC d_CC sR_CC reff_CC C6_CC S_CC rcut1_CC rcut2_CC
```

**`map.nep`:**
```
0 1 C.nep
2
0
0
```

The `0 0` in `C.ilp` specifies group_method 0 for both layers and sublayers (graphene has one sublayer per layer). In `map.nep`, the first `0` is the layer group method, `1` is the number of NEP files, `2` is the number of groups, and the final two `0`s map both groups to `NEP_0` (C.nep).

Sources: [nep_ilp.rst](doc/potentials/nep_ilp.rst#L142-L175), [hybrid_nep_ilp](potentials/hybrid_nep_ilp)

## NEP+ILP Example: h-BN / MoS₂ Heterostructure

**`BNMoS.ilp`:**
```
nep_ilp 4 B N Mo S
0 1
beta_BB alpha_BB ... rcut2_BB
beta_BN alpha_BN ... rcut2_BN
... (16 pair lines total for 4 elements)
```

**`map.nep`:**
```
0 2 BN.nep MoS.nep
2
1
0
```

Group 0 (MoS₂, `group_id = 0`) maps to `NEP_1` (MoS.nep), and group 1 (h-BN, `group_id = 1`) maps to `NEP_0` (BN.nep). The sublayer group method `1` distinguishes Mo, S-top, and S-bottom planes for normal vector computation.

Sources: [nep_ilp.rst](doc/potentials/nep_ilp.rst#L178-L209), [hybrid_nep_ilp](potentials/hybrid_nep_ilp)

## Design Rationale and Comparison

| Aspect | NEP+ILP | Tersoff+ILP | SW+ILP |
|--------|---------|-------------|--------|
| **Intralayer accuracy** | High (ML-fitted) | Moderate (empirical) | Moderate (empirical) |
| **Parameter effort** | Requires NEP training | Uses published parameters | Uses published parameters |
| **Heterostructure support** | ✅ Different NEP per layer | ✅ Different Tersoff per type | ❌ Homostructures only |
| **Material scope** | Broad (C, BN, TMDs) | Narrow (C, BN only) | Narrow (TMDs only) |
| **Group methods needed** | 2 (layers + sublayers) | 1 (layers) | 2 (layers + sublayers) |
| **Files in `potential` command** | 2 (ILP + NEP map) | 2 (ILP + Tersoff) | 2 (ILP + SW) |
| **ILP neighbor constant** | `MAX_ILP_NEIGHBOR`: 3 or 6 | `MAX_ILP_NEIGHBOR`: 3 | `MAX_ILP_NEIGHBOR`: 6 |

The NEP+ILP hybrid is the recommended choice for production simulations requiring high accuracy, particularly for heterostructures with dissimilar materials. Tersoff+ILP and SW+ILP serve as lightweight alternatives where well-tested empirical parameters exist and training data for NEP is unavailable.

Sources: [ilp_nep.cuh](src/force/ilp_nep.cuh#L34-L42), [ilp_tersoff.cuh](src/force/ilp_tersoff.cuh#L30-L36), [ilp_tmd_sw.cuh](src/force/ilp_tmd_sw.cuh#L30-L38)

## Suggested Reading

For the mathematical foundations of individual intralayer potentials, see [Empirical Potentials](11-empirical-potentials). For the NEP model architecture used in the NEP+ILP hybrid, see [NEP Model Architecture](8-nep-model-architecture). For details on how the force computation pipeline dispatches to these hybrids, see [Force and Potential System](5-force-and-potential-system).

# CUDA Kernel Design



GPUMD's computational engine is built on a carefully layered CUDA kernel architecture that maps molecular dynamics workloads directly onto GPU hardware with minimal abstraction overhead. Every force potential — from simple pairwise LJ to the multi-stage Neuroevolution Potential (NEP) — is expressed as a self-contained GPU kernel following a unified design philosophy: **one thread per atom**, register-heavy accumulation, and explicit multi-step decomposition for many-body interactions. This page dissects the kernel design patterns, execution strategies, and portability abstractions that make GPUMD's GPU acceleration both high-performance and maintainable.

## Kernel Launch Architecture

All force-computation kernels in GPUMD follow a consistent **one-thread-per-atom** mapping. Each CUDA thread is assigned a single atom index and iterates over that atom's neighbor list to accumulate contributions to force, potential energy, and virial stress. The thread-to-atom mapping is computed as:

```
int n1 = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x + N1;
```

where `N1` and `N2` define the active atom range `[N1, N2)`, enabling partial-domain execution for multi-GPU decomposition. The grid size is derived directly from the atom count and block size:

```
int grid_size = (N2 - N1 - 1) / BLOCK_SIZE_FORCE + 1;
```

Each potential selects its own **optimal block size** via a compile-time constant, tuned empirically for the kernel's register pressure and occupancy characteristics:

| Potential | Block Size | Rationale |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| LJ | 128 | Low register pressure; pairwise-only kernel |
| Tersoff-1989 | 64 | Higher register usage from bond-order precomputation |
| NEP | Varies | Descriptor dimension drives register pressure |

The kernel launch wrapper follows an identical pattern across all potentials — neighbor list construction, then kernel dispatch with `GPU_CHECK_KERNEL` error verification:

```cpp
gpu_find_force<<<grid_size, BLOCK_SIZE_FORCE>>>(
    lj_para, number_of_atoms, N1, N2, box,
    neighbor.NN.data(), neighbor.NL.data(), type.data(),
    position_per_atom.data(), position_per_atom.data() + number_of_atoms,
    position_per_atom.data() + number_of_atoms * 2,
    force_per_atom.data(), force_per_atom.data() + number_of_atoms,
    force_per_atom.data() + 2 * number_of_atoms,
    virial_per_atom.data(), potential_per_atom.data());
GPU_CHECK_KERNEL
```

Sources: [lj.cu](/src/force/lj.cu#L27-L28), [lj.cu](/src/force/lj.cu#L77-L95), [lj.cu](/src/force/lj.cu#L192-L219), [tersoff1989.cu](/src/force/tersoff1989.cu#L29-L29), [tersoff1989.cu](/src/force/tersoff1989.cu#L517-L518)

## Single-Step Kernel Pattern: Pair Potentials

Pairwise potentials (LJ, EAM) use a **single-kernel** design because force computation for atom *i* depends only on pairwise interactions with neighbors — no intermediate data structure is needed between neighbors. The LJ kernel exemplifies this pattern with its characteristic register accumulation strategy:

```cpp
static __global__ void gpu_find_force(
  LJ_Para lj, const int number_of_particles, const int N1, const int N2,
  const Box box, const int* g_neighbor_number, const int* g_neighbor_list,
  const int* g_type, const double* __restrict__ g_x, ...)
{
  int n1 = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x + N1;
  float s_fx = 0.0f;  float s_fy = 0.0f;  float s_fz = 0.0f;
  float s_pe = 0.0f;
  float s_sxx = 0.0f;  float s_sxy = 0.0f;  /* ... 9 virial components */
```

Three critical design decisions are visible here:

**1. Mixed-precision accumulation.** Position data arrives as `double` (the `g_x`, `g_y`, `g_z` arrays), but force, energy, and virial accumulators are `float` registers. The displacement computation casts implicitly to float (`float x12 = g_x[n2] - x1`), and all accumulation happens in single precision. The final write-back uses `+=` to the `double` output arrays, enabling mixed-precision accumulation that is both fast (float ALU throughput) and sufficient for MD accuracy requirements.

**2. `__restrict__` pointer qualifiers.** All read-only global memory pointers carry the `__restrict__` qualifier, signaling to the compiler that no aliasing exists between input and output arrays. This enables the NVCC compiler to perform read-write overlap optimizations and reduce unnecessary L1 cache invalidation.

**3. Inlined device functions for physics.** The pairwise potential evaluation is encapsulated in a `static __device__` function:

```cpp
static __device__ void
find_p2_and_f2(float s6e4, float s12e4, float d12sq, float& p2, float& f2)
{
  float d12inv2 = 1.0f / d12sq;
  float d12inv6 = d12inv2 * d12inv2 * d12inv2;
  f2 = 6.0f * (s6e4 * d12inv6 - s12e4 * 2.0f * d12inv6 * d12inv6) * d12inv2;
  p2 = s12e4 * d12inv6 * d12inv6 - s6e4 * d12inv6;
}
```

This keeps the kernel body clean while ensuring the compiler can inline aggressively. The precomputed parameters (`s6e4`, `s12e4` — σ⁶·4ε and σ¹²·4ε) are stored in a constant-size struct (`LJ_Para`) passed by value, placing them in kernel parameter cache rather than global memory.

Sources: [lj.cu](/src/force/lj.cu#L67-L74), [lj.cu](/src/force/lj.cu#L77-L181), [lj.cuh](/src/force/lj.cuh#L25-L29)

## Multi-Step Kernel Pattern: Many-Body Potentials

Many-body potentials (Tersoff, NEP, ADP) **cannot** compute forces in a single pass because the force on atom *i* from neighbor *j* depends on the environment of atom *i* (bond-order functions in Tersoff; descriptor vectors in NEP). GPUMD decomposes these into explicit multi-step kernel launches with intermediate GPU buffers.

### Tersoff Two-Step Decomposition

The Tersoff-1989 potential splits into two kernels plus a shared utility:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Neighbor List Build] --> B[Step 1 Kernel:<br/>find_force_tersoff_step1]
    B --> C[GPU Buffer:<br/>g_b, g_bp<br/>bond-order + derivative]
    C --> D[Step 2 Kernel:<br/>find_force_tersoff_step2]
    D --> E[GPU Buffer:<br/>g_f12x, g_f12y, g_f12z<br/>partial forces]
    E --> F[find_properties_many_body:<br/>Reduce to force + virial]
    
    style B fill:#2563eb,color:#fff
    style D fill:#2563eb,color:#fff
    style F fill:#16a34a,color:#fff
```

**Step 1** (`find_force_tersoff_step1`) computes the bond-order function *b_ij* and its derivative *∂b_ij/∂ζ_ij* for every (atom, neighbor) pair. For each atom `n1` and each neighbor `n2`, it sums the coordination environment:

```cpp
for (int i1 = 0; i1 < neighbor_number; ++i1) {
    // ... compute d12, cutoff fc, angular g-function
    for (int i2 = 0; i2 < neighbor_number; ++i2) {
        // triple loop: accumulate zeta from all n3 != n2
        zeta += fc13 * g123;
    }
    g_b[i1 * number_of_particles + n1] = b12;
    g_bp[i1 * number_of_particles + n1] = -b12 * bzn * 0.5 / ((1.0 + bzn) * zeta);
}
```

**Step 2** (`find_force_tersoff_step2`) consumes the precomputed `g_b` and `g_bp` arrays to evaluate the (i,j) pairwise part and the (i,j,k) three-body part of the force, writing partial forces `f12x/y/z` per neighbor pair.

**Step 3** (`find_properties_many_body`) is a **shared utility** that reduces the per-neighbor-pair partial forces into per-atom total forces and virial tensors, used by all many-body potentials.

The intermediate data buffers are allocated in the potential's constructor with sizes proportional to `num_atoms × max_neighbors`:

```cpp
const int num_of_neighbors = 50 * num_atoms;
tersoff_data.b.resize(num_of_neighbors);
tersoff_data.bp.resize(num_of_neighbors);
tersoff_data.f12x.resize(num_of_neighbors);
```

Sources: [tersoff1989.cu](/src/force/tersoff1989.cu#L141-L149), [tersoff1989.cu](/src/force/tersoff1989.cu#L337-L405), [tersoff1989.cu](/src/force/tersoff1989.cu#L408-L505), [tersoff1989.cu](/src/force/tersoff1989.cu#L508-L586)

### NEP Multi-Stage Pipeline

The NEP potential employs the most elaborate kernel pipeline, reflecting its neural network architecture:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Global Neighbor Build] --> B["Typewise Neighbor Split:<br/>Radial NL + Angular NL"]
    C["find_descriptor Kernel:<br/>Compute q-vector + ANN forward pass"]
    D["GPU Buffer: g_Fp<br/>∂E/∂q per atom per component"]
    E["find_force Kernel:<br/>Backprop-style force accumulation"]
    B --> C
    C --> D
    D --> E
    E --> F[Force + Virial Output]
    
    style B fill:#7c3aed,color:#fff
    style C fill:#2563eb,color:#fff
    style E fill:#2563eb,color:#fff
```

The NEP kernel pipeline has these distinguishing features:

**Typewise neighbor lists.** NEP maintains *two separate neighbor lists* — a radial list (larger cutoff `rc_radial`) and an angular list (smaller cutoff `rc_angular`) — because angular descriptor computation is far more expensive and benefits from a reduced neighbor count. A dedicated kernel (`find_neighbor_list_large_box`) splits the global neighbor list into these two typewise lists, computing type-averaged cutoffs on the fly:

```cpp
float rc_radial = (paramb.rc_radial[t1] + paramb.rc_radial[t2]) * 0.5f;
float rc_angular = (paramb.rc_angular[t1] + paramb.rc_angular[t2]) * 0.5f;
```

**Descriptor computation with stack arrays.** The `find_descriptor` kernel allocates the descriptor vector `q[MAX_DIM]` and its gradient `Fp[MAX_DIM]` as local arrays on the stack (which the compiler places in registers when possible). The radial and angular descriptor loops are structurally separate — radial descriptors sum over the radial neighbor list, angular descriptors sum over the angular neighbor list with spherical harmonic accumulation via `accumulate_s` and `find_q`.

**ANN forward pass in-register.** The neural network evaluation (`apply_ann_one_layer`) executes entirely within the kernel, reading weight matrices from global memory but accumulating the hidden layer in registers. This avoids any intermediate global memory round-trip for the per-atom energy prediction.

Sources: [nep.cu](/src/force/nep.cu#L436-L486), [nep.cu](/src/force/nep.cu#L488-L598), [nep.cu](/src/force/nep.cu#L379-L394)

## Neighbor List Traversal and Memory Layout

All force kernels traverse the neighbor list using a **column-major** (stride-by-N) layout for the neighbor list array `NL`:

```
n2 = g_neighbor_list[n1 + number_of_particles * i1]
```

Here, `i1` is the neighbor index (0 to NN[n1]-1), and `n1` is the atom index. The stride `number_of_particles` means all neighbors of atom `n1` occupy positions `n1`, `n1 + N`, `n1 + 2N`, ... in the flat array. This layout provides **coalesced memory access** when threads in the same warp read `NL[n1 + N * i1]` for the same `i1` but different `n1` — the addresses differ by 1, falling within the same cache line.

The virial tensor output uses a similar stride-by-N layout with 9 components stored as separate "rows":

```cpp
g_virial[n1 + 0 * number_of_particles] += s_sxx;  // component 0
g_virial[n1 + 1 * number_of_particles] += s_syy;  // component 1
// ... up to component 8
```

This ensures that when multiple threads write virial components for the same component index, their accesses are coalesced.

Sources: [lj.cu](/src/force/lj.cu#L118-L118), [lj.cu](/src/force/lj.cu#L168-L176)

## CUDA/HIP Portability Layer

GPUMD targets both NVIDIA (CUDA) and AMD (HIP) GPUs through a comprehensive **macro-based portability layer** in `gpu_macro.cuh`. The entire file is structured as a compile-time branch:

```
#ifdef USE_HIP  →  hipMalloc, hipMemcpy, hipLaunchKernel, ...
#else           →  cudaMalloc, cudaMemcpy, cudaLaunchKernel, ...
```

The abstraction covers six categories of GPU runtime APIs, each mapped to a `gpu`-prefixed macro:

| Category | CUDA Original | GPUMD Macro | HIP Counterpart |
|----------|--------------|-------------|-----------------|
| Memory | `cudaMalloc` | `gpuMalloc` | `hipMalloc` |
| Error | `cudaError_t` | `gpuError_t` | `hipError_t` |
| Device | `cudaSetDevice` | `gpuSetDevice` | `hipSetDevice` |
| Stream | `cudaStream_t` | `gpuStream_t` | `hipStream_t` |
| RAND | `curandState` | `gpurandState` | `hiprandState` |
| FFT | `cufftHandle` | `gpufftHandle` | `hipfftHandle` |

The layer also wraps cuBLAS/hipBLAS and cuSOLVER/hipSOLVER for the NEP training pipeline, plus cuFFT/hipFFT for Ewald and PPPM long-range electrostatics. This design avoids runtime API dispatch overhead — the preprocessor selects the entire backend at compile time, producing a binary that is either pure CUDA or pure HIP with zero abstraction cost.

> [!TIP]
> When adding a new force potential kernel, use the `gpu`-prefixed macros (e.g., `gpuMalloc`, `GPU_CHECK_KERNEL`) rather than raw CUDA calls to maintain HIP portability. The kernel launch syntax `<<<grid, block>>>` works identically under HIP's compilation mode.

Sources: [gpu_macro.cuh](/src/utilities/gpu_macro.cuh#L18-L199)

## Kernel Design Pattern Comparison

The following table summarizes the three distinct kernel design patterns employed across GPUMD's potential implementations:

| Pattern | Potentials | Kernel Steps | Intermediate GPU Buffers | Accumulation Precision |
|--------|-----------|-------------|------------------------|----------------------|
| **Single-step pair** | LJ, EAM | 1 | None | float registers → double output |
| **Two-step many-body** | Tersoff, SW | 2 + reduce | `b`, `bp`, `f12x/y/z` | double throughout |
| **Multi-stage NN** | NEP, DP | 3+ (neighbor split, descriptor, force) | `Fp`, `sum_fxyz`, `f12x/y/z`, separate NL | float descriptor → double output |

The choice between float and double accumulation reflects a precision-performance tradeoff tuned per potential: pair potentials tolerate float accumulation due to the smooth, well-conditioned nature of pairwise force sums; many-body potentials like Tersoff use double throughout because bond-order derivatives can vary over many orders of magnitude; NEP uses float for descriptor/ANN computation (matching the training precision) but double for final force accumulation.

Sources: [lj.cu](/src/force/lj.cu#L77-L181), [tersoff1989.cu](/src/force/tersoff1989.cu#L337-L586), [nep.cu](/src/force/nep.cu#L436-L598)

## Parameter Passing Strategies

GPUMD uses two distinct strategies for passing potential parameters into kernels, chosen based on parameter size and access patterns:

**Value-passed structs (small parameters).** The LJ potential passes its entire `LJ_Para` struct by value into the kernel. Because `LJ_Para` contains only three 10×10 float matrices (300 bytes total), it fits entirely in the kernel parameter cache — a small region of constant memory that broadcasts efficiently to all threads. Similarly, Tersoff passes its parameter structs (`Tersoff1989_Parameters`) by value.

**Pointer-passed arrays (large parameters).** The NEP potential's parameter set (ANN weights + descriptor coefficients) can exceed tens of kilobytes. These are stored in a `GPU_Vector<float>` (`nep_data.parameters`) and passed as device pointers. The `NEP::ANN` struct contains pointer fields (`w0[t]`, `b0[t]`, `w1[t]`) that are set up by `update_potential()` to point into the flat parameter array with correct offsets per atom type:

```cpp
void NEP::update_potential(float* parameters, ANN& ann) {
  float* pointer = parameters;
  for (int t = 0; t < paramb.num_types; ++t) {
    ann.w0[t] = pointer;  pointer += ann.num_neurons1 * ann.dim;
    ann.b0[t] = pointer;  pointer += ann.num_neurons1;
    ann.w1[t] = pointer;  pointer += ann.num_neurons1;
  }
  ann.b1 = pointer;
}
```

This pointer-chasing pattern is safe because the ANN struct is passed by **value** into the kernel — the struct itself is in parameter cache, but its pointer members reference global memory where the actual weight data resides. The kernel then reads weights through these cached pointers with standard global memory loads.

> [!TIP]
> The `update_potential` pointer-wiring pattern is critical for on-line potential updates (e.g., during HNEMD or multi-potential averaging). After modifying parameters on the host, call `update_potential` to re-wire the pointer offsets before the next kernel launch — the kernel reads whatever the pointers currently reference.

Sources: [lj.cuh](/src/force/lj.cuh#L25-L29), [nep.cu](/src/force/nep.cu#L402-L434), [lj.cu](/src/force/lj.cu#L78-L79)

## Minimum Image Convention and Box Handling

All kernels apply the **minimum image convention (MIC)** inline for every neighbor displacement using the `apply_mic(box, x12, y12, z12)` device function. The `Box` struct — passed by value into every kernel — contains the simulation cell parameters and triclinic transformation data needed for MIC computation. Because `Box` is small (a few dozen bytes) and read-only, it resides in kernel parameter cache and is accessible with zero latency from all threads.

The displacement computation follows a consistent pattern: read double-precision positions, compute the raw displacement, apply MIC, then (for float-accumulating kernels) implicitly narrow to float:

```cpp
double x1 = g_x[n1];
float x12 = g_x[n2] - x1;   // double subtraction → float narrowing
apply_mic(box, x12, y12, z12);
float d12sq = x12 * x12 + y12 * y12 + z12 * z12;
```

Sources: [lj.cu](/src/force/lj.cu#L110-L125)

## Next Steps

The kernel designs described here are inseparable from the memory layout and neighbor list construction that feed them. For a deep understanding of the column-major neighbor list format, typewise neighbor splitting, and the GPU_Vector memory management that underpins all kernel I/O, continue to [Neighbor List and Memory Layout](14-neighbor-list-and-memory-layout). For the NEP-specific neural network kernel internals and training-side kernel design, see [NEP Model Architecture](8-nep-model-architecture).

# Neighbor List and Memory Layout



GPUMD's performance hinges on two architectural pillars: an **O(N) cell-list-accelerated Verlet neighbor list** with a dual-resolution (global/local) strategy, and a **Structure-of-Arrays (SoA) memory layout** that aligns per-atom data for coalesced GPU access. This page dissects both systems — how neighbor lists are built, stored, and refreshed, and how all per-atom arrays are arranged in GPU memory to maximize throughput.

## Cell List Construction

The neighbor list algorithm begins by partitioning the simulation domain into a uniform grid of cells, each with side length **rc/2** (half the cutoff radius). This choice guarantees that any atom's neighbors within the cutoff must reside in one of the 27 adjacent cells (3×3×3 stencil for fully periodic systems). The cell list is built in three GPU-parallel phases:

1. **Count atoms per cell** — each atom computes its cell ID via fractional coordinate mapping and atomically increments the count for that cell.
2. **Exclusive prefix sum** — `thrust::exclusive_scan` converts per-cell counts into offsets, yielding `cell_count_sum[c]` = the starting index into a flat array for cell `c`.
3. **Populate cell contents** — atoms re-compute their cell IDs and write their global atom index into `cell_contents[cell_count_sum[cell_id] + ind]` using `atomicAdd` for the local offset `ind`.

The cell ID computation handles both orthogonal and triclinic boxes by transforming Cartesian coordinates into fractional (scaled) space using the inverse box matrix stored in `box.cpu_h[9..17]`, then applying `floor` to obtain integer cell indices. Periodic wrapping ensures indices remain within `[0, nx)`, `[0, ny)`, `[0, nz)` bounds.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Atom positions (SoA)"] --> B["find_cell_counts kernel"]
    B --> C["cell_count[c] = atoms in cell c"]
    C --> D["thrust::exclusive_scan"]
    D --> E["cell_count_sum[c] = prefix offset"]
    E --> F["find_cell_contents kernel"]
    F --> G["cell_contents[...] = atom indices"]
    G --> H["Cell list ready"]
    style A fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#2563eb
    style H fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#16a34a
```

Sources: [neighbor.cu](src/force/neighbor.cu#L42-L83), [neighbor.cuh](src/force/neighbor.cuh#L76-L110), [box.cuh](src/model/box.cuh#L32-L33)

## Verlet Neighbor List with Skin Distance

GPUMD implements a **Verlet-style neighbor list** with a configurable skin distance (`skin = 1.0` Å by default). The algorithm maintains two levels of resolution:

| List | Cutoff | Purpose | Rebuild Frequency |
|------|--------|---------|-------------------|
| **Global** | `rc + skin` | Persistent across timesteps | Only when any atom moves > skin/2 |
| **Local** | `rc` (exact) | Used by force kernels | Every timestep (cheap filter) |

The global list is built by `Neighbor::find_neighbor_global`, which first calls `check_atom_distance` to determine if any atom has drifted more than `skin/2` from its position at the last rebuild. If so, it invokes the full O(N) cell-list-based construction at the extended cutoff `rc + skin`, then snapshots all atom positions into `x0, y0, z0` for the next distance check. If no atom has moved beyond the threshold, the global list is reused — this is the key performance optimization that avoids rebuilding every step.

The local list is derived by `Neighbor::find_local_neighbor_from_global`, which simply iterates each atom's global neighbor entries and retains only those within the exact cutoff `rc`. This filter is extremely cheap (one distance comparison per global neighbor) and runs every timestep.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Timestep begins"] --> B{"Any atom moved > skin/2?"}
    B -->|Yes| C["Rebuild global NL at rc + skin"]
    C --> D["Snapshot positions to x0,y0,z0"]
    B -->|No| E["Reuse existing global NL"]
    D --> F["Filter global→local at exact rc"]
    E --> F
    F --> G["Force kernels use local NL"]
    style A fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#2563eb
    style G fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#16a34a
```

Sources: [neighbor.cu](src/force/neighbor.cu#L742-L823), [neighbor.cuh](src/force/neighbor.cuh#L153-L160)

## Neighbor List Storage: Column-Major Layout

The neighbor list is stored in two GPU arrays:

- **`NN`** — `GPU_Vector<int>` of size `N`, where `NN[i]` = number of neighbors of atom `i`.
- **`NL`** — `GPU_Vector<int>` of size `N × MN`, where `MN` is the maximum neighbors per atom.

The critical access pattern is **column-major**: the j-th neighbor of atom `i` is stored at `NL[N * j + i]`. This layout places all atoms' first neighbors contiguously, then all atoms' second neighbors, and so on. When a force kernel assigns one thread per atom, consecutive threads reading `NL[N * 0 + tid]`, `NL[N * 0 + tid + 1]`, ... access adjacent memory locations — achieving **coalesced global memory reads** on the GPU.

The maximum neighbor count `MN` is estimated during initialization as:

```
MN = num_neighbors × ((rc + skin) / rc)³
```

This scales the expected neighbor count by the cube of the cutoff ratio, accounting for the larger global cutoff volume. If an atom's actual neighbor count exceeds `MN`, the simulation will produce out-of-bounds access — the `num_neighbors` parameter must be chosen conservatively.

After construction, the neighbor list is **sorted** by the `gpu_sort_neighbor_list` kernel, which uses shared-memory bubble-sort logic to order each atom's neighbors by global index. This sorting improves access regularity in downstream force kernels.

Sources: [neighbor.cu](src/force/neighbor.cu#L85-L162), [neighbor.cu](src/force/neighbor.cu#L825-L834), [neighbor.cuh](src/force/neighbor.cuh#L112-L134)

## Specialized Neighbor List Variants

Three distinct neighbor-finding functions serve different potential families:

| Variant | Function | Filter Logic | Use Case |
|---------|----------|--------------|----------|
| **Standard** | `find_neighbor` | All pairs within `rc` | NEP, EAM, Tersoff, LJ |
| **ILP** | `find_neighbor_ilp` | Same-layer vs. different-layer separation | ILP-NEP, ILP-Tersoff hybrids |
| **SW** | `find_neighbor_SW` | Only same-group pairs | Stillinger-Weber in hybrids |

The **ILP variant** maintains two separate neighbor lists: the standard `NN/NL` for inter-layer pairs (different `group_label`) within the ILP cutoff, and `big_ilp_NN/big_ilp_NL` for intra-layer pairs (same `group_label`) within a larger cutoff. This dual-list structure reflects the physics of layered materials where intra-layer bonding (e.g., Tersoff or NEP) operates at a different range than inter-layer van der Waals interactions.

The **SW variant** filters neighbors by `group_label`, only including pairs within the same group — essential for Stillinger-Weber potentials where the three-body term requires all three atoms to belong to the same layer in hybrid ILP-SW models.

All three variants share the same cell-list infrastructure (`cell_count`, `cell_count_sum`, `cell_contents`) and the same column-major NL layout with post-construction sorting.

Sources: [neighbor.cu](src/force/neighbor.cu#L352-L440), [neighbor.cu](src/force/neighbor.cu#L509-L587), [neighbor.cuh](src/force/neighbor.cuh#L43-L74)

## Structure-of-Arrays (SoA) Memory Layout

The `Atom` class stores all per-atom quantities using the **Structure-of-Arrays** pattern via `GPU_Vector<T>`. Each physical quantity is a contiguous GPU array (or multiple arrays for vector/tensor quantities), with components laid out sequentially:

| Quantity | Type | Components | Memory Layout |
|----------|------|------------|---------------|
| `type` | `int` | 1 | `[t₀, t₁, ..., tₙ₋₁]` |
| `mass` | `double` | 1 | `[m₀, m₁, ..., mₙ₋₁]` |
| `charge` | `float` | 1 | `[q₀, q₁, ..., qₙ₋₁]` |
| `position_per_atom` | `double` | 3 | `[x₀..xₙ₋₁, y₀..yₙ₋₁, z₀..zₙ₋₁]` |
| `velocity_per_atom` | `double` | 3 | `[vx₀..vxₙ₋₁, vy₀..vyₙ₋₁, vz₀..vzₙ₋₁]` |
| `force_per_atom` | `double` | 3 | `[fx₀..fxₙ₋₁, fy₀..fyₙ₋₁, fz₀..fzₙ₋₁]` |
| `virial_per_atom` | `double` | 9 | `[v₀₀..v₀₀ₙ₋₁, v₀₁.., ..., v₂₂ₙ₋₁]` |
| `heat_per_atom` | `double` | 5 | `[h₀..hₙ₋₁, ..., h₄ₙ₋₁]` |
| `potential_per_atom` | `double` | 1 | `[p₀, p₁, ..., pₙ₋₁]` |

For a 3-component quantity like position, the x-coordinates of all N atoms occupy the first N elements, y-coordinates the next N, and z-coordinates the final N. Force kernels access these via offset arithmetic: `const double* x = position.data(); const double* y = position.data() + N; const double* z = position.data() + 2*N;`. This pattern — where thread `i` reads `x[i]`, `y[i]`, `z[i]` — maps directly to **coalesced memory transactions** on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs.

> [!TIP]
> SoA layout is non-negotiable for GPU performance. The alternative AoS (Array of Structures) would place xᵢ, yᵢ, zᵢ in adjacent memory, causing stride-3 access patterns where consecutive threads read non-adjacent addresses — severely degrading memory bandwidth utilization.

Sources: [atom.cuh](src/model/atom.cuh#L23-L56), [neighbor.cu](src/force/neighbor.cu#L177-L179)

## GPU_Vector: The Memory Abstraction

`GPU_Vector<T>` is GPUMD's primary GPU memory container, providing allocation, transfer, and initialization for both **global (device) memory** and **managed (unified) memory**:

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class GPU_Vector_T {
        +size_t size_
        +size_t memory_
        +Memory_Type memory_type_
        +T* data_
        +bool allocated_
        +resize(size, memory_type) void
        +resize(size, value, memory_type) void
        +copy_from_host(h_data) void
        +copy_from_device(d_data) void
        +copy_to_host(h_data) void
        +fill(value) void
        +data() T*
        +size() size_t
    }
    class Memory_Type {
        <<enum>>
        global
        managed
    }
    GPU_Vector_T --> Memory_Type
```

Key design choices:

- **Dual memory types**: `Memory_Type::global` uses `gpuMalloc` for standard device memory; `Memory_Type::managed` uses `gpuMallocManaged` for unified memory accessible from both host and device.
- **Fill optimization**: For global memory, `fill()` launches a GPU kernel (`gpu_fill`); for managed memory, it uses a simple CPU loop — exploiting the unified access model.
- **Offset-based transfers**: `copy_from_host(h_data, size, offset)` writes to `data_ + offset`, enabling partial updates to sub-arrays without staging buffers.
- **RAII lifecycle**: The destructor calls `gpuFree` if `allocated_` is true, preventing leaks. `resize()` frees existing allocation before reallocating.

All per-atom arrays in `Atom`, all neighbor list arrays (`NN`, `NL`), and all cell-list arrays (`cell_count`, `cell_count_sum`, `cell_contents`) are `GPU_Vector` instances — making this the universal memory backbone of the simulation.

> [!TIP]
> The `GPU_Vector` deliberately omits a copy constructor and assignment operator. Transferring GPU vectors should use `copy_from_device()` / `copy_to_host()` explicitly — implicit deep copies would hide costly device-to-host transfers and break performance reasoning.

Sources: [gpu_vector.cuh](src/utilities/gpu_vector.cuh#L32-L200)

## Cell List Memory Footprint

The cell list requires three auxiliary `GPU_Vector<int>` arrays:

| Array | Size | Purpose |
|-------|------|---------|
| `cell_count` | `N_cells` (= `nx × ny × nz`) | Number of atoms in each cell |
| `cell_count_sum` | `N_cells` | Exclusive prefix sum — starting offset into `cell_contents` |
| `cell_contents` | `N` | Flat array of atom indices, grouped by cell |

The cell grid dimensions `nx, ny, nz` are computed by `box.get_num_bins(rc_cell_list, num_bins)` where `rc_cell_list = rc / 2`. For a cubic box of side L with cutoff rc, this yields roughly `(2L/rc)³` cells. The `cell_contents` array is sized to N (the total number of atoms) since every atom belongs to exactly one cell. If `N_cells > N`, the `cell_count` and `cell_count_sum` arrays are resized dynamically — this can occur for small systems with large cutoffs where the cell grid is finer than the atom count.

The cell list is rebuilt every time the neighbor list is rebuilt (i.e., when atoms exceed the skin/2 displacement threshold). Between rebuilds, the cell list arrays are reused without reallocation, provided the cell count doesn't exceed the previously allocated capacity.

Sources: [neighbor.cu](src/force/neighbor.cu#L164-L215), [neighbor.cu](src/force/neighbor.cu#L297-L349), [neighbor.cuh](src/force/neighbor.cuh#L155-L157)

## Neighbor List Access Patterns in Force Kernels
