Force kernels follow a consistent access idiom. Each GPU thread handles one atom `n1` and iterates over its neighbors:

```
for (int i1 = 0; i1 < NN[n1]; ++i1) {
    int n2 = NL[static_cast<size_t>(N) * i1 + n1];
    // compute pair interaction between n1 and n2
}
```

The column-major NL layout means that for a fixed `i1` (neighbor index), all threads access `NL[N * i1 + tid]` where `tid` is the thread index — these are contiguous memory addresses, producing **coalesced 128-byte transactions** on GPUs with warp size 32. However, as `i1` varies within the inner loop, successive reads stride by `N` elements — these are non-coalesced but unavoidable in the neighbor-list iteration pattern. The sorting of neighbor indices (by `gpu_sort_neighbor_list`) partially mitigates this by improving spatial locality of the referenced atom data (`x[n2]`, `y[n2]`, `z[n2]`).

For potentials requiring three-body interactions (Tersoff, SW, ADP), the neighbor list of atom `n2` is also accessed within the inner loop, creating a **double-indirect** access pattern: `n3 = NL[N * i2 + n2]` where `n2` itself came from the neighbor list. This is the primary bottleneck for three-body potentials and benefits greatly from L1/L2 cache hit rates, which the sorted neighbor list improves.

Sources: [neighbor.cu](src/force/neighbor.cu#L85-L162), [potential.cuh](src/force/potential.cuh#L91-L112)

## Putting It All Together: Memory Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph SoA["SoA Per-Atom Data (GPU Global Memory)"]
        direction LR
        X["x[N]"]
        Y["y[N]"]
        Z["z[N]"]
        FX["fx[N]"]
        FY["fy[N]"]
        FZ["fz[N]"]
    end
    subgraph NL["Neighbor List (GPU Global Memory)"]
        direction LR
        NN_arr["NN[N]"]
        NL_arr["NL[N×MN]<br/>column-major"]
    end
    subgraph CL["Cell List (GPU Global Memory)"]
        direction LR
        CC["cell_count[NC]"]
        CCS["cell_count_sum[NC]"]
        CCO["cell_contents[N]"]
    end
    subgraph Cache["GPU Cache Hierarchy"]
        L1["L1 per-SM"]
        L2["L2 shared"]
    end
    NL -->|"i1-th neighbor<br/>coalesced for fixed i1"| SoA
    CL -->|"cell lookup<br/>atomicAdd during build"| SoA
    SoA -->|"position reads"| Cache
    NL -->|"NL reads"| Cache
    Cache -->|"force writes<br/>atomicAdd for f12"| SoA
    style SoA fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#2563eb
    style NL fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706
    style CL fill:#f3e8ff,stroke:#9333ea
```

The complete data flow for a force computation step: (1) the neighbor list module checks atom displacements against the skin threshold; (2) if triggered, it rebuilds the cell list and neighbor list entirely on the GPU; (3) the local neighbor list is filtered from the global list; (4) each force kernel reads positions via coalesced SoA access, traverses the column-major NL, and accumulates forces back into the SoA `force_per_atom` array using `atomicAdd` for the pairwise decomposition (`f12` pattern). The `Potential::find_properties_many_body` helper centralizes this force/virial accumulation logic across all many-body potentials.

This architecture — SoA layout for coalesced reads, column-major NL for neighbor traversal, Verlet skin for amortized rebuild cost, and cell lists for O(N) construction — represents the standard high-performance pattern for GPU molecular dynamics and is the foundation upon which GPUMD achieves its simulation throughput.

Sources: [neighbor.cuh](src/force/neighbor.cuh#L136-L160), [atom.cuh](src/model/atom.cuh#L23-L56), [potential.cuh](src/force/potential.cuh#L91-L112), [gpu_vector.cuh](src/utilities/gpu_vector.cuh#L37-L200)

## Next Steps

The neighbor list and memory layout form the substrate for all force computations. To understand how force kernels leverage this infrastructure on the GPU:

- **[CUDA Kernel Design](13-cuda-kernel-design)** — examines thread mapping strategies, shared memory usage, and kernel launch configurations that operate on the neighbor list and SoA data described here.
- **[Force and Potential System](5-force-and-potential-system)** — details the potential hierarchy and how each potential type consumes the neighbor list during force computation.
- **[Multi-GPU and MDI Interface](17-multi-gpu-and-mdi-interface)** — covers how the neighbor list is decomposed across multiple GPUs in the `NEP_MULTIGPU` variant.

# Heat Transport Methods



GPUMD implements a comprehensive suite of heat transport simulation methods spanning equilibrium, homogeneous nonequilibrium, and direct nonequilibrium approaches — all GPU-accelerated. These methods enable thermal conductivity calculation for bulk 3D materials, 2D layered systems, and multicomponent alloys, with additional capabilities for spectral decomposition and mode-resolved analysis. The unifying computational primitive across all equilibrium and HNEMD methods is the **per-atom heat current**, calculated from virial and velocity data on the GPU.

Sources: [compute_heat.cuh](/src/measure/compute_heat.cuh#L1-L30), [measure directory](/src/measure)

## Architectural Overview

The heat transport system is organized as a set of `Property` subclasses within the measurement pipeline, each implementing the `preprocess → process → postprocess` lifecycle. A shared `compute_heat` GPU kernel produces per-atom heat current data that feeds into the HAC (Green-Kubo), HNEMD, HNEMDEC, and SHC computations. Separately, the `MODAL_ANALYSIS` class implements GKMA and HNEMA, while the integrator layer provides direct nonequilibrium heat bath and two-temperature-model (TTM) ensembles.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Heat Current Computation"
        CH[compute_heat GPU kernel] --> PAH[Per-atom heat current<br/>J_x^in, J_x^out, J_y^in, J_y^out, J_z]
    end

    subgraph "Equilibrium Methods (EMD)"
        PAH --> HAC[HAC class<br/>Heat Auto-Correlation]
        HAC --> RTC[Running Thermal Conductivity<br/>hac.out]
    end

    subgraph "Homogeneous NEMD Methods"
        PAH --> HNEMD[HNEMD class<br/>Driving force F_e]
        PAH --> HNEMDEC[HNEMDEC class<br/>Evans-Cummings algorithm]
        HNEMD --> KOUT[kappa.out]
        HNEMDEC --> OOUT[onsager.out]
    end

    subgraph "Spectral Decomposition"
        PAH --> SHC[SHC class<br/>Spectral Heat Current]
        SHC --> SHOUT[shc.out<br/>K(t) and J_q(omega)]
    end

    subgraph "Modal Analysis"
        MA[MODAL_ANALYSIS class] --> GKMA[GKMA method<br/>Green-Kubo Modal]
        MA --> HNEMA[HNEMA method<br/>HNEMD Modal]
        GKMA --> HMOUT[heatmode.out]
        HNEMA --> KMOUT[kappamode.out]
    end

    subgraph "Direct NEMD (Integrator Layer)"
        EH[ensemble heat_nhc/heat_bdp/heat_lan] --> DIRECT[Direct heat bath method]
        TTM[ensemble ttm/heat_ttm] --> TTMOUT[Two-Temperature Model]
    end

    VPA[Virial per atom] --> CH
    VEL[Velocity per atom] --> CH
```

Sources: [hac.cuh](/src/measure/hac.cuh#L1-L66), [hnemd_kappa.cuh](/src/measure/hnemd_kappa.cuh#L1-L68), [hnemdec_kappa.cuh](/src/measure/hnemdec_kappa.cuh#L1-L76), [shc.cuh](/src/measure/shc.cuh#L1-L81), [modal_analysis.cuh](/src/measure/modal_analysis.cuh#L1-L155)

## Per-Atom Heat Current Kernel

The `compute_heat` function is the foundational GPU kernel shared by the HAC, HNEMD, HNEMDEC, and SHC methods. It computes the **potential part** of the per-atom heat current from the per-atom virial tensor and velocity, following the formalism established in [Fan et al., Phys. Rev. B 92, 094301 (2015)]. Two overloads exist: one using only virial and velocity (producing the 5-component in-plane/out-of-plane decomposition used by HAC, HNEMD, and SHC), and one that additionally includes mass and per-atom potential energy (producing the full 3-component heat current used by HNEMDEC).

The 5-component variant decomposes each Cartesian heat current into in-plane and out-of-plane contributions — critical for 2D materials where basal-plane and cross-plane transport differ fundamentally. The virial tensor is stored in a compact 9-element layout per atom (`xx, yy, zz, xy, xz, yz, yx, zx, zy` mapped to indices `0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8`), and the kernel maps these to the heat current components:

| Heat Component | Formula | Physical Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| J_x^in | S_xx·v_x + S_xy·v_y | In-plane x heat current |
| J_x^out | S_xz·v_z | Out-of-plane x heat current |
| J_y^in | S_yx·v_x + S_yy·v_y | In-plane y heat current |
| J_y^out | S_yz·v_z | Out-of-plane y heat current |
| J_z | S_zx·v_x + S_zy·v_y + S_zz·v_z | Total z heat current |

The 3-component overload computes `J_α = (E_i + S_αα)·v_α + Σ_{β≠α} S_αβ·v_β` where `E_i = ½m_i|v_i|² + φ_i` is the total energy per atom, yielding the full heat current including convective contributions for multicomponent systems.

> [!TIP]
> For 3D isotropic systems, sum the in-plane and out-of-plane columns: κ_x^tot = κ_x^in + κ_x^out. The decomposition is only meaningful for 2D/layered materials where the basal plane is in the xy directions.

Sources: [compute_heat.cu](/src/measure/compute_heat.cu#L1-L167)

## Green-Kubo Method (EMD): `compute_hac`

The **Heat Auto-Correlation (HAC)** method computes thermal conductivity via the Green-Kubo linear response formalism in equilibrium molecular dynamics. The thermal conductivity is obtained from the time integral of the heat current autocorrelation function: `κ = (1/Vk_BT) ∫₀^∞ ⟨J(0)·J(t)⟩ dt`. In practice, GPUMD computes the **Running Thermal Conductivity (RTC)** — the cumulative integral as a function of upper limit — which should converge to the true κ at sufficiently long correlation time.

**Syntax:** `compute_hac <sampling_interval> <correlation_steps> <output_interval>`

| Parameter | Description | Constraints |
|---|---|---|
| `sampling_interval` | Steps between heat current samples | ≥ 1 |
| `correlation_steps` | Maximum correlation steps (Nc) | Typically ~10% of total samples |
| `output_interval` | Averaging window before writing output | 1 = no averaging |

The implementation follows a three-phase pipeline: (1) **preprocess** allocates GPU memory for `5 × N_frames` heat current components; (2) **process** computes per-atom heat current via `compute_heat`, then reduces across atoms using a `gpu_sum_heat` kernel with shared-memory reduction (launching 5 blocks of 1024 threads); (3) **postprocess** computes the autocorrelation via `gpu_find_hac` (launching Nc blocks of 128 threads with shared-memory accumulation), then integrates via the trapezoidal rule in `find_rtc` on the CPU. The HAC kernel computes cross-terms between in-plane and out-of-plane components and attributes them equally, as justified in [Fan2019].

**Output** (`hac.out`): 11 columns — correlation time (ps), 5 HAC components (eV³/amu), 5 RTC components (W/mK). The in/out decomposition allows extracting total conductivity for 3D systems by simple column summation.

Sources: [hac.cu](/src/measure/hac.cu#L1-L200), [compute_hac.rst](/doc/gpumd/input_parameters/compute_hac.rst#L1-L52), [hac_out.rst](/doc/gpumd/output_files/hac_out.rst#L1-L49)

## Homogeneous NEMD: `compute_hnemd`

The **HNEMD** method applies a fictitious external driving force **F**_e to all atoms, creating a homogeneous heat current without spatial temperature gradients. This avoids the finite-size effects inherent in direct NEMD. The thermal conductivity is extracted from the steady-state heat current: `κ_μα = ⟨J_α⟩ / (V·T·F_e,μ)`. The method is described in [Fan et al., Phys. Rev. B 99, 064308 (2019)].

**Syntax:** `compute_hnemd <output_interval> <Fe_x> <Fe_y> <Fe_z>`

| Parameter | Description | Units |
|---|---|---|
| `output_interval` | Steps between averaged outputs | steps |
| `Fe_x, Fe_y, Fe_z` | Driving force components | Å⁻¹ |

The driving force direction determines which conductivity tensor components are measured. A nonzero F_e,x yields κ_xx, κ_yx, κ_zx; F_e,y yields κ_xy, κ_yy, κ_zy; F_e,z yields κ_xz, κ_yz, κ_zz. The magnitude |**F**_e| must be small enough for linear response (typically 10⁻⁵ Å⁻¹) but large enough for sufficient signal-to-noise.

The HNEMD class calls `force.set_hnemd_parameters(fe_x, fe_y, fe_z)` during construction, which modifies the force computation to include the driving force. The **process** method samples heat current every step (not at a configurable interval — unlike HAC), accumulates over `output_interval` steps, then computes `κ = KAPPA_UNIT_CONVERSION / (output_interval × V × T × |F_e|) × ΣJ` and appends to `kappa.out`. A Nose-Hoover chain thermostat must be used to control temperature; Langevin thermostats are incompatible because they alter dynamical correlations.

Sources: [hnemd_kappa.cu](/src/measure/hnemd_kappa.cu#L1-L185), [compute_hnemd.rst](/doc/gpumd/input_parameters/compute_hnemd.rst#L1-L60)

## HNEMD for Multicomponent Systems: `compute_hnemdec`

The **HNEMDEC** method extends HNEMD to multicomponent (alloy) systems using the **Evans-Cummings algorithm**, which accounts for the coupling between heat and mass diffusion. In multicomponent systems, the Onsager transport coefficients form a matrix relating heat flux and mass flux to thermodynamic driving forces. HNEMDEC computes these cross-coupling Onsager coefficients by applying either a thermal driving force (producing heat flux) or a diffusive driving force (producing momentum flux for a specific element).

**Syntax:** `compute_hnemdec <driving_force> <output_interval> <Fe_x> <Fe_y> <Fe_z>`

| Parameter | Description | Values |
|---|---|---|
| `driving_force` | Type of driving force | 0 = thermal; i > 0 = diffusive for element (i-1) |
| `output_interval` | Steps between output | steps |
| `Fe_x, Fe_y, Fe_z` | Driving force components | Å⁻¹ (thermal) or eV/Å (diffusive) |

When `driving_force = 0`, heat flux is the dissipative flux and F_e is in Å⁻¹. When `driving_force = i` (positive integer), a momentum flux of the (i-1)th element is produced as dissipative flux, and F_e is in eV/Å. The implementation uses the 3-component `compute_heat` overload (with mass and per-atom potential) to compute the full heat current including convective terms. It simultaneously accumulates diffusion currents (mass-weighted velocity sums per atom type) via the `gpu_sum_heat_and_diffusion` kernel. The `FACTOR` variable corrects for reduced-mass effects in the color conductivity formulation.

**Output** (`onsager.out`): Onsager coefficient matrix elements relating heat and mass transport — essential for predicting alloy thermal conductivity including the mass-diffusion contribution.

Sources: [hnemdec_kappa.cu](/src/measure/hnemdec_kappa.cu#L1-L200), [compute_hnemdec.rst](/doc/gpumd/input_parameters/compute_hnemdec.rst#L1-L61)

## Spectral Heat Current: `compute_shc`

The **Spectral Heat Current (SHC)** method decomposes the total thermal conductivity into frequency-resolved contributions, yielding the spectral thermal conductivity κ(ω). This reveals which phonon frequencies carry the most heat — invaluable for understanding scattering mechanisms and designing materials. The method computes the non-equilibrium virial-velocity correlation function K(t) and its Fourier transform to obtain J_q(ω), following Eq. (18) and Eq. (20) of [Fan2019].

**Syntax:** `compute_shc <sample_interval> <Nc> <transport_direction> <num_omega> <max_omega> [group <grouping_method> <group_id>]`

| Parameter | Description | Constraints |
|---|---|---|
| `sample_interval` | Steps between correlation samples | 1–10 |
| `Nc` | Total correlation steps | 100–1000 |
| `transport_direction` | Heat transport direction | 0=x, 1=y, 2=z |
| `num_omega` | Number of frequency points | ≥ 1 |
| `max_omega` | Maximum angular frequency | THz |
| `group` (optional) | Restrict to atom group | grouping_method + group_id |

The implementation stores Nc frames of velocity (vx, vy, vz) and virial (sx, sy, sz) data per atom in the group, consuming `6 × group_size × Nc` doubles of GPU memory. The correlation kernel `gpu_find_k` computes the in-plane and out-of-plane virial-velocity correlations using shared-memory reduction. The `find_shc` function performs the discrete Fourier transform to obtain the spectral heat current. Setting `group_id = -1` computes SHC for all groups except group 0, allowing selective analysis while reducing memory by assigning unneeded atoms to group 0.

**Output** (`shc.out`): Angular frequency (THz), in-plane SHC, out-of-plane SHC — providing the spectral decomposition of thermal conductivity.

Sources: [shc.cu](/src/measure/shc.cu#L1-L200), [compute_shc.rst](/doc/gpumd/input_parameters/compute_shc.rst#L1-L100)

## Modal Analysis: `compute_gkma` and `compute_hnema`

Modal analysis methods resolve thermal transport to individual phonon modes or frequency bins, requiring eigenvector data from a separate phonon calculation. The `MODAL_ANALYSIS` class implements both **Green-Kubo Modal Analysis (GKMA)** [Lv2016] and **Homogeneous NEMD Modal Analysis (HNEMA)** [Gabourie2021], selected by the keyword used.

### GKMA: `compute_gkma`

Computes modal heat currents in equilibrium using the Green-Kubo formalism projected onto phonon modes.

**Syntax:** `compute_gkma <sample_interval> <first_mode> <last_mode> <bin_option> <size>`

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| `sample_interval` | Steps between modal heat current samples |
| `first_mode`, `last_mode` | Mode range from eigenvector.in |
| `bin_option` | `bin_size` (count) or `f_bin_size` (frequency in THz) |
| `size` | Modes per bin or bin width in THz |

**Output** (`heatmode.out`): Modal heat current data per bin per sample — can be very large (many GB).

### HNEMA: `compute_hnema`

Computes modal thermal conductivity using a driving force, analogous to HNEMD but mode-resolved.

**Syntax:** `compute_hnema <sample_interval> <output_interval> <Fe_x> <Fe_y> <Fe_z> <first_mode> <last_mode> <bin_option> <size>`

| Parameter | Description | Units |
|---|---|---|
| `sample_interval` | Must divide `output_interval` | steps |
| `output_interval` | Output averaging window | steps |
| `Fe_x, Fe_y, Fe_z` | Driving force components | Å⁻¹ |
| Remaining | Same as GKMA | — |

**Output** (`kappamode.out`): Mode-resolved thermal conductivity per bin.

Both methods use cuBLAS (or hipBLAS for AMD GPUs) for eigenvector-matrix multiplications. The eigenvectors are loaded from `eigenvector.in` as single-precision floats. Memory requirements scale with the eigenvector file size. GKMA and HNEMA are **mutually exclusive** within a single run — the last keyword parsed takes precedence.

Sources: [modal_analysis.cuh](/src/measure/modal_analysis.cuh#L1-L155), [compute_gkma.rst](/doc/gpumd/input_parameters/compute_gkma.rst#L1-L76), [compute_hnema.rst](/doc/gpumd/input_parameters/compute_hnema.rst#L1-L83)

## Direct NEMD: Heat Bath Ensembles

Beyond the homogeneous methods, GPUMD provides direct nonequilibrium simulation via localized heat source/sink thermostats. These create an explicit temperature gradient across the simulation domain, and thermal conductivity is extracted from the steady-state heat flux and temperature profile via Fourier's law.

| Ensemble | Thermostat | Command |
|---|---|---|
| `heat_nhc` | Nose-Hoover chain | `ensemble heat_nhc <T> <T_coup> <delta_T> <source> <sink>` |
| `heat_bdp` | Bussi-Donadio-Parrinello | `ensemble heat_bdp <T> <T_coup> <delta_T> <source> <sink>` |
| `heat_lan` | Langevin | `ensemble heat_lan <T> <T_coup> <delta_T> <source> <sink>` |

The source region is thermostatted at T + δT and the sink at T − δT, producing a temperature difference of 2δT. Both `source` and `sink` labels reference grouping method 0. The `T_coup` parameter controls thermostat coupling strength (same meaning as in NVT ensembles). The integrator implementation lives in `ensemble_heat_hybrid.cu`, which combines the velocity Verlet integration with local thermostat application only to atoms in the source/sink groups.

Sources: [ensemble_heat.rst](/doc/gpumd/input_parameters/ensemble_heat.rst#L1-L59), [ensemble_heat_hybrid.cuh](/src/integrate/ensemble_heat_hybrid.cuh#L1-L1)

## Two-Temperature Model: `ensemble ttm` and `ensemble heat_ttm`

The **Two-Temperature Model (TTM)** couples the ionic system to an electron temperature grid, enabling simulation of electron-phonon coupling effects critical in metals and laser-heated systems. The electron temperature evolves on a separate grid according to a diffusion equation with source terms from electron-phonon energy exchange.

**TTM syntax:** `ensemble ttm <grouping_method> <group_id> <Ce> <rho_e> <kappa_e> <gamma_p> <gamma_s> <v_0> <nx> <ny> <nz> <T_e_init> [options]`

**Heat+TTM syntax:** `ensemble heat_ttm <T> <T_coup> <delta_T> <source> <sink> <grouping_method> <group_id> <Ce> <rho_e> <kappa_e> <gamma_p> <gamma_s> <v_0> <nx> <ny> <nz> <T_e_init> [options]`

| Parameter | Description | Units |
|---|---|---|
| `Ce` | Electron specific heat per electron | eV/K |
| `rho_e` | Electron number density | Å⁻³ |
| `kappa_e` | Electron thermal conductivity | eV/(ps·K·Å) |
| `gamma_p`, `gamma_s` | Friction coefficients | amu/ps |
| `v_0` | Threshold velocity | Å/ps |
| `nx, ny, nz` | Electron grid dimensions | cells |
| `T_e_init` | Initial electron temperature | K |

Optional arguments include: `ttm_out_interval` (output frequency), `ttm_infile` (initial electron temperature profile), `ttm_properties_file` (per-cell properties overriding uniform values), `ttm_source` (volumetric heat source in eV/(ps·Å³)), and `ttm_active_x/y/z` (active grid ranges). The `ensemble_ttm.cu` integrator handles both pure TTM and combined heat-bath+TTM simulations.

**Output** (`ttm_electron_temperature.out`): Electron temperature per grid cell over time.

Sources: [ensemble_ttm.rst](/doc/gpumd/input_parameters/ensemble_ttm.rst#L1-L136), [ensemble_ttm.cuh](/src/integrate/ensemble_ttm.cuh#L1-L1)

## Method Selection Guide

| Method | Type | κ Components | Spectral Info | System Type | Finite-Size Issues | Key Output |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **HAC** (Green-Kubo) | EMD | All (via in/out decomp.) | No | Bulk 3D, 2D | Minimal | `hac.out` |
| **HNEMD** | Homogeneous NEMD | 3 per run (via F_e direction) | No | Bulk 3D, 2D | Minimal | `kappa.out` |
| **HNEMDEC** | Homogeneous NEMD | Onsager matrix | No | Multicomponent alloys | Minimal | `onsager.out` |
| **SHC** | EMD correlation | One direction per run | Yes: κ(ω) | Bulk, interfaces | Minimal | `shc.out` |
| **GKMA** | EMD modal | Mode-resolved | Yes: per-mode | Crystalline | Minimal | `heatmode.out` |
| **HNEMA** | HNEMD modal | Mode-resolved | Yes: per-mode | Crystalline | Minimal | `kappamode.out` |
| **heat_nhc/bdp/lan** | Direct NEMD | One direction per run | No | Any | **Significant** | Temperature profile |
| **TTM / heat_ttm** | Direct NEMD + e-ph | Electron + phonon | No | Metals | **Significant** | `ttm_electron_temperature.out` |

> [!TIP]
> For bulk crystalline or amorphous systems, start with HNEMD — it converges faster than Green-Kubo HAC and avoids finite-size effects. Use HAC to validate. For alloys, use HNEMDEC. For 2D materials, leverage the in/out decomposition by orienting the basal plane in xy. For spectral analysis, SHC is more general (no eigenvectors needed); GKMA/HNEMA provide mode-resolved detail but require phonon eigenvectors.

Sources: [hac.cuh](/src/measure/hac.cuh#L1-L66), [hnemd_kappa.cuh](/src/measure/hnemd_kappa.cuh#L1-L68), [hnemdec_kappa.cuh](/src/measure/hnemdec_kappa.cuh#L1-L76), [shc.cuh](/src/measure/shc.cuh#L1-L81), [modal_analysis.cuh](/src/measure/modal_analysis.cuh#L1-L155)

## Inter-Method Dependencies and Constraints

Several constraints govern which heat transport computations can coexist in a single run. The HNEMD driving force modifies the force computation globally via `force.set_hnemd_parameters()`, meaning HNEMD-based methods (HNEMD, HNEMDEC, HNEMA) are mutually exclusive with equilibrium methods that assume unmodified dynamics (HAC, GKMA). GKMA and HNEMA are explicitly mutually exclusive. The direct NEMD ensembles (heat_nhc/bdp/lan) operate at the integrator level and are compatible with output computations that don't assume equilibrium, but the thermal conductivity extraction requires post-processing of temperature profiles rather than built-in κ calculation.

The `compute_heat` kernel is invoked within the `process()` method of HAC, HNEMD, HNEMDEC, and SHC, meaning these measurements occur on-line during the MD loop. In contrast, the direct NEMD methods require separate post-processing of dumped temperature data. The modal analysis methods load eigenvectors during `preprocess()` and use cuBLAS for on-line modal heat current computation during `process()`.

For deeper understanding of the force computation that feeds into heat current calculations, see [Force and Potential System](5-force-and-potential-system). For the integration schemes used with heat transport (NHC, BDP, Langevin), see [Integration and Ensemble Methods](6-integration-and-ensemble-methods). For the GPU kernel patterns used in correlation and reduction computations, see [CUDA Kernel Design](13-cuda-kernel-design).


# Monte Carlo and PIMD



GPUMD implements two distinct classes of advanced sampling methods that extend molecular dynamics beyond classical equilibrium ensembles: **Monte Carlo–Molecular Dynamics (MCMD)** for alloy phase-space exploration and **Path Integral Molecular Dynamics (PIMD)** for quantum nuclear effects. Both subsystems are tightly integrated with the GPU-accelerated NEP potential engine, enabling production-scale simulations of composition-dependent thermodynamics and quantum-statistical properties on a single GPU.

## Architectural Overview

The MC and PIMD subsystems occupy different layers of the simulation pipeline. MC operates as an **interleaved trial step** between MD integration steps — it does not replace the integrator but mutates atomic identities in-place. PIMD, by contrast, is a **full integrator replacement** that evolves a ring-polymer representation of the quantum partition function. The following diagram captures this structural asymmetry:

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Simulation Loop"
        MD[MD Integration Step] --> MC_Check{MC Enabled?<br/>step % md_steps == 0}
        MC_Check -->|Yes| MC_Trial[MC Trial Steps<br/>Type Swap + Energy Eval]
        MC_Check -->|No| Next[Continue MD]
        MC_Trial --> Next
    end

    subgraph "PIMD Pipeline (Replaces MD)"
        Force_Beads[Force on Each Bead] --> Transform[Normal-Mode Transform<br/>Cayley Integrator]
        Transform --> Langevin[Mode-Resolved Langevin<br/>Thermostat]
        Langevin --> Barostat[Pressure Control<br/>Berendsen / SCR]
    end

    style MC_Trial fill:#e8f4e8,stroke:#2d7d2d
    style Transform fill:#e8e8f4,stroke:#2d2d7d
    style Langevin fill:#e8e8f4,stroke:#2d2d7d
```

Sources: [mc.cuh](/src/mc/mc.cuh#L1-L57), [ensemble_pimd.cuh](/src/integrate/ensemble_pimd.cuh#L1-L99)

## Monte Carlo–Molecular Dynamics (MCMD)

### Concept and Scope

MCMD interleaves Monte Carlo trial moves into an ongoing MD trajectory, enabling the system to sample **configurational space** that pure MD cannot efficiently reach — specifically, atom-type swaps in multicomponent systems. This is essential for studying alloy thermodynamics, precipitation, and order–disorder transitions. The MC module supports three statistical ensembles, each governing how atom identities are mutated:

| Ensemble | Trial Move | Governs | Key Use Case |
|----------|-----------|---------|--------------|
| **Canonical** | Swap types of two atoms (i, j) | Fixed composition | Order–disorder transitions at fixed stoichiometry |
| **SGC** (Semi-Grand Canonical) | Change type of one atom | Fixed Δμ between species | Concentration–chemical potential mapping |
| **VCSGC** (Variance-Constrained SGC) | Change type of one atom | Fixed φ, κ (concentration + variance) | Full composition range, miscibility gaps |

The canonical ensemble performs **swap moves** — exchanging the types of two randomly selected atoms of different species — preserving total composition. The SGC and VCSGC ensembles perform **identity-change moves** on a single atom, where acceptance depends on chemical potential differences (SGC) or the constrained φ/κ parameters (VCSGC).

> [!TIP]
> MCMD requires a NEP potential. The `NEP_Energy` class evaluates the local energy change for each MC trial by computing per-atom NEP energies for the affected neighborhood only — not the entire system — which is what makes GPU-accelerated MCMD tractable.

Sources: [mc_ensemble_canonical.cuh](/src/mc/mc_ensemble_canonical.cuh#L1-L38), [mc_ensemble_sgc.cuh](/src/mc/mc_ensemble_sgc.cuh#L1-L57), [mc.rst](/doc/gpumd/input_parameters/mc.rst#L1-L112)

### MC Class Hierarchy

The MC module follows a polymorphic design with a strategy pattern:

```
MC (driver)
 └── MC_Ensemble (abstract base)
      ├── MC_Ensemble_Canonical  (swap moves)
      └── MC_Ensemble_SGC        (identity-change moves, also covers VCSGC)
```

The `MC` driver class holds scheduling parameters (`num_steps_md`, `num_steps_mc`, temperature ramp) and delegates trial computation to the appropriate `MC_Ensemble` subclass via `std::unique_ptr<MC_Ensemble>`. The driver's `compute` method fires MC trials only when `(step + 2) % num_steps_md == 0`, using a linearly interpolated temperature from `T_initial` to `T_final`.

Sources: [mc.cuh](/src/mc/mc.cuh#L1-L57), [mc_ensemble.cuh](/src/mc/mc_ensemble.cuh#L1-L72)

### GPU-Accelerated Trial Evaluation

Each MC trial involves a **local energy evaluation** — only the neighborhood of the trial atom(s) needs re-evaluation. The implementation leverages GPU parallelism through these kernel stages:

1. **Neighbor identification**: CUDA kernels `get_neighbors_of_i_and_j` (canonical) or `get_neighbors_of_i` (SGC) find atoms within the NEP radial cutoff of the trial site(s), storing them in `NL_ij`.
2. **Type arrays**: Before/after type arrays are constructed via `get_types` and `find_local_types` kernels, enabling differential energy computation.
3. **NEP energy**: The `NEP_Energy` class computes per-atom energies for both before and after the proposed change, using the same NEP parameter structure as the MD force engine.
4. **Acceptance & commit**: A host-side Metropolis criterion determines acceptance; if accepted, the `exchange` kernel (canonical) or analogous kernel (SGC) updates atom types, masses, and velocities on the GPU.

Sources: [mc_ensemble_canonical.cu](/src/mc/mc_ensemble_canonical.cu#L1-L200), [nep_energy.cuh](/src/mc/nep_energy.cuh#L1-L100)

### MC Input Syntax

The `mc` keyword in `run.in` supports three forms:

**Canonical ensemble:**
```
mc canonical <md_steps> <mc_trials> <T_i> <T_f> [group <grouping_method> <group_id>]
```

**SGC ensemble:**
```
mc sgc <md_steps> <mc_trials> <T_i> <T_f> <num_species> {<species_0> <mu_0> ...} [group ...]
```

**VCSGC ensemble:**
```
mc vcsgc <md_steps> <mc_trials> <T_i> <T_f> <num_species> {<species_0> <phi_0> ...} <kappa> [group ...]
```

| Parameter | Description | Constraints |
|-----------|-------------|-------------|
| `md_steps` | MD steps between MC trial batches | Positive integer |
| `mc_trials` | Number of MC trials per batch | Positive integer |
| `T_i`, `T_f` | Initial/final MC temperature (K) | Positive; linearly ramped |
| `num_species` | Species count in SGC/VCSGC | 2–4 |
| `mu_i` | Chemical potential of species i (eV) | Only Δμ matters |
| `phi_i` | Dimensionless concentration parameter | Typically −1.2 to +1.2 |
| `kappa` | Variance constraint parameter | Positive; ~100 typical, increase for miscibility gaps |
| `group` | Restrict MC to a subgroup | Optional; requires grouping_method and group_id |

**Concrete examples:**
```
mc canonical 100 200 500 100 group 1 3     # 200 swaps every 100 MD steps, T: 500→100 K, group 3 of method 1
mc sgc 100 1000 300 300 2 Cu 0 Au 0.6      # SGC at 300 K, Δμ(Au−Cu) = 0.6 eV
mc vcsgc 200 1000 500 500 2 Al -2 Ag 0 10000  # VCSGC at 500 K, κ=10000
```

Sources: [mc.rst](/doc/gpumd/input_parameters/mc.rst#L23-L112), [mc.cu](/src/mc/mc.cu#L200-L334)

---

## Path Integral Molecular Dynamics (PIMD)

### Quantum Nuclear Effects via Ring Polymers

PIMD approximates the quantum canonical partition function by mapping each quantum particle onto a **ring polymer** of `P` classical beads connected by harmonic springs. The effective spring constant is `ω_P = P k_B T / ℏ`, and the classical ring-polymer Hamiltonian exactly reproduces quantum thermodynamics as P → ∞. GPUMD supports four PIMD variants that differ in how the ring-polymer modes are thermostatted:

| Variant | Internal Modes | Centroid Mode | Barostat | Physical Regime |
|---------|---------------|---------------|----------|-----------------|
| **pimd** | Langevin thermostat | Langevin thermostat | Berendsen or SCR | Equilibrium quantum statistics (NVT/NPT) |
| **pimd_scr** | Langevin thermostat | Langevin thermostat | Stochastic cell rescaling | NPT with better volume sampling |
| **rpmd** | Free (no thermostat) | Free (no thermostat) | None | Approximate quantum rate theory (NVE) |
| **trpmd** | Langevin thermostat | Free (no thermostat) | None | Improved quantum dynamics [Rossi2014] |

Sources: [ensemble_pimd.rst](/doc/gpumd/input_parameters/ensemble_pimd.rst#L1-L66), [ensemble_pimd.cu](/src/integrate/ensemble_pimd.cu#L1-L50)

### Normal-Mode Integration Scheme

The integration follows the **Ceriotti et al. (2010)** scheme with a Cayley-modified free-polymer propagator for numerical stability. The time-stepping algorithm decomposes into:

1. **Half-kick**: `v += (Δt/2m) · f` for all beads
2. **Normal-mode transform**: Positions and velocities are rotated into the staging/normal-mode basis via the precomputed `transformation_matrix` (a discrete cosine/sine transform of size P × P)
3. **Free-polymer drift**: In normal-mode space, each mode k evolves as a harmonic oscillator with frequency `ω_k`. The centroid (k=0) drifts freely. Internal modes use the **Cayley approximation** rather than exact trigonometric functions:
   - `cos_factor = (1 − (ω_k Δt/2)²) / (1 + (ω_k Δt/2)²)`
   - `sin_factor = ω_k Δt / (1 + (ω_k Δt/2)²)`
   
   This Cayley form is more stable than `cos(ω_k Δt)` for stiff modes, following [Korol et al., J. Chem. Phys. 151, 124103 (2019)].
4. **Inverse transform**: Back to bead representation
5. **Force evaluation**: Compute forces on all beads (P independent NEP evaluations)
6. **Second half-kick**: `v += (Δt/2m) · f`

The Langevin thermostat is applied in normal-mode space between the half-kicks, with mode-dependent friction: the centroid uses a user-specified coupling time `T_coup`, while internal mode k uses friction proportional to `ω_k`.

Sources: [ensemble_pimd.cu](/src/integrate/ensemble_pimd.cu#L200-L399), [ensemble_pimd.cuh](/src/integrate/ensemble_pimd.cuh#L1-L99)

### Ring-Polymer Memory Layout

Each bead stores its own position, velocity, force, potential, and virial arrays. The `Ensemble_PIMD` class maintains **GPU arrays of GPU pointers** — `position_beads`, `velocity_beads`, `force_beads`, `virial_beads` — each of length `P`, where element `k` points to the device memory for bead `k`. This double-indirection pattern allows a single CUDA kernel to iterate over all beads efficiently:

```
GPU_Vector<double*> position_beads;  // P pointers, one per bead
// position_beads[k] → atom.position_beads[k].data() on GPU
```

The first PIMD run allocates bead storage in the `Atom` object and initializes all beads to the classical configuration. Subsequent runs (e.g., RPMD after PIMD equilibration) reuse the same bead arrays — the number of beads cannot change between runs.

Sources: [ensemble_pimd.cu](/src/integrate/ensemble_pimd.cu#L120-L198), [ensemble_pimd.cuh](/src/integrate/ensemble_pimd.cuh#L64-L80)

### Eco-PIMD: Economised Path-Integral Frequencies

The standard Trotter discretization uses internal-mode frequencies `ω_k = 2ω_P sin(kπ/P)`, which reproduce the quantum partition function but require many beads for high-frequency modes. **Eco-PIMD** [Zeng & Manolopoulos, arXiv:2607.06414 (2026)] replaces these with optimised frequencies that minimise the error in Matsubara correlation functions while using far fewer beads.

The optimisation solves a nonlinear least-squares problem: minimize the RMSE between the exact and ring-polymer Matsubara correlation function over a grid of dimensionless frequencies `x = βℏω`, subject to the constraint that the highest physical frequency `ω_max` (supplied in cm⁻¹) is faithfully reproduced. The solver uses:

- **Newton's method** with a shifted Hessian (eigendecomposition via Jacobi solver on GPU) for the Newton direction
- **Line search** for step-size control
- **Small-x series expansion** to avoid cancellation in the objective function
- **Relative convergence test** that terminates in the flat valley of an already-converged fit

The `update_eco_modes` method recalculates Eco frequencies whenever the temperature changes beyond a tolerance, using the previous solution as the Newton starting point — enabling efficient temperature-ramped simulations.

> [!TIP]
> Eco-PIMD is available only for `pimd` and `pimd_scr`; RPMD and TRPMD always use Trotter frequencies. The `eco` option is rejected at parse time for `rpmd`/`trpmd` with a clear error message.

Sources: [eco_pimd.cu](/src/integrate/eco_pimd.cu#L1-L200), [eco_pimd.cuh](/src/integrate/eco_pimd.cuh#L1-L39), [ensemble_pimd.cu](/src/integrate/ensemble_pimd.cu#L200-L248)

### PIMD Input Syntax

**PIMD (NVT or NPT with Berendsen barostat):**
```
ensemble pimd <num_beads> <T_1> <T_2> <T_coup> [{pressure_params}] [eco <omega_max>]
```

**PIMD with stochastic cell rescaling (NPT):**
```
ensemble pimd_scr <num_beads> <T_1> <T_2> <T_coup> {pressure_params} [eco <omega_max>]
```

**Ring-Polymer MD (NVE-like):**
```
ensemble rpmd <num_beads>
```

**Thermostatted Ring-Polymer MD:**
```
ensemble trpmd <num_beads>
```

| Parameter | Description | Constraints |
|-----------|-------------|-------------|
| `num_beads` | Number of ring-polymer beads | Positive even integer ≤ 128 |
| `T_1`, `T_2` | Initial/final target temperature (K) | Positive; linearly ramped |
| `T_coup` | Langevin coupling time (steps) | Positive; controls centroid thermostat |
| `eco omega_max` | Highest wavenumber to reproduce (cm⁻¹) | Only for `pimd`/`pimd_scr` |
| Pressure params | Same forms as `npt_ber` or `npt_scr` | Isotropic, orthogonal, or triclinic |

**Concrete example:**
```
ensemble pimd 32 300 300 100 eco 3500   # 32 beads, 300 K, coupling=100 steps, Eco up to 3500 cm⁻¹
ensemble rpmd 32                       # RPMD with 32 beads (must follow a prior PIMD run)
```

Sources: [ensemble_pimd.rst](/doc/gpumd/input_parameters/ensemble_pimd.rst#L17-L66), [test_eco_pimd.py](/tests_pytest/test_eco_pimd.py#L1-L74)

---

## Implementation Comparison

| Aspect | MCMD | PIMD |
|--------|------|------|
| **Module path** | `src/mc/` | `src/integrate/` |
| **Integration role** | Interleaved adjunct to MD | Full integrator replacement |
| **State mutation** | Atom type, mass, velocity | All bead positions & velocities |
| **Potential calls** | Local NEP energy (affected neighborhood) | Full NEP force × P beads |
| **GPU parallelism** | Within-trial neighbor search + energy | Bead-level parallelism + normal-mode transforms |
| **NEP dependency** | Required (exclusive) | Any potential supporting per-bead evaluation |
| **Output** | `mcmd.out` (composition tracking) | `thermo.out`, `dump_beads` |
| **Group support** | Yes (restrict MC to subgroup) | No (all atoms participate) |
| **Temperature control** | Linear ramp T_i → T_f | Linear ramp + mode-resolved Langevin |

Sources: [mc.cuh](/src/mc/mc.cuh#L1-L57), [ensemble_pimd.cuh](/src/integrate/ensemble_pimd.cuh#L1-L99)

## Testing and Validation

The Eco-PIMD implementation is validated by `test_eco_pimd.py`, which verifies two properties: (1) the Eco RMSE is strictly less than the Trotter RMSE for the same bead count, confirming that the optimisation improves fidelity; and (2) the `eco` suffix is correctly rejected for `rpmd` and `trpmd` ensembles, preventing invalid configurations. MCMD correctness is implicitly validated through the NEP energy local-evaluation path, which shares its core with the production NEP force engine.

Sources: [test_eco_pimd.py](/tests_pytest/test_eco_pimd.py#L1-L74)

## Related Topics

- The NEP potential engine that both MCMD and PIMD depend on: [NEP Model Architecture](8-nep-model-architecture)
- The integration framework that PIMD plugs into: [Integration and Ensemble Methods](6-integration-and-ensemble-methods)
- GPU kernel patterns used in both modules: [CUDA Kernel Design](13-cuda-kernel-design)
- Measurement outputs for PIMD trajectories: [Measurement and Output](7-measurement-and-output)

# Multi-GPU and MDI Interface



GPUMD extends beyond single-GPU standalone simulation through two complementary architectural strategies: the **MolSSI Driver Interface (MDI)** for inter-code coupling, and a **modular executable topology** that isolates MDI concerns into a dedicated build target. The MDI integration positions GPUMD as an **ENGINE** in the MolSSI ecosystem — an MD integrator whose force evaluation can be delegated to an external **DRIVER** (e.g., VASP for QM forces), enabling hybrid QM/MD workflows without modifying GPUMD's core simulation loop. This page examines the architectural design, command protocol, data marshalling between GPU and MDI layers, and the concrete VASP–GPUMD coupling that ships as a reference implementation.

## Architectural Overview: Executable Topology

GPUMD does not bolt MDI support onto the main `gpumd` executable. Instead, it produces a **separate `gpumd-mdi` binary** from a dedicated source tree under `src/main_mdi/`, sharing the bulk of the simulation kernel code with `src/main_gpumd/` but replacing the entry point and `Run` class with MDI-aware variants. This architectural decision yields three concrete advantages: (1) the standard `gpumd` binary carries zero MDI dependency overhead; (2) the MDI build can conditionally link against the MDI library via compile-time flags without polluting the default build; and (3) the `Run` class in `main_mdi` extends its `main_gpumd` counterpart with MDI-specific member functions and state without risking regression in standalone simulations.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Source Topology"
        A["src/main_gpumd/<br/>run.cu, run.cuh, main.cu"] --> B["gpumd executable<br/>(standalone)"]
        C["src/main_mdi/<br/>run.cu, run.cuh, main.cu<br/>mdi_stub.cu, mdi_fallback.h"] --> D["gpumd-mdi executable<br/>(MDI-enabled)"]
    end

    subgraph "Shared Kernel Code"
        E["src/force/"] 
        F["src/integrate/"]
        G["src/measure/"]
        H["src/model/"]
        I["src/utilities/"]
    end

    A --> E & F & G & H & I
    C --> E & F & G & H & I

    subgraph "MDI External Dependencies"
        J["MDI Library<br/>(libmdi)"]
        K["mdi_fallback.h<br/>(stub declarations)"]
    end

    C -.->|USE_MDI=1| J
    C -.->|compile-time| K
```

The `main_mdi/main.cu` entry point introduces a **dual-mode dispatch**: if `--mdi` is present on the command line, the `Run` object is constructed with `skip_run = true` (suppressing `run` commands in `run.in`) and control transfers to `mdi_engine_main()`; otherwise, the binary behaves identically to the standard `gpumd` executable. This means `gpumd-mdi` is a **strict superset** — it can always substitute for `gpumd` in standalone mode.

Sources: [main.cu](/src/main_mdi/main.cu#L48-L67), [makefile_mdi](/src/makefile_mdi#L1-L170)

## MDI Command Protocol

The MDI standard defines a **command-exchange protocol** between a DRIVER and an ENGINE over a transport layer (TCP, MPI, or plugin). GPUMD's ENGINE registers a single node `@DEFAULT` and exposes nine commands, split into **outbound queries** (the DRIVER requests data from GPUMD) and **inbound directives** (the DRIVER pushes data into GPUMD):

| Command | Direction | Payload | Units | Purpose |
|---------|-----------|---------|-------|---------|
| `<NATOMS` | ENGINE → DRIVER | 1 × `MDI_INT` | — | Report atom count |
| `<COORDS` | ENGINE → DRIVER | N×3 × `MDI_DOUBLE` | Bohr | Send current positions |
| `>COORDS` | DRIVER → ENGINE | N×3 × `MDI_DOUBLE` | Bohr | Override positions |
| `<FORCES` | ENGINE → DRIVER | N×3 × `MDI_DOUBLE` | MDI force units | Compute & send forces |
| `>FORCES` | DRIVER → ENGINE | N×3 × `MDI_DOUBLE` | MDI force units | Inject external (QM) forces |
| `<ENERGY` | ENGINE → DRIVER | 1 × `MDI_DOUBLE` | MDI energy units | Compute & send total energy |
| `>ENERGY` | DRIVER → ENGINE | 1 × `MDI_DOUBLE` | MDI energy units | Inject external energy |
| `>STRESS` | DRIVER → ENGINE | 9 × `MDI_DOUBLE` | eV/Å³ | Inject 3×3 stress tensor |
| `EXIT` | DRIVER → ENGINE | — | — | Terminate MDI loop |

The protocol follows a strict **synchronous request-response** pattern: the DRIVER sends a command string via `MDI_Send_Command`, then either sends or receives the associated data buffer. The ENGINE sits in a blocking `MDI_Recv_command` loop until `EXIT` arrives. This design is inherently **step-serial** — each MD step requires a full round-trip — which is appropriate for QM/MD coupling where the QM evaluation dominates wall-clock time.

Sources: [mdi_stub.cu](/src/main_mdi/mdi_stub.cu#L85-L100), [mdi_stub.cu](/src/main_mdi/mdi_stub.cu#L117-L240)

## MDI Engine Implementation: The Command Loop

The `mdi_engine_main()` function in `mdi_stub.cu` orchestrates the ENGINE lifecycle in four phases: **initialization**, **registration**, **communication**, and **finalization**. After `MDI_Init` parses the `--mdi` options string (encoding role, name, method, hostname, port), the ENGINE calls `run->mdi_initialize_for_mdi()` to set up the integrator, MC, and measurement subsystems for **single-step operation** (`one_steps = 1`). This is a critical architectural choice: unlike `perform_a_run()` which loops internally over `number_of_steps`, the MDI mode steps **one integration step at a time**, with the DRIVER dictating when to advance.

The command loop itself is a `while (!exit_flag)` dispatch over received command strings. For outbound queries (`<NATOMS`, `<COORDS`, `<FORCES`, `<ENERGY`), the ENGINE calls the corresponding `mdi_get_*` or `mdi_compute_forces()` method, marshals data from GPU memory to a host `std::vector<double>`, and sends via `MDI_Send`. For inbound directives (`>COORDS`, `>FORCES`, `>ENERGY`, `>STRESS`), the ENGINE receives into a host buffer and calls the corresponding `mdi_set_*` method, which copies into GPU memory. The `>FORCES` command is the most consequential: after receiving external forces, the ENGINE immediately calls `mdi_step_one()`, performing a single velocity-Verlet integration step using the injected forces rather than the internal potential.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant D as DRIVER (e.g., VASP)
    participant E as ENGINE (GPUMD)

    E->>E: mdi_initialize_for_mdi()
    E->>D: Register @DEFAULT + commands
    D->>E: Accept communicator

    loop Each MD Step
        D->>E: <COORDS
        E->>D: positions (N×3 doubles)
        Note over D: Run VASP QM calculation
        D->>E: >ENERGY
        D->>E: energy (1 double)
        D->>E: >STRESS
        D->>E: stress (9 doubles)
        D->>E: >FORCES
        D->>E: forces (N×3 doubles)
        Note over E: mdi_step_one() with QM forces
        Note over E: Dump/measure outputs written
    end

    D->>E: EXIT
    E->>E: mdi_finalize_for_mdi()
```

Sources: [mdi_stub.cu](/src/main_mdi/mdi_stub.cu#L62-L116), [mdi_stub.cu](/src/main_mdi/mdi_stub.cu#L145-L210)

## Run Class Extensions for MDI

The `Run` class in `main_mdi/run.cuh` extends the standalone version with **ten public MDI methods** and **six private MDI state variables**. The class diff reveals the architectural pattern: MDI support is achieved by adding a **single-step integration pathway** (`mdi_step_one()`) that mirrors the logic of `perform_a_run()` but executes exactly one iteration, and by introducing **external-data pending flags** that override the internal force computation when the DRIVER has supplied QM quantities.

| MDI Method | Operation | GPU ↔ Host Direction |
|------------|-----------|---------------------|
| `mdi_get_natoms()` | Return `atom.number_of_atoms` | — |
| `mdi_get_positions()` | Copy `position_per_atom` to host vector | Device → Host |
| `mdi_set_positions()` | Copy host array to `position_per_atom` | Host → Device |
| `mdi_compute_forces()` | Call `force.compute()` on current positions | GPU internal |
| `mdi_get_forces()` | Copy `force_per_atom` to host vector | Device → Host |
| `mdi_get_potential()` | Copy `potential_per_atom` to host vector | Device → Host |
| `mdi_set_forces()` | Copy host array to `force_per_atom`, set `external_forces_pending = true` | Host → Device |
| `mdi_set_energy()` | Store `external_total_energy`, set `external_energy_pending = true` | — |
| `mdi_set_stress()` | Store 9-component stress, set `external_stress_pending = true` | — |
| `mdi_step_one()` | Execute one integration step (see below) | — |

The **pending-flag pattern** is the key mechanism that reconciles MDI-driven stepping with GPUMD's internal force pipeline. When `mdi_set_forces()` is called, it copies the QM forces directly into `atom.force_per_atom` on the GPU and sets `external_forces_pending = true`. Inside `mdi_step_one()`, the force computation is **conditionally skipped**:

```cpp
if (!external_forces_pending) {
  mdi_compute_forces();  // internal potential
} else {
  // use forces already present (set by mdi_set_forces)
}
```

After integration completes, `external_forces_pending` is cleared. This design ensures that the integrator's `compute1()` and `compute2()` halves see consistent forces without any special-case branching in the integrator code itself.

> [!TIP]
> The `mdi_step_one()` method also handles external energy and stress by distributing the total energy evenly across per-atom potential arrays and converting the 3×3 stress tensor into GPUMD's per-atom virial convention (W = −σ·V/N), so that thermodynamic outputs (`dump_thermo`, `dump_xyz`) remain physically consistent when QM quantities are used instead of the internal potential.

Sources: [run.cuh](/src/main_mdi/run.cuh#L45-L107), [run.cu](/src/main_mdi/run.cu#L399-L570)

## MDI Step Internals: Single-Step Integration Path

The `mdi_step_one()` method reproduces the per-iteration logic of `perform_a_run()` with two modifications: (1) force computation is conditional on `external_forces_pending`, and (2) the step counter is `mdi_step_counter` (a dedicated MDI-local counter) rather than the `step` variable from the `perform_a_run` loop. The complete sequence within a single `mdi_step_one()` call is:

1. **Velocity correction** — `velocity.correct_velocity()` applies constraints (fixed groups, etc.)
2. **Integration half-step 1** — `integrate.compute1()` advances velocities by half a time step
3. **Force evaluation** — conditional: internal `force.compute()` or use pending external forces
4. **External energy/stress injection** — distribute `external_total_energy` and `external_stress` into per-atom arrays, then clear pending flags
5. **Auxiliary force modifiers** — `electron_stop`, `add_force`, `add_spring`, `add_random_force`, `add_efield`
6. **Integration half-step 2** — `integrate.compute2()` completes the velocity-Verlet step
7. **Monte Carlo** — `mc.compute()` handles MC moves if configured
8. **Measurement & output** — `measure.process()` triggers all `dump_*` and `compute_*` outputs
9. **Step counter increment** — `mdi_step_counter++`

This ensures that **all GPUMD output keywords work identically** in MDI mode. The `dump_xyz`, `dump_thermo`, and other diagnostic outputs fire at the same intervals and write the same quantities — except that forces, energy, and virial now reflect the QM-supplied values rather than the internal potential.

> [!TIP]
> When `skip_run_commands = true` (MDI mode), the `execute_run_in()` parser skips any `run` keyword it encounters. This means the `run.in` file can still contain `potential`, `velocity`, `ensemble`, `time_step`, `dump_*`, and `compute_*` directives for initialization, but the actual simulation stepping is entirely under DRIVER control via the MDI command loop.

Sources: [run.cu](/src/main_mdi/run.cu#L510-L570), [run.cu](/src/main_mdi/run.cu#L163-L198)

## Build System and Compilation

GPUMD offers two build paths for the MDI-enabled executable. The **Makefile path** (`src/makefile_mdi`) is the primary method, designed to be invoked from the `src/` directory:

```bash
cd src
make -f makefile_mdi USE_MDI=1 MDI_LIB=1 \
  MDI_LIB_PATH=/path/to/MDI_Library/install/lib64 \
  MDI_INC_PATH=/path/to/MDI_Library/install/include
```

The Makefile links source files from both `main_mdi/` and selected modules from `main_gpumd/` (velocity, cohesive, add_efield, add_force, add_spring, add_random_force, electron_stop, replicate), creating a `gpumd-mdi` executable. The `USE_MDI=1` flag injects `-DUSE_MDI` into the compiler, activating the `#ifdef USE_MDI` guards throughout the codebase. The `MDI_LIB=1` flag adds the MDI library include path and links `-lmdi`.

| Build Variable | Effect | Default |
|---------------|--------|---------|
| `USE_MDI` | Defines `USE_MDI` preprocessor macro | Off |
| `MDI_LIB` | Enables MDI library linking | Off |
| `MDI_LIB_PATH` | Adds `-L<path>` to linker | — |
| `MDI_INC_PATH` | Adds `-I<path>` to compiler | — |
| `CUDA_ARCH` | Sets `-arch=sm_XX` | `sm_60` |

The **CMake path** (`CMakeLists.txt`) currently builds `gpumd`, `nep`, and `gnep` targets but does **not** yet include a `gpumd-mdi` target. Users who prefer CMake must either add a custom target or fall back to the Makefile.

The `mdi_fallback.h` header provides **stub declarations** for the full MDI API (all `MDI_*` functions, types, and constants) so that `mdi_stub.cu` compiles even when the actual MDI library headers are unavailable. At link time, the real library must be present when `USE_MDI=1` and `MDI_LIB=1` are both set.

Sources: [makefile_mdi](/src/makefile_mdi#L1-L170), [mdi_fallback.h](/src/main_mdi/mdi_fallback.h#L1-L152), [CMakeLists.txt](/CMakeLists.txt#L1-L69)

## VASP–GPUMD Reference Implementation

GPUMD ships a complete **QM/MD coupling pipeline** using VASP as the DRIVER and GPUMD as the ENGINE. The implementation consists of three layers:

### Layer 1: Shell Orchestrator (`run_mdi_vasp_gpumd.sh`)

The shell script handles process lifecycle management: it starts `gpumd-mdi` as a background ENGINE process with the `--mdi` flag and TCP options, waits for initialization, then launches the Python DRIVER in the foreground. On completion (or error), it saves logs to a persistent `.gpumd_logs/` directory and optionally cleans up the `.gpumd_vasp_tmp/` intermediate directory.

```bash
# ENGINE (background)
gpumd-mdi --mdi "-role ENGINE -name gpumd -method TCP -hostname localhost -port 8021" -in run.in &

# DRIVER (foreground)
python3 vasp_mdi_driver.py --vasp-cmd "vasp_std" --port 8021 --steps 100
```

### Layer 2: Python MDI Driver (`vasp_mdi_driver.py`)

The driver implements two classes: `VASPCalculator` (VASP I/O wrapper) and `VASPMDIDriver` (MDI communication logic). The MD loop follows a fixed choreography per step:

1. Send `<COORDS` → receive positions from GPUMD
2. Write POSCAR from received coordinates + cell template
3. Execute VASP via `subprocess.run`
4. Parse `vasprun.xml` for energy, forces, stress
5. Send `>ENERGY` with QM energy
6. Send `>STRESS` with 3×3 stress tensor (kbar → eV/Å³ conversion)
7. Send `>FORCES` with QM forces → triggers `mdi_step_one()` in GPUMD

The stress conversion uses `KBAR_TO_EV_PER_ANG3 = 0.00062415091` to translate VASP's kbar output into GPUMD's eV/Å³ convention.

### Layer 3: GPUMD Configuration (`examples/gpumd_mdi/`)

The example provides a minimal Cu system with NEP potential, NVE ensemble, and standard dump keywords:

```
potential   ../../potentials/nep/nep89_20250409/nep89_20250409.txt
velocity    1
ensemble nve
time_step  0.5
dump_xyz 1 dump.xyz force precision double
dump_thermo 1
run 5
```

Note that `run 5` is parsed but **skipped** in MDI mode (`skip_run_commands = true`). The `potential`, `ensemble`, `time_step`, and `dump_*` directives still configure the simulation — the DRIVER simply replaces the internal force loop with QM evaluations.

| File | Role |
|------|------|
| `model.xyz` | Initial atomic structure (Cu dimer) |
| `run.in` | GPUMD initialization (potential, ensemble, dumps) |
| `INCAR_template` | VASP DFT parameters |
| `POSCAR_template` | VASP cell + species template |
| `KPOINTS` | VASP k-point mesh |
| `POTCAR` | VASP pseudopotential |

Sources: [run_mdi_vasp_gpumd.sh](/tools/gpumd-mdi/run_mdi_vasp_gpumd.sh#L1-L255), [vasp_mdi_driver.py](/tools/gpumd-mdi/vasp_mdi_driver.py#L1-L200), [run.in](/examples/gpumd_mdi/run.in#L1-L10)

## Extending to Other Driver Codes

The MDI protocol is **code-agnostic by design**. The ENGINE-side logic in GPUMD has no VASP-specific knowledge — it simply responds to the nine standard commands. To couple GPUMD with any other QM or MM code, one needs only a DRIVER that:

1. Initializes MDI in DRIVER role (`MDI_Init` with `-role DRIVER`)
2. Accepts a communicator to the GPUMD ENGINE
3. Repeats: request coordinates (`<COORDS`), compute forces externally, send forces (`>FORCES`), optionally send energy (`>ENERGY`) and stress (`>STRESS`)
4. Sends `EXIT` when done

The transport layer is configurable at launch time: TCP (for single-node or networked execution), MPI (for HPC environments where both codes share an MPI communicator), or plugin (for in-process coupling via `dlopen`). The current VASP example uses TCP, which requires no MPI dependency between the DRIVER and ENGINE processes.

| Transport | Latency | Use Case | Configuration |
|-----------|---------|----------|---------------|
| TCP | ~100 µs/msg | Single-node, codes launched separately | `-method TCP -port 8021` |
| MPI | ~10 µs/msg | HPC, shared MPI_COMM_WORLD | `-method MPI` |
| Plugin | ~1 µs/msg | In-process, shared address space | `-method plugin -path <so>` |

Sources: [mdi_fallback.h](/src/main_mdi/mdi_fallback.h#L74-L78), [mdi_stub.cu](/src/main_mdi/mdi_stub.cu#L62-L80)

## Multi-Executable Design and Future Multi-GPU Considerations

GPUMD's current architecture is fundamentally **single-GPU per process**. The MDI interface does not directly address multi-GPU domain decomposition; instead, it enables a different form of parallelism — **heterogeneous coupling** where GPUMD runs on one GPU handling MD integration while a separate code (potentially on another GPU or CPU cluster) computes forces. This is a form of **functional decomposition** rather than spatial decomposition.

The executable topology hints at how multi-GPU support could evolve: the `main_mdi/` directory demonstrates that GPUMD's `Run` class can be extended with external control interfaces while preserving the core simulation pipeline intact. A future multi-GPU extension could follow the same pattern — a `main_mgpu/` directory with a `Run` subclass that partitions atoms across GPUs, with inter-GPU communication handled in the force computation and neighbor list stages. The MDI interface itself is already compatible with multi-GPU engines, since the MDI standard supports MPI-based communicators where each ENGINE rank can handle its own domain.

| Strategy | Current Status | Mechanism |
|----------|---------------|-----------|
| Single GPU, standalone | ✅ Supported | Default `gpumd` executable |
| Single GPU + MDI coupling | ✅ Supported | `gpumd-mdi` executable |
| Multi-GPU spatial decomposition | ❌ Not yet implemented | Would require domain partitioning in `force.compute()` |
| Multi-GPU via MDI (each rank = 1 GPU) | ⚠️ Theoretically possible | MPI transport + one ENGINE per GPU |

Sources: [run.cuh](/src/main_mdi/run.cuh#L1-L107), [makefile_mdi](/src/makefile_mdi#L37-L56)
